1. Object-Oriented Programming & SOLID

At 12 years of experience nobody will ask you to define encapsulation and stop there. They ask it to see whether you can connect the definition to design decisions: why a field is private, why an interface exists, why inheritance hurt a codebase you worked on. Every answer below gives the textbook line first (say it in one sentence), then the depth that separates a senior engineer from a junior one.

1.1 The mental model: objects are state + behaviour + identity

An object has three things:

Part Meaning Java mechanism
State The data it holds right now Instance fields
Behaviour What it can do Instance methods
Identity Which one it is, independent of its state Reference (heap address), ==

run1 == run2 is false (two identities) even though run1.equals(run2) may be true (same state, if equals compares id). Interviewers love this distinction because it leads straight into equals/hashCode, JPA entities and HashMap keys.

1.2 The four pillars, with the depth interviewers want

Encapsulation

One line: bundle data with the methods that operate on it and hide the data behind those methods.

Senior depth: encapsulation is not "private fields with getters and setters". A class with a public setter for every field is not encapsulated; it is a struct with extra steps. Real encapsulation protects invariants — rules that must always hold.

// Not encapsulated: anyone can put the run into an impossible state
public class ReconRun {
    private String status;
    public void setStatus(String s) { this.status = s; }
}

// Encapsulated: the class owns its lifecycle rules
public class ReconRun {
    private RunStatus status = RunStatus.QUEUED;
    private Instant startedAt;

    public void start(Clock clock) {
        if (status != RunStatus.QUEUED) throw new IllegalStateException("Run already " + status);
        status = RunStatus.RUNNING;
        startedAt = clock.instant();
    }
    public void complete(int matched, int breaks) { /* only from RUNNING */ }
    public RunStatus status() { return status; }
}

RefinePoint: a reconciliation run moves QUEUED → RUNNING → COMPLETED/FAILED. If any service could write status directly, a crashed worker could leave a run "COMPLETED" without results. Putting the transition rules in the entity (and the DB claim in FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) means the rule lives in one place.

Abstraction

One line: expose what something does and hide how.

Senior depth: abstraction is about choosing the right level of detail for the caller. Interfaces are the main tool, but a well-named method is also an abstraction. The test: can the implementation change without the caller changing?

public interface LlmClient {               // the abstraction
    LlmResponse complete(LlmRequest request);
}
class AnthropicClient implements LlmClient { ... }      // detail 1
class OpenAiCompatibleClient implements LlmClient { ... } // detail 2

RefinePoint: the AI service talks to LlmClient. Switching from a local GGUF model to Claude is a config change (ai.provider=anthropic), and no business code (rule drafting, break explanation) changed. That is abstraction paying for itself.

Abstraction vs encapsulation (asked constantly): encapsulation hides data to protect invariants; abstraction hides complexity to simplify use. Encapsulation is implementation-level (access modifiers), abstraction is design-level (interfaces, abstract classes).

Inheritance

One line: a class acquires fields and methods of a parent class (extends), modelling an is-a relationship.

Senior depth:

  • Java supports single inheritance of classes, multiple inheritance of type (interfaces).
  • Inheritance creates the tightest coupling in Java: the subclass depends on the parent's implementation, not just its contract (the fragile base class problem).
  • Prefer inheritance for genuine type hierarchies with shared invariants (e.g., BaseEntity holding id, createdAt), and composition for reusing behaviour.
@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class BaseEntity {        // id, createdAt, updatedAt
    @Id @GeneratedValue private UUID id;
    private Instant createdAt;
}
@MappedSuperclass
public abstract class BaseOrgEntity extends BaseEntity {   // + org_id tenant column
    @Column(name = "org_id", nullable = false) private UUID orgId;
}

RefinePoint: every tenant-scoped table extends BaseOrgEntity, so "every row has an org_id" is enforced by the type system instead of code review.

Fragile base class example (classic from Effective Java):

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    int added = 0;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); }
}
CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>();
s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(s.added); // 6, not 3 — HashSet.addAll calls add() internally

The subclass broke because it depended on an undocumented implementation detail of the parent. Fix: composition (wrap a Set and forward calls).

Polymorphism

One line: one interface, many forms — the same call behaves differently depending on the object.

Two kinds:

Compile-time (static) Runtime (dynamic)
Mechanism Method overloading Method overriding
Decided by Compiler, from declared (static) types of arguments JVM, from actual object type at runtime
Bytecode Exact method chosen at compile time invokevirtual / invokeinterface resolved via vtable/itable

How runtime polymorphism works internally: each class has a virtual method table (vtable) — an array of method pointers. A subclass copies the parent's table and replaces entries it overrides. A call shape.area() compiles to invokevirtual Shape.area; at runtime the JVM looks at the object's class pointer (in the object header), goes to that class's vtable, picks slot n. The JIT usually removes this lookup by inline caching: if a call site has only ever seen one type (monomorphic), it inlines that method directly with a cheap type guard.

Tricky overloading questions:

void print(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
void print(String s)  { System.out.println("String"); }
print(null);          // "String" — most specific applicable method wins
Object o = "hi";
print(o);             // "Object" — overloading uses the STATIC type

void m(long x) {}  void m(Integer x) {}  void m(int... x) {}
m(5);   // m(long): widening beats boxing beats varargs

Overload resolution phases: (1) exact/widening without boxing or varargs, (2) allow boxing/unboxing, (3) allow varargs.

1.3 Class relationships

Relationship Meaning Lifetime Example
Association Uses / knows about Independent ReconService uses RunClient
Aggregation Has-a, parts can exist alone Independent Workspace has Users
Composition Owns-a, part dies with whole Dependent ReconProcess owns its FieldMappings
Inheritance Is-a — BaseOrgEntity is a BaseEntity
Dependency Uses temporarily (parameter) Method call only export(Writer w)

1.4 Composition over inheritance

Why prefer it:

  1. Coupling only to the interface of the component, not its implementation.
  2. Behaviour can be swapped at runtime (strategy).
  3. Avoids class explosion (LoggingCachingRetryingClient extends ...).
  4. Testability: inject a fake component.
// Inheritance explosion
class RetryingHttpClient extends HttpClient { }
class LoggingRetryingHttpClient extends RetryingHttpClient { }

// Composition / decorator
LlmClient client = new RetryingLlmClient(new LoggingLlmClient(new AnthropicClient(props, http)));

When inheritance is right: a true is-a that obeys Liskov, the parent is designed and documented for extension (template method), or the framework requires it (@MappedSuperclass, OncePerRequestFilter).

1.5 Abstract class vs interface (Java 8 → 21)

Feature Abstract class Interface
Multiple inheritance No (single extends) Yes (many implements)
State (instance fields) Yes No (only public static final constants)
Constructors Yes No
Method bodies Yes default, static (Java 8), private (Java 9)
Access modifiers on methods Any public (and private helpers)
Use when Sharing state + code among closely related classes Defining a capability/contract across unrelated classes

Diamond problem with default methods:

interface A { default String hello() { return "A"; } }
interface B { default String hello() { return "B"; } }
class C implements A, B {
    @Override public String hello() { return A.super.hello() + B.super.hello(); } // must resolve
}

Rules: (1) class methods win over interface defaults, (2) more specific interface wins (if B extends A, B's default wins), (3) otherwise the class must override.

1.6 SOLID with real examples

S — Single Responsibility Principle

"A class should have one reason to change" — i.e., one actor who asks for changes.

Bad: ReconciliationService that loads data, matches records, writes Excel and emails the result. Finance asks for a new Excel column → you touch the matcher's class.

Good (RefinePoint shape): ReconEngine matches, ExportWriter writes files, ExportWorker schedules exports, Notifier sends mail. Each changes for one reason.

O — Open/Closed Principle

"Open for extension, closed for modification." Add new behaviour by adding code, not editing tested code.

public interface DataConnector {                 // ryfn-plugin-api
    ConnectorDescriptor descriptor();
    ConnectorResult fetch(ConnectorContext ctx);
}
// A new source (e.g., SAP) is a new jar with META-INF/services/com.ryfnflow.plugin.connector.DataConnector
// Plugins.load(DataConnector.class) finds it via ServiceLoader — core code never changes.

L — Liskov Substitution Principle

Subtypes must be usable wherever the parent is expected without breaking the caller's expectations: no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions, preserve invariants, no new unchecked exceptions the caller can't expect.

Classic violation — Square extends Rectangle:

void resize(Rectangle r) { r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert r.area() == 20; } // fails for Square

Java's own violation: List.of(...) returns a List whose add throws UnsupportedOperationException. The contract documents it as "optional operation", which is how the JDK legalises it — but it is a frequent source of production bugs.

I — Interface Segregation Principle

Clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Split fat interfaces into role interfaces.

// Fat
interface Repository<T> { T find(); void save(T t); void delete(T t); void bulkImport(Stream<T> s); void reindex(); }
// Segregated
interface Reader<T> { Optional<T> find(UUID id); }
interface Writer<T> { void save(T t); }

Spring Data does this well: Repository (marker) → CrudRepository → ListCrudRepository → PagingAndSortingRepository. You can extend just Repository and declare only the methods you need.

D — Dependency Inversion Principle

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both depend on abstractions. Abstractions are owned by the high-level policy.

DIP (principle) ≠ DI (dependency injection, a technique) ≠ IoC (inversion of control, the broader idea that a framework calls your code). Spring's container is an IoC container that performs DI, which makes DIP easy.

1.7 Other design principles you should name-drop correctly

  • DRY — every piece of knowledge has one representation. Duplicated code that changes for different reasons is not a DRY violation.
  • KISS, YAGNI — do not build what you do not need yet.
  • Law of Demeter — talk to friends, not strangers: order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity() is a train wreck; ask order.shippingCity().
  • Tell, don't ask — tell an object to do something rather than asking for its data and deciding outside it.
  • High cohesion, low coupling.
  • Program to an interface, not an implementation.

1.8 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is OOP and why use it over procedural programming?

OOP models a program as interacting objects, each owning its data and behaviour. Benefits: invariants protected in one place (encapsulation), replaceable implementations (polymorphism), reuse through composition, and code organised around domain concepts that non-programmers recognise. Procedural code works well for small scripts or data pipelines; it degrades when many functions share and mutate the same data because any function can break any rule. In practice modern Java blends both: OOP for the domain model, functional style (streams, records, immutability) for data transformation.

Q2. Is Java 100% object-oriented?

No. Primitives (int, double, …) are not objects, static members belong to the class not an instance, and Java 21 records/pattern matching lean toward data-oriented programming. Wrapper classes and autoboxing bridge primitives to objects. Project Valhalla (value classes) aims to close the gap.

Q3. Difference between a class and an object?

A class is a blueprint (loaded once per class loader into metaspace); an object is an instance on the heap with its own copy of instance fields. new allocates memory (usually in the thread's TLAB in Eden), zeroes fields, runs initialisers and the constructor, and returns a reference.

Q4. What happens step by step when you write new ReconRun()?

  1. If ReconRun is not loaded, the class loader loads, links (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialises it (static blocks run).
  2. JVM allocates memory — fast path is a pointer bump in the thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB).
  3. Fields are set to default values (0/null/false); object header written (mark word + class pointer).
  4. Instance initialisers and field initialisers run in textual order, after the super(...) call.
  5. Constructor body runs.
  6. Reference returned. (With escape analysis the JIT may skip heap allocation entirely — scalar replacement.)

Q5. Can a constructor be private? Why?

Yes: singletons, static factory methods (List.of), utility classes (private Util() {}), and builders. Private constructors also prevent subclassing (subclass constructors must call a super constructor).

Q6. Can constructors be inherited, overridden, final, static, or abstract?

None of those. Constructors are not members, so they are not inherited or overridden. The first statement is always this(...) or super(...) (implicit super() if omitted). Java 22+ previews statements before super(...), but in Java 21 the call must be first.

Q7. Order of initialisation in an inheritance chain?

class P { static { print("P static"); } { print("P instance"); } P() { print("P ctor"); } }
class C extends P { static { print("C static"); } { print("C instance"); } C() { print("C ctor"); } }
new C(); new C();

Output: P static, C static, P instance, P ctor, C instance, C ctor, P instance, P ctor, C instance, C ctor. Static blocks run once at class initialisation, parent first; instance initialisers run right before each constructor body, parent chain first.

Q8. What happens if you call an overridable method from a constructor?

The subclass override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised:

class Base { Base() { init(); } void init() {} }
class Child extends Base { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); @Override void init() { items.add("x"); } }
new Child(); // NullPointerException: items is still null

Rule: never call overridable methods from constructors (Effective Java item 19).

Q9. Method overloading vs overriding — every rule.

Overloading: same name, different parameter list (type/number/order), in the same class or subclass; return type alone is not enough; resolved at compile time. Overriding: same signature in subclass; return type same or covariant (subtype); access cannot be more restrictive; cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions; static, private, final methods cannot be overridden; resolved at runtime. Use @Override so the compiler catches signature mistakes.

Q10. Can we override a static method? What is method hiding?

No. A static method with the same signature in a subclass hides the parent's. Which one runs depends on the reference type, not the object:

class A { static String who() { return "A"; } }
class B extends A { static String who() { return "B"; } }
A ref = new B(); ref.who(); // "A"

Q11. Can private methods be overridden? What about final?

Private methods are not visible to subclasses, so a same-named method in the subclass is a new method. final methods cannot be overridden (compile error). The JIT can inline final and private methods without guards, but modern JITs inline virtual methods too, so final is about design intent, not speed.

Q12. What is covariant return type?

An override may return a subtype of the parent's return type. Object.clone() returns Object, but MyClass.clone() can return MyClass. The compiler generates a bridge method with the original signature that delegates to the new one.

Q13. What is dynamic method dispatch?

Choosing the overriding method at runtime based on the actual object, via invokevirtual/invokeinterface and vtables/itables. Fields are not polymorphic: Parent p = new Child(); p.name reads Parent.name if both declare name.

Q14. Abstract class with no abstract methods — useful?

Yes — prevents direct instantiation while sharing code. HttpServlet is abstract with no abstract methods; you are meant to subclass and override what you need.

Q15. Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can an interface?

Abstract class: yes (called via super() from subclasses, used to initialise shared state). Interface: no.

Q16. When choose abstract class vs interface in a real system?

Interface for a capability many unrelated types implement or for something you want to mock/swap (LlmClient, DataConnector, Notifier). Abstract class when subclasses share state and a fixed algorithm skeleton (template method), e.g., an AbstractImporter with read() → validate() → persist() where only read() varies. Often both: an interface for the contract plus an abstract skeletal implementation (AbstractList for List).

Q17. What is the diamond problem and how does Java handle it?

Ambiguity when a class inherits the same member from two paths. Java avoids it for state (no multiple class inheritance) and resolves it for default methods with explicit rules (class wins, more specific interface wins, else must override and may call X.super.m()).

Q18. Explain this and super.

this = current instance (disambiguate fields, call another constructor this(...), pass self). super = parent's members (super.method(), super(...)). Neither can be used in static context.

Q19. What is a marker interface? Alternatives?

An interface with no methods that tags a type: Serializable, Cloneable, RandomAccess. The JVM/libraries check instanceof. Annotations are the modern alternative, but marker interfaces have one advantage: they define a type the compiler can check (void write(Serializable s)).

Q20. Explain Cloneable and why it is considered broken.

Object.clone() is protected and does a shallow field copy only if the class implements Cloneable (else throws CloneNotSupportedException). It bypasses constructors, does not work with final fields that need deep copy, and the interface does not even declare clone(). Prefer copy constructors or static factories: new ArrayList<>(other), Map.copyOf(map), record with-style methods.

Q21. Shallow vs deep copy?

Shallow copy duplicates the top-level object but shares referenced objects; deep copy recursively copies the graph. A shallow copy of a ReconDefinition that holds a mutable List<Rule> lets two definitions share — and corrupt — one rule list. Use immutable collections to make shallow copies safe.

Q22. What is an immutable class and how do you create one?

State cannot change after construction. Steps: class final (or private constructor + factories), all fields private final, no setters, defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs, do not leak this during construction. Records give you most of it, but you still need defensive copies of mutable components:

public record MatchRule(String name, List<String> keys) {
    public MatchRule { keys = List.copyOf(keys); }   // compact constructor: defensive, unmodifiable
}

Benefits: thread-safe without locks, safe as map keys, cacheable, simpler reasoning.

Q23. Why is String immutable?

String pool safety (shared literals), security (class names, file paths, URLs cannot change after validation), thread safety, cached hashCode (great as HashMap keys), and class-loading correctness. (Details in chapter 2.)

Q24. Explain association, aggregation and composition with an example from your work.

In RefinePoint: ReconService associates with RunClient (calls it); a Workspace aggregates users (a user can belong elsewhere and survives the workspace); a ReconProcess is composed of field mappings and rules (deleting the process deletes them — orphanRemoval = true, CascadeType.ALL).

Q25. What is coupling and cohesion?

Coupling — how much one module depends on another's internals (aim low). Cohesion — how related the responsibilities inside a module are (aim high). Microservices boundaries are the same idea at deployment scale: high cohesion inside a service, low coupling (async events, versioned APIs) between them.

Q26. Explain each SOLID principle with a violation you fixed.

Have one story per letter. Example DIP story: "Our AI features called the OpenAI SDK directly from five services. When we wanted a local model for privacy-sensitive customers, every call site had to change. I introduced an LlmClient interface owned by the AI module with two adapters, chosen by configuration. Switching provider became a property change; tests use a stub client."

Q27. Does SOLID conflict with simplicity (KISS/YAGNI)?

It can. An interface with exactly one implementation that will never change is ceremony. Apply OCP/DIP at volatile boundaries (external providers, I/O, plug-in points), not everywhere. Senior answer: principles are heuristics to manage change cost; apply them where change is likely.

Q28. What is the Law of Demeter? Does a fluent builder/stream violate it?

"Only talk to your immediate friends." Builders and streams return the same object or a value of the same abstraction, so chaining is fine; the law targets reaching through different objects' internals (a.getB().getC().doX()).

Q29. What is an object's hashCode by default? Is it the memory address?

Not necessarily. HotSpot's default identity hash is a random/thread-local xorshift number generated on first call and stored in the object header (mark word). Objects move during GC, so it cannot be the address. Once computed, it is fixed for the object's lifetime. (Calling it on a lock-biased object historically revoked the bias; biased locking was removed in JDK 18.)

Q30. equals and hashCode contract — and what breaks if you violate it?

equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and x.equals(null) == false. If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() (the reverse is not required). Violate it and HashMap/HashSet lose entries: an object put in a set is not found because its hash lands in a different bucket.

Set<Point> s = new HashSet<>();
s.add(new Point(1, 2));
s.contains(new Point(1, 2)); // false if equals overridden without hashCode

Mutable fields in hashCode are equally dangerous: mutate a key after insertion and it is "lost" in the wrong bucket.

Q31. How should JPA entities implement equals/hashCode?

Do not use all fields (lazy proxies, collections). Do not use a generated ID naïvely: before persist it is null, after persist it changes, so a HashSet containing the new entity breaks. Options: (a) business key that never changes, (b) ID-based equals with a constant hashCode (getClass().hashCode()), (c) assign UUIDs in the constructor (RefinePoint uses UUID ids) so the id exists before persisting. Also compare with Hibernate.getClass()/instanceof rather than getClass() because of proxy subclasses.

Q32. instanceof vs getClass() in equals?

getClass() keeps symmetry strict (a subclass is never equal to a parent), instanceof allows subclass equality but risks symmetry/transitivity violations if subclasses add state. With Hibernate proxies, getClass() fails because the proxy is a subclass. Records use getClass-like semantics automatically and are final, so the problem disappears.

Q33. What is the difference between == and equals()?

== compares references for objects (identity) and values for primitives. equals() compares logical equality as defined by the class (defaults to == in Object). Watch for Integer cache: Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true, but for 128 it is false (cache is -128..127 by default, tunable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax).

Q34. What is an inner class, static nested class, local and anonymous class?

Static nested: no reference to the outer instance (preferred, like Map.Entry). Inner (non-static): holds an implicit Outer.this reference — can cause memory leaks (e.g., an inner Runnable keeps a large outer object alive). Local: declared in a method. Anonymous: inline subclass/implementation, largely replaced by lambdas. Details in chapter 3.

Q35. What is the difference between final, finally, and finalize?

final: constant variable / non-overridable method / non-extendable class. finally: block that always runs after try (except System.exit, JVM crash, or infinite loop in try). finalize: deprecated (Java 9) and removed for removal (JEP 421, Java 18) GC callback; unpredictable, slow, can resurrect objects. Use try-with-resources and java.lang.ref.Cleaner instead.

Q36. What is "programming to an interface"?

Declare variables, parameters and return types with the most general type that provides the needed operations (List<Run> runs = new ArrayList<>(), Map not HashMap). The implementation can change without callers changing, and tests can supply doubles.

Q37. How does polymorphism help in Spring?

Spring injects by interface; at runtime the bean may be your class, a JDK dynamic proxy or a CGLIB subclass that adds transactions, security or caching. Your code calls service.save() polymorphically and gets cross-cutting behaviour for free. Collections of implementations can be injected (List<DataConnector>, Map<String, MatchStrategy>), giving strategy dispatch with zero if/else.

Q38. Replace a large switch on a type with polymorphism — and when not to.

Classic refactor: move each branch into an implementation of a common interface (Replace Conditional with Polymorphism). But Java 21 sealed interfaces + pattern-matching switch make the switch exhaustive and compiler-checked, which is better when the set of types is closed and operations are many (data-oriented programming). Rule of thumb: open set of types → polymorphism; closed set of types with many operations → sealed + switch (the expression problem).

Q39. What is the expression problem?

OOP makes adding new types easy (new subclass) but adding new operations hard (touch every class). Functional/sealed-switch style makes new operations easy (new function) but new types hard (touch every switch). Knowing this shows architectural maturity.

Q40. How do you design a class for extension vs prohibit it?

Either document self-use and provide protected hooks (template method), or make the class final/sealed. Effective Java: "Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it." Java 17 sealed lets you allow a specific list of subclasses: sealed interface Result permits Matched, Break, Ignored.

Q41. What are access modifiers and their scopes?

Modifier Class Package Subclass (other pkg) World
private ✓
(default) ✓ ✓
protected ✓ ✓ ✓ (through inheritance)
public ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
Top-level classes can only be public or package-private. Modules (Java 9) add another layer: public is only visible outside the module if the package is exportsed.

Q42. Why is multiple inheritance of classes not allowed?

To avoid ambiguity in state and method resolution (diamond) and complexity in constructors/initialisation order. Java chose single inheritance of implementation plus multiple inheritance of type (interfaces) — and since Java 8, limited inheritance of behaviour via defaults, without state.

Q43. How would you explain OOP design to a junior using a real feature?

Pick a feature end to end: "Matching strategies — MatchStrategy interface (abstraction), ExactMatch, ToleranceMatch, FuzzyNameMatch implementations (polymorphism), each immutable and configured from MatchRuleConfig (encapsulation), engine composed with a list of strategies (composition), new strategy = new class (OCP)."

Q44. What is object slicing? Does Java have it?

In C++, assigning a derived object to a base value copies only the base part. Java has no value-type objects (references only), so no slicing — a Parent p = child still refers to the full Child object.

Q45. What is a God class and how do you break it?

A class that knows/does too much (thousands of lines, dozens of dependencies). Break it by identifying responsibilities (look at which fields each method uses — clusters reveal hidden classes), extract classes, introduce facades for callers, and move behaviour next to the data it uses. Do it incrementally behind tests.

Q46. Is getter/setter on every field good OOP?

Not by default. It exposes internals and invites anaemic models. Expose behaviour (run.start()), keep getters for read models/DTOs, and use records for pure data carriers. JPA needs a no-arg constructor and field access, not setters.

Q47. Anaemic domain model vs rich domain model?

Anaemic: entities are data bags, all logic in services (procedural code in OO clothing). Rich: entities hold behaviour and invariants. In large Spring apps a pragmatic middle ground is common: entities guard their own state transitions, services orchestrate across aggregates, transactions and I/O.

Q48. What are value objects?

Small immutable objects defined by their value, not identity: Money(amount, currency), OrgCode, DateRange. They validate on construction, so invalid values cannot exist. Records are perfect value objects. Using BigDecimal amount + String currency everywhere instead of Money is "primitive obsession".

Q49. Explain the "is-a" vs "has-a" test with a mistake you've seen.

Stack extends Vector in the JDK — a stack is not a vector, yet it inherits add(index, e) which breaks LIFO. Also Properties extends Hashtable allowing non-String values. Both should have used composition.

Q50. What does "favour immutability" buy you in a multi-threaded Spring app?

Singleton beans are shared across request threads. If a bean holds mutable instance state (e.g., a SimpleDateFormat field or a per-request list), you get race conditions. Immutable beans and immutable DTOs/records eliminate a whole class of bugs without synchronisation.

2. Core Language Internals

Core-language rounds are where senior candidates lose points they should never lose. The questions sound basic ("is Java pass-by-reference?", "why is String immutable?"), but the interviewer is listening for the mechanism: the string pool and invokedynamic, the Integer cache, how finally interacts with return, why new BigDecimal(0.1) is wrong. This chapter walks through each mechanism once with a picture, then drills it with output-prediction and production questions.

2.1 JDK, JRE, JVM — and what happens when you run a program

Term What it is Contains
JVM A specification + an implementation (HotSpot, OpenJ9) that executes bytecode Class loader subsystem, runtime data areas (heap, stacks, metaspace), execution engine (interpreter, JIT, GC)
JRE Runtime environment to run Java programs JVM + core class libraries (java.base, …)
JDK Development kit to build Java programs JRE + tools: javac, jar, javadoc, jshell, jlink, jcmd, jfr, jpackage

Since Java 11 Oracle no longer ships a separate JRE download. You either install a JDK or build a trimmed runtime with jlink containing only the modules your app needs (common in Docker images).

Execution engine in one paragraph: the JVM starts interpreting bytecode. Methods that are called often (invocation and back-edge counters) are compiled by C1 with profiling, then by C2 using that profile (inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling). If a speculative assumption breaks — a new subclass is loaded and a call site is no longer monomorphic — the code is deoptimised back to the interpreter. This is tiered compilation and is why Java services need a warm-up period and why microbenchmarks need JMH.

Write once, run anywhere works because .class files contain platform-neutral bytecode; only the JVM is platform-specific.

2.2 Primitive types and conversions

Type Size Default (field) Range / notes
byte 8 bit 0 -128 … 127
short 16 bit 0 -32,768 … 32,767
char 16 bit unsigned '\u0000' 0 … 65,535 (a UTF-16 code unit, not a "character")
int 32 bit 0 ±2.1 billion
long 64 bit 0L ±9.2 × 10^18
float 32 bit IEEE 754 0.0f ~7 decimal digits
double 64 bit IEEE 754 0.0d ~15–16 decimal digits
boolean JVM-dependent (int on stack, byte in arrays) false true/false

Local variables have no default — the compiler refuses to read an unassigned local ("definite assignment").

Widening (safe, implicit): byte → short → int → long → float → double, and char → int. Note long → float is "widening" yet can lose precision: (float) 123456789L is 1.23456792E8.

Narrowing (explicit cast): keeps the low-order bits. (byte) 200 is -56; (int) 3.99 is 3 (truncation toward zero); (int) Double.NaN is 0; (int) 1e20 is Integer.MAX_VALUE (floating-to-int saturates).

Arithmetic promotion: any arithmetic on byte, short, char is done in int.

byte a = 10, b = 20;
byte c = a + b;        // compile error: int cannot be converted to byte
byte d = (byte)(a + b);
a += b;                // compiles: compound assignment hides a cast — (byte)(a + b)
char ch = 'A' + 1;     // compiles: constant expression fits in char → 'B'

Overflow is silent for integers: Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 == Integer.MIN_VALUE. Use Math.addExact, Math.multiplyExact, Math.toIntExact when overflow must fail loudly (counting rows, computing offsets). Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.

Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.30000000000000004; 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN and NaN != NaN; 1.0 / 0 is Infinity but 1 / 0 throws ArithmeticException; -0.0 == 0.0 is true but Double.valueOf(-0.0).equals(0.0) is false.

2.3 Wrapper classes, autoboxing and the Integer cache

Every primitive has a wrapper (Integer, Long, Character, …). The compiler inserts conversions:

Integer x = 5;        // compiles to Integer.valueOf(5)   — boxing
int y = x;            // compiles to x.intValue()         — unboxing

Integer.valueOf(int) returns a cached instance for -128…127 (Integer.IntegerCache, built at class initialisation). The upper bound is tunable with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=<n> (or java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high).

Wrapper Cached by valueOf
Byte, Short, Long -128 … 127
Integer -128 … 127 (upper bound configurable)
Character 0 … 127
Boolean TRUE, FALSE
Float, Double none

Autoboxing traps you must be able to explain:

Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;
a == b;                         // false — two objects
a.equals(b);                    // true

Long total = 0L;
for (long i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) total += i;   // boxes a new Long every iteration

Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
int n = counts.get("missing");  // NullPointerException on unboxing null

Integer i = null;
int r = flag ? i : 0;           // NPE: mixed Integer/int ternary unboxes i

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
list.remove(1);                 // removes INDEX 1 → [1, 3]
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));// removes VALUE 1

Constructors like new Integer(5) are deprecated for removal (Java 9/16) because they defeat the cache and will clash with value classes (Project Valhalla). Use valueOf or rely on autoboxing.

2.4 String internals

Layout and immutability

public final class String implements Serializable, Comparable<String>, CharSequence {
    @Stable private final byte[] value;   // Java 9+: bytes, not char[]
    private final byte coder;             // LATIN1 = 0, UTF16 = 1
    private int hash;                     // cached hashCode, 0 until computed
    private boolean hashIsZero;           // Java 13+: distinguishes "computed as 0"
}

Compact strings (JEP 254, Java 9): if every character fits in Latin-1, the string stores one byte per char; otherwise two bytes (UTF-16). Most business strings (codes, IDs, English text) halve their memory. Turn it off with -XX:-CompactStrings (rarely useful).

Why immutable (have all five reasons ready):

  1. String pool — literals are shared; if one caller could mutate "USD", every other user would see it.
  2. Security — file paths, class names, URLs, SQL validated once cannot be changed after the check (time-of-check/time-of-use).
  3. Thread safety — share freely without locks.
  4. Cached hash — computed once, perfect as HashMap keys.
  5. Class loading — class names passed to loaders must not change.

The string pool

The pool (StringTable) is a native hash table of references to String objects that live in the heap (moved from PermGen to heap in Java 7, so pooled strings are garbage-collectable). Its size is -XX:StringTableSize (default 65,536 buckets in recent JDKs).

  • Literals are resolved through the constant pool to the same pooled instance (ldc instruction), so s1 == s2.
  • new String("ACME") always creates a new object (the literal is still pooled) — s1 != s3.
  • intern() returns the pooled instance, adding this one if absent — s1 == s4.
  • Compile-time constants are folded: "AC" + "ME" is the literal "ACME". A final String a = "AC" local is also a constant variable, so a + "ME" == "ACME". A non-final variable is not, so the result is a new object.

Interning in production: useful to dedupe millions of repeated values (currency codes, country codes) parsed from files — but each intern() call is a native hash lookup, and a huge pool slows GC root scanning. G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication deduplicates the backing arrays of long-lived strings in the background without changing identity, which is usually the safer choice.

RefinePoint: a large bank statement can repeat five currency codes across millions of rows. Held as Java objects, that is millions of equal Strings, which is one reason large files are processed in DuckDB rather than on the heap. For repeated values that do stay on the heap, a small Map<String, String> canonicaliser keeps one instance per value without touching the global pool.

Concatenation: +, StringBuilder, invokedynamic

Before Java 9, a + b + c compiled to new StringBuilder().append(a).append(b).append(c).toString(). Since Java 9 (JEP 280) it compiles to a single invokedynamic call bootstrapped by StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. At first execution the JVM builds an optimised method handle that pre-computes the exact length and coder, allocates the byte[] once and copies parts in — fewer allocations, and the strategy can improve in future JDKs without recompiling your code.

But inside a loop, += still creates a new String on every iteration (O(n²) copying). Use one StringBuilder (or String.join, Collectors.joining).

String csv = "";
for (String s : values) csv += s + ",";          // O(n^2): copies the whole string every time

var sb = new StringBuilder(values.size() * 16);    // presize to avoid array growth
for (String s : values) sb.append(s).append(',');
String StringBuilder StringBuffer
Mutability Immutable Mutable Mutable
Thread-safe Yes (immutable) No Yes (synchronized methods)
Speed New object per change Fastest Slower (lock per call)
Since 1.0 1.5 1.0
Use Values, keys Building strings in one thread (99% of cases) Legacy APIs only

StringBuilder starts with capacity 16 and grows to (old * 2) + 2 when full, copying the array. StringBuffer's locking is almost never useful: sharing a builder between threads is a design smell.

Other String facts worth knowing

  • substring copies the range (since 7u6). Before that, it shared the parent array, causing leaks when a small substring kept a huge string alive.
  • strip() (Java 11) is Unicode-aware; trim() removes only chars ≤ ' '. isBlank(), lines(), repeat(), indent(), formatted() and text blocks (""") are Java 11–15 additions.
  • switch on String uses hashCode() then equals() — compiled to a lookupswitch on the hash.
  • String.valueOf((char[]) null) throws NullPointerException, but String.valueOf((Object) null) returns "null". A bare String.valueOf(null) picks the char[] overload (most specific) and throws.
  • Store passwords in char[], not String: a char array can be wiped; a String stays in memory (and maybe the pool) until GC.

2.5 Methods of java.lang.Object

Method Purpose / key fact
equals(Object) Logical equality; default is ==
hashCode() Must agree with equals; default is an identity hash stored in the object header
toString() Default ClassName@hexIdentityHash
getClass() Runtime Class object; final
clone() protected, shallow copy, needs Cloneable
wait(), notify(), notifyAll() Monitor condition methods; must hold the object's monitor (synchronized) or get IllegalMonitorStateException
finalize() Deprecated for removal (JEP 421); use Cleaner / try-with-resources

2.6 Java is always pass-by-value

Java passes a copy of the value in the variable. For a primitive the value is the number; for an object the value is the reference (a pointer). The method gets its own copy of the pointer: it can mutate the object the pointer refers to, but reassigning the parameter does not affect the caller.

void rename(Workspace w) { w.setName("Finance"); }     // visible to caller (same object)
void replace(Workspace w) { w = new Workspace("Ops"); } // invisible to caller (local copy reassigned)
void swap(Integer a, Integer b) { Integer t = a; a = b; b = t; } // swaps nothing

2.7 static, final and initialisation

static fields belong to the class. Since Java 8 they live in the heap inside the java.lang.Class mirror object (not PermGen/metaspace). One copy per class per class loader — two web apps in one Tomcat each get their own "singleton".

A class is initialised (static blocks run, in textual order with static field initialisers) on its first active use: new, static method call, non-constant static field access, Class.forName(name), reflection, or initialising a subclass. Accessing a static final compile-time constant does not initialise the class because the value is inlined at the call site.

Lazy holder idiom — thread-safe lazy singleton using class-initialisation guarantees (the JVM holds an init lock):

public final class FxRates {
    private FxRates() {}
    private static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = load(); }
    public static FxRates get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }  // Holder initialised on first call
}

final meanings:

  • final variable: assigned once. A blank final field must be assigned in every constructor path.
  • final reference ≠ immutable object: final List<String> l = new ArrayList<>(); l.add("x"); is legal.
  • final method: cannot be overridden. final class: cannot be extended (String, wrappers, records).
  • Effectively final: a local never reassigned; lambdas and inner classes may capture only effectively final locals because they capture a copy of the value.
  • JMM guarantee: fields that are final are safely published after the constructor finishes (if this didn't escape), so other threads never see their default values.

Trap: public static final int MAX_ROWS = 500_000; in a shared library is inlined into every caller's bytecode. Change it to 1,000,000 and redeploy only the library: services compiled against the old jar still use 500,000. Expose values that may change through a static method or a configuration property. In RefinePoint, a change to ryfn-platform is followed by mvn clean package on every service, so no service keeps a stale platform jar or a stale inlined constant.

2.8 Exceptions

Hierarchy

Checked Unchecked
Types Exception and subclasses except RuntimeException RuntimeException, Error and subclasses
Compiler Must be caught or declared in throws No requirement
Meaning Recoverable condition outside the program's control (I/O, network) Programming bugs or unrecoverable state
JVM level No difference — checking is purely a javac feature Same

Checked exceptions do not compose with lambdas (Function cannot throw IOException), which is a big reason modern frameworks (Spring, JPA, Jackson's newer APIs) use unchecked exceptions. Spring translates SQLException into the unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy.

try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions

try (var in = Files.newInputStream(path);
     var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in))) {
    return parse(reader);
}   // reader.close() then in.close() — reverse order of declaration

The compiler generates the finally logic: resources (anything AutoCloseable) are closed in reverse order, even if the body throws. If the body throws and close() throws, the close exception is attached to the primary one via addSuppressed() instead of replacing it (the pre-Java-7 finally { close(); } pattern lost the original error).

Java 9 allows effectively final variables in the header: try (conn) { ... }.

finally edge cases

int f() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }        // returns 2, and swallows any exception
int g() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 99; } } // returns 1: value saved before finally runs
void h() { try { System.exit(0); } finally { log("never"); } } // finally does not run

finally does not run on System.exit, Runtime.halt, JVM crash, the thread being killed by the OS, or an infinite loop/deadlock inside try. A return or throw in finally discards the pending exception — never do it.

Custom exceptions, translation and chaining

public class CreditLimitExceededException extends RuntimeException {
    private final String limit;
    public CreditLimitExceededException(String limit, long allowed) {
        super("Credit limit reached: " + limit + " (allowed " + allowed + ")");
        this.limit = limit;
    }
    public String limit() { return limit; }
}

try {
    return sftp.download(path);
} catch (SftpException e) {
    throw new IngestFailedException("Cannot fetch " + path, e);   // translate + chain the cause
}

Guidelines: extend RuntimeException for domain errors; carry structured fields (code, limit) not just text; always pass the cause; translate low-level exceptions at layer boundaries so the controller does not know about SFTP or JDBC.

RefinePoint: the shared GlobalExceptionHandler in ryfn-platform (@RestControllerAdvice) maps domain exceptions to the ApiResponse error envelope: PlanLimitExceededException becomes HTTP 402, ConflictException a conflict, RateLimitExceededException a 429. Services throw meaningful exceptions, controllers have no try/catch boilerplate, and every service returns errors in the same shape.

The cost of exceptions

Creating an exception is expensive mostly because the constructor calls fillInStackTrace(), which walks the stack. Throwing and catching within the same compiled method is cheap. For high-frequency, expected control flow (validation of millions of rows) either avoid exceptions (return a result object) or create exceptions without stack traces:

public class RowRejected extends RuntimeException {
    public RowRejected(String msg) { super(msg, null, false, false); } // no suppression, no stack trace
}

HotSpot's -XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow (on by default) replaces repeatedly thrown implicit exceptions (NPE, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds) in hot compiled code with a preallocated exception without a stack trace — the reason production logs sometimes show java.lang.NullPointerException with no lines. Look further back in the logs for the first occurrence, or run with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow.

2.9 var, operators and output-prediction traps

var (Java 10) is local-variable type inference — static typing still applies; the type is fixed at compile time. Allowed: locals with initialisers, for loops, try-with-resources, lambda parameters (Java 11, so you can annotate them). Not allowed: fields, method parameters, return types, var x;, var x = null;, array initialisers var a = {1,2}, lambdas without target type. var list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object> — a trap. var is a reserved type name, not a keyword, so a variable named var still compiles.

Operator facts that output questions exploit:

int i = 5; i = i++;            // 5: old value saved, i incremented, then old value assigned
int j = 5; j = j++ + ++j;      // 5 + 7 = 12
System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");   // "33": left to right, numeric add first
System.out.println("1" + 2 + 3);   // "123"
System.out.println('a' + 'b');     // 195: char + char is int
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b');// "ab"
System.out.println(-7 % 3);        // -1: sign follows the dividend
System.out.println(-8 >> 1);       // -4: arithmetic shift keeps sign
System.out.println(-8 >>> 28);     // 15: logical shift fills zeros
System.out.println(Math.round(-2.5)); // -2: rounds half up (floor(x + 0.5))
System.out.println(Math.round(2.5));  // 3
System.out.println(1.0 / 0);       // Infinity
System.out.println(0.1f == 0.1);   // false: float widened to double differs
Object o = true ? 1 : "s";         // Integer
System.out.println(true ? 1 : 2.0);// 1.0: binary numeric promotion in ternary

Short-circuit: &&/|| skip the right side; &/| on booleans evaluate both. Precedence trap: a + b * c, x == 1 || y == 2 && z == 3 (&& binds tighter).

2.10 The main method

public static void main(String[] args) — public so the launcher can call it from outside the package, static so no instance is needed, void because the exit status is set with System.exit(int), String[] for command-line arguments. String... args and final String[] args are also valid; overloaded main methods are allowed but only the standard signature is the entry point.

Newer launchers:

  • Java 11: run a single source file directly — java Hello.java (compiles in memory).
  • Java 21: unnamed classes and instance main methods in preview (JEP 445): void main() { System.out.println("hi"); } with --enable-preview. They became final in Java 25.

In Spring Boot, main calls SpringApplication.run(App.class, args); the fat jar's real Main-Class is Spring Boot's JarLauncher, which sets up a class loader over BOOT-INF/lib and then calls your main via the Start-Class manifest attribute.

2.11 BigDecimal for money

double is binary floating point: 0.1 has no exact representation, so sums drift (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3). Money must be exact. BigDecimal = unscaled BigInteger value × 10^-scale: 123.45 is unscaled 12345, scale 2.

new BigDecimal(0.1);          // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
new BigDecimal("0.1");        // 0.1  — use the String constructor
BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1);      // 0.1  — uses Double.toString, fine for literals

new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"));    // false: scale differs
new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00")); // 0: numerically equal

BigDecimal.ONE.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3));            // ArithmeticException: non-terminating
BigDecimal.ONE.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), 10, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // 0.3333333333
amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);              // banker's rounding

Rules: construct from String or valueOf; compare with compareTo (and beware HashSet<BigDecimal> treats 2.0 and 2.00 as different — normalise with stripTrailingZeros() first); always give a scale and RoundingMode for division; keep the currency next to the amount (a Money record); map to NUMERIC(19,4) in PostgreSQL. BigDecimal is immutable — amount.add(x) without assigning the result does nothing.

RefinePoint: tolerance checks in ryfn-engine compare exactly, as in the balance control expected.subtract(b).abs().compareTo(tol) > 0, never with double. FxRates holds rates as BigDecimal, and when only the opposite direction is quoted it derives the rate with BigDecimal.ONE.divide(rate, 10, RoundingMode.HALF_UP): an explicit scale and rounding mode, because a bare divide would throw on a non-terminating result. A reconciliation that says "matched" because two doubles were "close enough" would be a correctness bug in a finance product.

2.12 Date and time (java.time)

The legacy java.util.Date (a mutable instant with a misleading toString), Calendar (months from 0) and SimpleDateFormat (not thread-safe — a shared static formatter corrupts dates under load) were replaced in Java 8 by java.time (JSR-310): immutable, thread-safe, clearly separated concepts.

Type Represents Example use
Instant A point on the UTC timeline (seconds + nanos since epoch) createdAt, event timestamps, audit logs
LocalDate A calendar date, no time, no zone Value date, statement date, month-end
LocalDateTime Date + time without zone — not a moment "Run every day at 02:00" in some zone
ZonedDateTime Date + time + ZoneId (DST rules) Scheduling in a user's zone
OffsetDateTime Date + time + fixed offset (+05:30) APIs, JDBC timestamptz mapping
Duration / Period Time-based (seconds) / date-based (days, months) amount Timeouts / "3 months"
ZoneId / ZoneOffset Asia/Kolkata (rules) / +05:30 (fixed)
Clock Injectable source of "now" Testable code

Rules for backend systems:

  • Store moments as Instant / timestamptz in UTC. Convert to a zone only for display or for business rules that depend on a local calendar.
  • LocalDateTime is not a moment — "2026-03-29 01:30" in Europe/London does not exist (DST gap) and "2026-10-25 01:30" happens twice.
  • Period.ofMonths(1) added to Jan 31 gives Feb 28 (clamped); Duration.ofDays(1) across a DST change is 24 hours, Period.ofDays(1) is one calendar day (23 or 25 hours).
  • Inject Clock instead of calling Instant.now() directly so tests can freeze time.
  • Format with DateTimeFormatter (immutable and thread-safe); ISO_INSTANT for APIs.
  • Jackson needs JavaTimeModule (Spring Boot registers it) and WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS=false for ISO strings.

RefinePoint: FX quotes are LocalDate-keyed because a rate belongs to a calendar date, while execution times are Instants. In job-service each job stores an IANA time_zone; Schedule computes the next due time in that ZoneId, and it is stored as next_run_at, an absolute moment that the claim query compares with now(). A 02:00 job in New York and one in Kolkata both fire at the right moment, and the zone rules handle DST rather than our code.

2.13 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is the difference between JDK, JRE and JVM?

The JVM executes bytecode, the JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries needed to run programs, and the JDK is the JRE plus development tools (javac, jar, jlink, jcmd, jfr). The JVM is platform-specific; bytecode is not, which gives "write once, run anywhere". Since Java 11 there is no separate JRE download — production images either use a full JDK base image or a jlink-built minimal runtime.

Q2. Is the JVM an interpreter or a compiler?

Both. HotSpot starts by interpreting bytecode, profiles it, and compiles hot methods to native code with the C1 then C2 JIT compilers (tiered compilation). Optimisations are speculative (based on observed types), so code can be deoptimised when assumptions break. GraalVM can additionally compile ahead of time into a native image (Spring Boot supports it with AOT processing).

Q3. What are the class loaders and what is parent delegation?

Bootstrap (native, loads java.base), Platform (other JDK modules), and Application/System (your classpath). A loader first asks its parent; only if the parent cannot find the class does it try itself. This prevents application code from replacing java.lang.String and ensures one copy of core classes. A class's identity is (class name + defining loader), so the same class loaded by two loaders gives ClassCastException: X cannot be cast to X. Spring Boot DevTools uses a restart class loader for your code, which is why that error appears there sometimes.

Q4. Why is char 2 bytes in Java?

Java was designed around UCS-2/UTF-16, so char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji, some CJK) need two chars (a surrogate pair), so an emoji string has length() 2. Use codePointCount / codePoints() when you need real character counts. Compact strings changed how String stores text, not the size of char.

Q5. What is the output: byte b = (byte) 130; System.out.println(b);?

-126. Narrowing keeps the low 8 bits: 130 is 1000 0010, which in two's complement is -126.

Q6. Why does short s = 1; s = s + 1; fail but s += 1; compile?

s + 1 is an int expression (binary numeric promotion), and assigning int to short needs an explicit cast. Compound assignment operators include an implicit cast: s += 1 is s = (short)(s + 1). That hidden cast can also hide overflow.

Q7. Is long → float widening? Can it lose data?

Yes, it is a widening primitive conversion and yes, it can lose precision: a float has only 24 bits of mantissa, so large long values are rounded. Widening guarantees no loss of magnitude, not of precision.

Q8. What is the Integer cache and why does Integer a = 128, b = 128; a == b print false?

Integer.valueOf (used by autoboxing) returns cached objects for -128…127; outside that range each boxing creates a new object, so == compares two different references. Always compare wrappers with equals (or unbox). The high bound can be raised with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, which is why code relying on == may pass on one machine and fail on another.

Q9. What happens when you unbox null?

NullPointerException, thrown from the compiler-inserted intValue() call. Common sources: int x = map.get(key), if (entity.getCount() > 0) when the column is nullable, and mixed ternaries cond ? wrapper : 0. Use primitives for required values and Optional or explicit null checks for nullable ones.

Q10. Explain the ternary NPE: Integer i = null; Integer r = true ? i : 0;

When one operand is Integer and the other is int, the conditional expression's type is int (binary numeric promotion), so i is unboxed — NPE — and then reboxed. Fix: make both operands Integer (Integer.valueOf(0)) or use an if.

Q11. list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> — what is removed?

The element at index 1, because remove(int) is an exact match and overload resolution prefers it over boxing to remove(Object). Use list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove the value.

Q12. Why is String immutable? Give at least four reasons.

Pool sharing (literals are shared safely), security (validated paths, URLs, class names cannot change after checks), thread safety without locks, cached hash code for fast HashMap lookups, and safe use in class loading. Immutability also makes strings safe keys and safe to pass across API boundaries without defensive copies.

Q13. How many objects are created by String s = new String("abc");?

Up to two: the literal "abc" is placed in the string pool when the class's constant is resolved (if not already there), and new creates a second String on the heap. In modern JDKs both share the same byte[], so the second object costs only its header and fields. If "abc" was already pooled, only one new object is created by this statement.

Q14. What does intern() do and where is the string pool?

intern() returns the canonical pooled instance for the string's content, adding it if absent. The pool is a native hash table (StringTable) whose entries point at String objects in the heap (since Java 7; earlier it was in PermGen and could cause OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space). Pooled strings that are unreachable are garbage-collected.

Q15. Predict the output.

String a = "hello";
String b = "hel" + "lo";
String c = "hel";
String d = c + "lo";
final String e = "hel";
String f = e + "lo";
System.out.println(a == b);           // true  — constant folded at compile time
System.out.println(a == d);           // false — runtime concat creates a new String
System.out.println(a == f);           // true  — e is a constant variable
System.out.println(a == d.intern());  // true

Q16. How is string concatenation compiled since Java 9?

To a single invokedynamic instruction bootstrapped by StringConcatFactory (JEP 280). On first call the JVM links a method handle that computes the final length and coder, allocates once, and copies parts. It is faster and produces less garbage than the old StringBuilder chain, and the JDK can improve the strategy without you recompiling. It does not fix concatenation in loops, which still creates a new string per iteration.

Q17. StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?

Same API; StringBuffer synchronises every method, StringBuilder does not. Use StringBuilder — builders are almost always method-local, so locking is pure overhead. StringBuffer remains only for legacy APIs.

Q18. What are compact strings?

Since Java 9, String stores a byte[] plus a coder flag: Latin-1 strings use 1 byte per char, others UTF-16 (2 bytes). For typical business data this halves string memory, and strings are often 25–40% of a Java heap. Methods check the coder and use specialised intrinsics.

Q19. Why prefer char[] over String for passwords?

A char[] can be overwritten (Arrays.fill(pw, '\0')) as soon as you are done; a String is immutable, may be interned, and stays readable in a heap dump until garbage-collected. It also won't accidentally appear in logs via toString(). Console.readPassword() and KeyStore APIs use char[] for this reason.

Q20. == vs equals() vs equalsIgnoreCase vs compareTo for strings?

== compares references; equals compares content; equalsIgnoreCase compares content case-insensitively per char; compareTo is lexicographic by UTF-16 code unit and returns negative/zero/positive. For user-facing sorting in a locale, use Collator. Put the literal first ("USD".equals(code)) or use Objects.equals to be null-safe.

Q21. Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Always pass-by-value. For objects, the value copied is the reference, so the method can mutate the shared object but cannot make the caller's variable point to a different object. A swap(a, b) method therefore cannot swap the caller's variables.

Q22. What does this print?

static void change(StringBuilder sb, String s) { sb.append("!"); s = s + "!"; sb = new StringBuilder("new"); }
var sb = new StringBuilder("hi"); var s = "hi";
change(sb, s);
System.out.println(sb + " " + s);  // "hi! hi"

The append mutated the shared builder before the parameter was reassigned; the String reassignment and builder reassignment only changed local copies.

Q23. List the methods of Object.

equals, hashCode, toString, getClass, clone (protected), wait() (three overloads), notify, notifyAll, and the deprecated finalize. getClass, wait, notify, notifyAll are final.

Q24. Why are wait/notify in Object and not in Thread?

Because every object can be a monitor: the condition waited on belongs to the shared object, not to the thread. A thread calls wait() on the object whose monitor it holds; it releases that monitor and parks in the object's wait set. Today prefer java.util.concurrent (locks with Condition, queues, latches).

Q25. When is a class initialised? Does referencing a static final constant trigger it?

On first active use: instance creation, static method call, assignment or read of a non-constant static field, reflection/Class.forName, subclass initialisation, or being the main class. Reading a compile-time constant (static final primitive or String with a constant initialiser) does not initialise the class because the value is inlined. Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads without initialising; ClassName.class also does not initialise.

Q26. What is the order of static blocks, instance blocks and constructors?

Static field initialisers and static blocks run once, in textual order, when the class is initialised (parent class first). For each new: the parent constructor chain runs first; then the class's instance field initialisers and instance blocks in textual order; then the constructor body.

Q27. Can a static method access instance variables? Can it be overridden?

It cannot access instance members directly (there is no this); it needs an object reference. It cannot be overridden, only hidden — the call is bound at compile time to the declared type.

Q28. What does final mean on a variable, method, class and parameter?

Variable: assigned exactly once (a reference stays pointed at the same object, but the object can still change). Method: cannot be overridden. Class: cannot be subclassed. Parameter: cannot be reassigned within the method. A final field also gets JMM safe-publication guarantees.

Q29. What is "effectively final" and why do lambdas require it?

A local variable that is never reassigned after initialisation. Lambdas and inner classes capture the value of locals (copied into the lambda object), not the variable itself; allowing later reassignment would create two diverging copies and invite data races. To accumulate inside a lambda, use an AtomicInteger or, better, a stream reduction.

Q30. Checked vs unchecked exceptions — which do you use and why?

Checked: subclasses of Exception except RuntimeException; the compiler forces handling. Unchecked: RuntimeException/Error. I use unchecked for domain and infrastructure errors because callers usually cannot recover locally, checked exceptions leak implementation details through signatures, and they do not work with lambdas/streams. Checked exceptions are reasonable for low-level APIs where the immediate caller can genuinely recover. Spring's @Transactional rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default, but not on checked ones unless you set rollbackFor.

Q31. Error vs Exception — should you catch OutOfMemoryError?

Error signals a serious problem the application should not try to handle (OOM, StackOverflowError, LinkageError). Catching OOM to log and exit can be acceptable, but continuing is dangerous because invariants may be broken mid-operation. In production set -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError so the container restarts cleanly and you get a dump to analyse.

Q32. What does this method return?

static int test() {
    try { throw new RuntimeException("boom"); }
    catch (RuntimeException e) { return 1; }
    finally { return 2; }
}

2. The finally return replaces the catch's return. If the catch had thrown instead, the exception would be discarded too. Compilers warn about this ("finally block does not complete normally").

Q33. Does finally always execute?

It runs after try/catch on normal completion, return, break, continue and exceptions. It does not run if the JVM exits (System.exit, Runtime.halt), the process is killed (kill -9, container OOM-kill), the JVM crashes, or the try never finishes (infinite loop, deadlock). For a daemon thread, finally may not run when the JVM shuts down.

Q34. What are suppressed exceptions?

Exceptions thrown while closing resources after a primary exception. try-with-resources attaches them with Throwable.addSuppressed, so the primary cause is preserved and the close failures are still visible via getSuppressed() and in the printed stack trace ("Suppressed: ..."). You can call addSuppressed yourself when cleaning up multiple resources manually.

Q35. In what order are resources closed in try-with-resources, and what if a constructor fails?

Reverse order of declaration. If the second resource's initialisation throws, the first (already opened) resource is still closed. Resources whose initialiser returned null are skipped. Watch wrapping: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f)) declared as one resource leaks the FileReader if the BufferedReader constructor throws — declare each as its own resource.

Q36. How do you write a good custom exception?

Extend RuntimeException (or a domain base exception), provide constructors with message and cause, carry structured data (error code, entity id, limit) as fields, keep it immutable, and document when it is thrown. Name it after the problem (PlanLimitExceededException, RunAlreadyStartedException), not the layer. Map it centrally to an HTTP status in a @RestControllerAdvice.

Q37. What is exception chaining and translation?

Translation: catching a low-level exception and throwing one meaningful at the current abstraction level (SftpException → IngestFailedException). Chaining: passing the original as the cause so the full trail ("Caused by: ...") survives. Losing the cause (throw new X(e.getMessage())) is one of the most common production debugging blockers.

Q38. Why are exceptions expensive, and how do you make them cheaper?

The cost is mostly fillInStackTrace() walking the thread's stack at construction time, plus the stack-trace array. Use exceptions for exceptional cases; for expected validation failures in hot loops return a result type. If you must throw frequently, use the 4-argument constructor with writableStackTrace=false or reuse a preallocated instance (only for exceptions with no varying state).

Q39. Why does a production log show NullPointerException with no stack trace?

HotSpot's OmitStackTraceInFastThrow optimisation: after an implicit exception is thrown many times from the same compiled code, the JIT throws a preallocated instance without a stack trace. Search earlier in the logs for the first occurrences (which have traces) or restart with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow. Java 14+ helpful NPE messages (JEP 358) tell you exactly which reference was null (because "run.getOwner()" is null) when the trace is present.

Q40. Can you catch multiple exceptions in one block? Any restriction?

Yes, catch (IOException | SQLException e). The types must not be subclasses of each other (compile error), and e is implicitly final. Java 7 also added precise rethrow: rethrowing a caught Exception e from a block whose try only throws IOException lets the method declare just throws IOException.

Q41. Can a try block exist without catch?

Yes, with finally (try { } finally { }) or as try-with-resources (try (r) { }). A plain try { } with neither is a compile error.

Q42. What happens if an exception is thrown in a static initialiser?

Class initialisation fails with ExceptionInInitializerError (wrapping the cause). Any later attempt to use the class throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X — which confuses people because the class file exists. Look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in the logs.

Q43. ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from explicit loading by name (Class.forName, loadClass) when the class is not on the classpath. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error when a class that was present at compile time cannot be found or initialised at runtime (missing jar, failed static init). In Spring Boot it often means a dependency version conflict — inspect with mvn dependency:tree.

Q44. What are the rules and pitfalls of var?

Only for local variables with an initialiser (plus loop/try-with-resources variables and lambda parameters). The type is inferred at compile time and fixed. Pitfalls: var list = new ArrayList<>() becomes ArrayList<Object>; var x = 1 is int when you wanted long; it hides types when the right side is a method call, hurting readability. Use it when the type is obvious from the right side.

Q45. Predict: int i = 0; i = i++ + i++; System.out.println(i);

1. The first i++ yields 0 (i becomes 1), the second yields 1 (i becomes 2), and the sum 0 + 1 = 1 is assigned to i, overwriting 2.

Q46. Predict: 10 == 10.0, 'a' + 1, (char)('a' + 1).

true (int promoted to double), 98 (char promoted to int), b.

Q47. Why does 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3, and how do you compare doubles?

0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point; their sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with an epsilon (Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9) for scientific values, or use BigDecimal for money. Double.compare handles NaN and -0.0 consistently, unlike ==.

Q48. Why not use double for money? How do you use BigDecimal correctly?

Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions, so totals drift and rounding is uncontrolled. Use BigDecimal built from String/valueOf, compare with compareTo, specify scale and RoundingMode (typically HALF_EVEN) for division and final rounding, reassign results (it is immutable), and store as NUMERIC in the DB. Alternatively store minor units in a long (cents) when all currencies' scales are known and no fractional rates apply.

Q49. Why is new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) false?

equals compares value and scale; compareTo compares only the numeric value. This bites HashSet/HashMap keys and assertions in tests. Normalise with stripTrailingZeros() or use compareTo.

Q50. What is RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN and why do banks use it?

"Banker's rounding": round to the nearest neighbour, and if exactly halfway, round to the even digit (2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4). Over many operations the rounding errors cancel out instead of biasing upward as HALF_UP does. Use what the business specifies — some tax rules mandate HALF_UP.

Q51. Instant vs LocalDateTime vs ZonedDateTime — when to use each?

Instant is an absolute moment in UTC — use it for timestamps you store and compare. LocalDateTime is a wall-clock date-time with no zone, not a moment — use it for user-entered schedules where the zone is stored separately. ZonedDateTime combines local date-time with zone rules — use it for calendar arithmetic that must respect DST, then convert to Instant to store. In PostgreSQL map Instant/OffsetDateTime to timestamptz.

Q52. Why was SimpleDateFormat a production problem?

It is mutable and not thread-safe: it stores the Calendar being parsed in a field. A static final SimpleDateFormat shared by request threads produces wrong dates or NumberFormatException under concurrency — intermittent and hard to reproduce. Fixes then were ThreadLocal or per-call instances; today use the immutable, thread-safe DateTimeFormatter.

Q53. How do you make time-dependent code testable?

Inject a java.time.Clock (a Spring bean Clock.systemUTC()) and call Instant.now(clock) / LocalDate.now(clock). Tests use Clock.fixed(...) or a mutable test clock to simulate month-end, expiry, or DST transitions without sleeping.

Q54. Duration vs Period?

Duration is an exact amount of time in seconds and nanoseconds (timeouts, SLAs). Period is a calendar amount in years, months and days (subscription length, "due in 30 days"). Adding Period.ofDays(1) to a ZonedDateTime keeps the same wall-clock time across a DST change; adding Duration.ofHours(24) keeps the exact elapsed time.

Q55. How do you handle time zones in a multi-tenant SaaS?

Store all instants in UTC (timestamptz), store each tenant's ZoneId as an IANA name (Europe/London, never a fixed offset), convert at the edges (API formatting, reports, scheduling), and compute business dates such as month-end in the tenant's zone. Keep the JVM default zone at UTC (-Duser.timezone=UTC) so nothing silently depends on the server's location.

Q56. Describe a real bug caused by a core-language detail.

Tell one that really happened to you, in the order symptom, mechanism, fix, prevention. The shape interviewers want: "Totals built from 33.37 + 33.37 + 33.36 failed to equal a ledger's 100.10, because the amounts had passed through double. We parsed from the original string into BigDecimal, compared with compareTo against a tolerance, and made it a rule that amounts never pass through double, including in JSON (Jackson USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS)." Other good candidates are == on Long ids that worked in tests only because the values were under 128, and a shared SimpleDateFormat.

Q57. What is the main method signature and can you overload it or omit static?

public static void main(String[] args) (varargs allowed). You may overload main, but only that signature is the launcher's entry point. In the Java 21 preview (final in Java 25), instance void main() methods are allowed for simple programs; production apps still use the classic form.

Q58. What does System.exit(0) do inside a Spring Boot app, and is it safe?

It starts JVM shutdown: shutdown hooks run (Spring's hook closes the context, calling @PreDestroy and graceful shutdown), then the JVM halts; finally blocks of the calling thread do not run. In CLI-style apps prefer SpringApplication.exit(context, () -> code) and then System.exit; in services let the orchestrator stop the process with SIGTERM so graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests.

3. Generics, Enums, Annotations, Reflection & Nested Classes

This chapter covers the language features that frameworks are built from. Spring's @Transactional is an annotation, read by reflection, applied by a generated proxy. Jackson binds JSON through generic type tokens because erasure removes the type arguments. Interviewers use these topics to separate people who use frameworks from people who can debug them. For each feature, know what the compiler does, what survives into the class file, and what happens at runtime.

3.1 Generics and type erasure

Generics give compile-time type safety without casts. They are implemented by erasure: the compiler checks the types, then removes them. The JVM sees no type arguments in ordinary objects, and List<String> and List<Integer> share the single class List.

The erasure rules are:

  1. Replace each type parameter with its leftmost bound: T becomes Object, and T extends Comparable<T> becomes Comparable.
  2. Insert casts where a value of the erased type is used as a more specific type.
  3. Generate bridge methods to preserve overriding after erasure.
// Source
public class Box<T extends Comparable<T>> {
    private T value;
    public T get() { return value; }
}
String s = new Box<String>().get();

// After erasure, conceptually
public class Box {
    private Comparable value;
    public Comparable get() { return value; }
}
String s = (String) new Box().get();    // the cast is added here

Why erasure? Migration compatibility. Java 5 had to run existing non-generic code and let it interoperate with generic libraries, which required identical class files. The cost is a list of things generics cannot do:

Not allowed Why Workaround
new T() T unknown at runtime Pass a Supplier<T> or Class<T>
new T[10], new List<String>[10] Arrays check element types at runtime and need a reifiable type (T[]) new Object[n], or use a List
x instanceof List<String> Type argument is erased x instanceof List<?>; Java 16+ allows it when the compiler can prove the cast
List<int> Type arguments must be references List<Integer>, IntStream; Valhalla aims to change this
static T field Static belongs to the erased class Generic static method
catch (T e), class X<T> extends Exception Exception dispatch happens at runtime Pass a class token
Overloads f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>) Same erasure: "name clash" Rename the methods

What does survive erasure? Generic declarations are kept in the Signature attribute of the class file: a field's declared type, a method's signature, and a class's generic superclass. Erased are the type arguments of an object instance. That gap is what makes the super type token work:

// new X<...>(){} creates an anonymous subclass whose generic superclass is recorded
List<ReconDraftSpec> specs = mapper.readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<ReconDraftSpec>>() {});

Type t = new TypeReference<List<ReconDraftSpec>>() {}.getType();  // List<ReconDraftSpec>, intact

Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference and ResolvableType work the same way, which is how Spring can autowire Repository<Order> differently from Repository<User>.

Bridge methods

class Node<T> { void set(T v) { } }
class IntNode extends Node<Integer> {
    @Override void set(Integer v) { }
}
