After erasure, Node has set(Object) while IntNode has set(Integer), which is an overload and not an override, so polymorphism would break. The compiler adds a synthetic bridge:

Bridges also implement covariant return types. You see them as extra frames in stack traces and as Method.isBridge() in reflection, and passing a String through a raw Node reference fails with ClassCastException at the bridge's cast.

Bounds, wildcards and PECS

Generics are invariant: List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. If it were, you could add a Double to a list of integers. Arrays are covariant, and pay for it at runtime:

Object[] objs = new String[1];
objs[0] = 1;                    // compiles, throws ArrayStoreException at runtime

List<Object> list = new ArrayList<String>();   // compile error: the safer design
Syntax Meaning Read as Write
List<Number> Exactly Number Number Number and subtypes
List<? extends Number> Some unknown subtype of Number Number Nothing except null
List<? super Integer> Some unknown supertype of Integer Object Integer and subtypes
List<?> Some unknown type Object Nothing except null
List (raw) Legacy, generics switched off Object Anything, unchecked

PECS, Producer Extends, Consumer Super: if a parameter produces values you read, use extends; if it consumes values you write, use super.

public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) {
    for (T item : src) dest.add(item);       // src produces, dest consumes
}
List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<>();
copy(nums, List.of(1, 2));                   // T inferred, works
copy(nums, List.of(1.5));

public static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c) { ... }

Comparable<? super T> in that last signature lets max work when the compareTo is defined on a parent class (java.sql.Timestamp inherits Comparable<Date>).

Generic method syntax: the type parameter precedes the return type, public static <T> List<T> listOf(T a), and the compiler infers it from arguments and target type. Explicit form: Util.<String>listOf("a"). Multiple bounds use &: <T extends Number & Comparable<T>>, with the class first; T erases to the first bound. Recursive bounds such as Enum<E extends Enum<E>> let the base class refer to its own subclass type.

Heap pollution and reifiable types

A type is reifiable when its full type is available at runtime: primitives, non-generic classes, raw types, unbounded wildcards (List<?>), and arrays of those. List<String> is not reifiable. Heap pollution happens when a variable of a parameterised type refers to an object that is not of that type, and it surfaces later as a ClassCastException at a line with no visible cast.

List raw = new ArrayList<String>();
raw.add(42);                         // unchecked warning
List<String> names = raw;            // heap pollution
String s = names.get(0);             // ClassCastException here, far from the cause

Generic varargs are the classic source. void f(List<String>... lists) creates a List[] at runtime, so the method can write the wrong thing into it. @SafeVarargs is your promise that the method does not store into the array or expose it. Collections.checkedList adds runtime checks when you need to catch pollution at the point of insertion.

3.2 Enums

An enum compiles to a final class extending java.lang.Enum, with one public static final field per constant, created in the static initialiser.

enum Status { QUEUED, RUNNING }
// compiles, conceptually, to
final class Status extends Enum<Status> {
    public static final Status QUEUED = new Status("QUEUED", 0);
    public static final Status RUNNING = new Status("RUNNING", 1);
    private static final Status[] $VALUES = { QUEUED, RUNNING };
    public static Status[] values() { return $VALUES.clone(); }
    public static Status valueOf(String n) { return Enum.valueOf(Status.class, n); }
    private Status(String name, int ordinal) { super(name, ordinal); }
}

Consequences follow directly from that shape:

  • Constants are singletons, so == is safe, null-safe and fast. Class initialisation makes creation thread-safe.
  • values() clones an array on each call, so cache it on a hot path.
  • Enums cannot extend a class (they already extend Enum) but can implement interfaces.
  • A constant with a body compiles to an anonymous subclass (Status$1). In that case getClass() differs from getDeclaringClass().
  • A non-constant static field cannot be read from an enum constructor, since constants are built before other statics are initialised.
  • Serialization writes only the constant's name and resolves it back through valueOf, and reflection refuses to instantiate enums, which makes them the safest singleton.
public enum Registry {                 // enum singleton
    INSTANCE;
    private final Map<String, Plugin> plugins = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    public void add(String k, Plugin p) { plugins.put(k, p); }
}

Strategy enum, behaviour per constant:

public enum Rounding {
    NONE { @Override BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal v) { return v; } },
    CENTS { @Override BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal v) { return v.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); } };
    abstract BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal v);
}

Switch on enums. The compiler builds a synthetic $SwitchMap$... int array in a helper class, indexed by ordinal(), so reordering constants does not break already compiled switches. A Java 21 switch expression over an enum must be exhaustive, and the compiler adds a default that throws MatchException (IncompatibleClassChangeError in code compiled for releases before 21) if a new constant appears at runtime without recompiling.

String label = switch (status) {
    case QUEUED -> "Waiting";
    case RUNNING -> "In progress";
};  // no default: adding a constant becomes a compile error here

EnumMap and EnumSet are the right collections for enum keys, and are much faster and smaller than the hash versions:

EnumMap<Status, V>                EnumSet<Status> (RegularEnumSet, up to 64 constants)
keyUniverse = Status.values()     long elements = 0b...0101
vals[]  index = ordinal           bit n set = constant with ordinal n present
[ v0 | null | v2 | ... ]          add = elements |= 1L << ordinal
No hashing, no entry objects      Over 64 constants: JumboEnumSet with long[]

Trap: never persist ordinal(). With JPA, @Enumerated defaults to ORDINAL, so inserting a new constant in the middle silently re-maps existing rows. Use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING), or a stable code column with an AttributeConverter.

RefinePoint: MatchStrategy is a plain enum (EXACT, NUMERIC_TOLERANCE, JARO_WINKLER, LEVENSHTEIN, …), and ReconDefinition declares Cardinality, FieldRole and ControlType as nested enums. A process's definition is stored as JSON in the definition_json jsonb column and read back with Jackson, so renaming a constant would break saved reconciliations. Constant names are part of the persisted format.

3.3 Annotations

An annotation is an interface (@interface, which extends java.lang.annotation.Annotation) with metadata stored in the class file. It does nothing by itself: something must read it, which is either a compile-time annotation processor or runtime reflection.

Meta-annotations:

Meta-annotation Purpose
@Retention SOURCE (dropped by javac, @Override, Lombok), CLASS (in class file, not at runtime; the default), RUNTIME (visible to reflection)
@Target Where it can go: TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, TYPE_USE, RECORD_COMPONENT, and others
@Inherited Subclasses inherit it, for class-level annotations only, not from interfaces or methods
@Documented Included in Javadoc
@Repeatable Can appear several times, wrapped in a container annotation

Attribute types are limited to primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations, and one-dimensional arrays of those, and values must be compile-time constants. An attribute named value can be written without its name.

How Spring processes annotations

Plain Java reflection does not treat annotations as composable, but Spring's MergedAnnotations / AnnotatedElementUtils follow meta-annotations. @Service works because it is itself annotated with @Component, and @AliasFor lets a composed annotation pass attributes down.

// Real, from ryfn-platform: a composed security annotation
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@PreAuthorize("@orgAuth.isAdmin()")
public @interface CanManageOrganization { }

RefinePoint: @CanManageOrganization on a controller method replaces a repeated SpEL string. Spring Security's method-security advisor finds the meta-present @PreAuthorize and evaluates it against the orgAuth bean, so the rule has one name and one definition.

Writing a custom annotation and aspect

@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface Audited { String action(); }

@Aspect @Component
class AuditedAspect {
    private final AuditWriter writer;
    AuditedAspect(AuditWriter writer) { this.writer = writer; }

    @Around("@annotation(audited)")
    Object around(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Audited audited) throws Throwable {
        Object result = pjp.proceed();
        writer.record(audited.action(), pjp.getArgs());
        return result;
    }
}

It must have RUNTIME retention, the annotated method must be called through the proxy (self-invocation skips the aspect), and private methods are not advised.

Compile-time annotation processors

A processor extends AbstractProcessor, is registered through META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor, and runs inside javac in rounds. It sees source elements and can generate new files or report errors, but officially cannot modify existing classes. Examples: MapStruct, Hibernate JPA Metamodel, Spring Boot's configuration processor. Lombok is the exception, as it patches javac's internal AST.

@SupportedAnnotationTypes("com.example.Audited")
@SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21)
public class AuditedProcessor extends AbstractProcessor {
    @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> types, RoundEnvironment env) {
        for (Element e : env.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Audited.class)) {
            if (e.getModifiers().contains(Modifier.PRIVATE)) {
                processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR,
                    "@Audited has no effect on private methods", e);
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
}

3.4 Reflection

Reflection inspects and invokes classes at runtime through Class, Method, Field, and Constructor.

Class<?> c = Class.forName("com.acme.refinepoint.AcmeFunctions");   // loads and initialises
Object o = c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
Method m = c.getMethod("functions");                 // public, including inherited
Method p = c.getDeclaredMethod("helper");            // any access, this class only
p.setAccessible(true);                               // bypass the access check
Object r = m.invoke(o);                              // wraps failures in InvocationTargetException

setAccessible and modules. Since Java 16 and finalised by Java 17 (JEP 403), strong encapsulation means setAccessible(true) on JDK internals fails with InaccessibleObjectException unless the package is opened with --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED. This was the classic failure when moving old libraries to Java 17.

Performance. Lookup (getMethod) is expensive because it searches and copies metadata, so cache Method objects. Invocation used to start in a native accessor and switch to generated bytecode after 15 calls ("inflation"). Since Java 18 (JEP 416), core reflection is reimplemented on method handles. Costs remaining: argument boxing, an Object[] allocation, and access checks unless accessible, plus limits on JIT inlining when the Method is not a constant.

MethodHandle and VarHandle

MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();
MethodHandle len = lookup.findVirtual(String.class, "length", MethodType.methodType(int.class));
int n = (int) len.invokeExact("hello");      // signature-polymorphic, no boxing

class Counter {
    private volatile int value;
    private static final VarHandle VALUE;
    static {
        try { VALUE = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Counter.class, "value", int.class); }
        catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); }
    }
    void increment() { VALUE.getAndAdd(this, 1); }   // atomic, replaces sun.misc.Unsafe
}
Reflection MethodHandle VarHandle
Access check At each call, unless accessible Once, at lookup Once, at lookup
Boxing Yes No with invokeExact No
JIT inlining Limited Full when static final Full when static final
Use for Frameworks, dynamic discovery Fast dynamic calls, invokedynamic targets Atomic field and array access, memory-order modes

Dynamic proxies

LlmClient proxy = (LlmClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    LlmClient.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class<?>[] { LlmClient.class },
    (self, method, args) -> {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try { return method.invoke(target, args); }
        catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); }  // unwrap, or callers see the wrapper
        finally { metrics.record(method.getName(), System.nanoTime() - start); }
    });

The JDK generates a class named like $Proxy42 at runtime, implementing the interfaces, with each method forwarding to your InvocationHandler. CGLIB and ByteBuddy instead generate a subclass of the target.

JDK Proxy CGLIB / ByteBuddy
Needs At least one interface A non-final class
How Implements interfaces Subclasses and overrides
Cannot intercept Methods outside the interfaces final, private, static methods
Self-invocation Not intercepted Not intercepted
Injectable as concrete class No, ClassCastException or injection error Yes
Used by Spring when proxyTargetClass=false, Spring Data repositories Spring Boot default (proxyTargetClass=true), Hibernate proxies (ByteBuddy), Mockito

Spring uses Objenesis to create a CGLIB proxy instance without calling the target's constructor, which is why proxy fields stay null and why reading a field directly through a proxy reference gives null.

3.5 ServiceLoader and the SPI pattern

An API is what callers use; a Service Provider Interface is what implementers provide. ServiceLoader finds implementations by reading META-INF/services/<interface name> from every jar visible to a class loader (or provides ... with in a module), and instantiates them lazily. JDBC drivers, javax.annotation.processing.Processor and logging bindings all work this way.

// Trimmed from ryfn-plugin-api
public static <T> List<Found<T>> load(Class<T> extensionPoint) {
    List<Found<T>> found = new ArrayList<>();
    var it = ServiceLoader.load(extensionPoint, loader()).stream().iterator();
    while (true) {
        try {
            if (!it.hasNext()) break;
            ServiceLoader.Provider<T> p = it.next();
            found.add(new Found<>(p.get(), source(p.type())));
        } catch (ServiceConfigurationError | RuntimeException | LinkageError e) {
            LOG.log(ERROR, "A plugin could not be loaded and is left out: " + e.getMessage(), e);
        }
    }
    return found;
}

RefinePoint: ryfn-plugin-api defines DataConnector and FunctionPlugin. Dropping a jar into the plugins folder and restarting adds connectors, or rule-language functions that the rule builder, checker and DuckDB SQL all pick up. Two design choices matter: a broken plugin is logged and left out rather than stopping the service, which is why ServiceConfigurationError and LinkageError are caught; and the plugin class loader's parent is the service's, so plugins share the API classes. Plugins run with the service's permissions, so only server operators install them.

ServiceLoader vs Spring's auto-configuration: ServiceLoader instantiates with a no-arg constructor and knows nothing about dependency injection or conditions. Spring Boot's META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports lists configuration classes that go through full bean processing with @ConditionalOn.... Same discovery idea, more machinery.

3.6 Nested classes and memory leaks

Kind Declared Holds outer instance Can access Typical use
Static nested static class in a class No Outer statics; private members via an instance Builders, Map.Entry, DTO parts
Inner Non-static member Yes, this$0 All outer members Iterators bound to a collection
Local Inside a method Yes, in an instance method Plus effectively final locals Rare
Anonymous Expression new X() { } Yes, in an instance method Plus effectively final locals Largely replaced by lambdas 
class Outer {
    class Inner { }                     // compiled to Outer$Inner with a constructor taking Outer
    static class Nested { }
}
Outer.Inner i = new Outer().new Inner();
Outer.Nested n = new Outer.Nested();

The leak: an inner class instance keeps its outer instance alive, even when it never uses it. Hand one to something long-lived (an executor, a cache, a listener registry, a ThreadLocal) and the outer object cannot be collected. Since JDK 18, javac omits this$0 from an inner class that never uses it (unless the class is serialisable without a serialVersionUID), which removes some of these leaks but is not something to rely on. Lambdas differ: they capture this only if they actually use an instance member, and a non-capturing lambda is a shared singleton. Anonymous classes always create a new object, and this inside one means the anonymous object, whereas in a lambda it means the enclosing instance.

3.7 Java serialization

Serializable is a marker interface. ObjectOutputStream writes the class descriptor and field values, walking the object graph with reflection; ObjectInputStream creates the instance without calling its constructor (only the first non-serializable superclass's no-arg constructor runs), then sets the fields directly.

  • serialVersionUID: a version identity. If it does not match on read you get InvalidClassException. If not declared, it is computed from the class structure, so any change such as a new method breaks old data. Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;.
  • transient: excluded field, restored to its default. static fields are never serialised.
  • Custom hooks: private writeObject / readObject, writeReplace / readResolve (singleton protection), and readObjectNoData.
  • Externalizable: you write everything with writeExternal / readExternal. It needs a public no-arg constructor, which is called.

Why Java serialization is dangerous. Deserialising untrusted bytes can instantiate any class on the classpath with attacker-controlled fields, and "gadget chains" in libraries turn that into remote code execution (the Apache Commons Collections exploit of 2015). Controls: never deserialise untrusted data, use ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290, JEP 415) as a whitelist. Mark Reinhold, the Java platform's chief architect, has called serialization a horrible mistake. Other problems are fragile versioning, hidden constructors bypassing invariants, and large output. Use JSON or Protobuf instead. Records are the safer serialisable shape, since their deserialisation always goes through the canonical constructor.

JSON with Jackson

ObjectMapper is expensive to configure and thread-safe once configured, so share one (Spring Boot provides a bean and customises it through Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer). Since it builds serialisers using reflection and caches them, creating a new mapper per request throws away the cache and is a known performance bug. Key annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true), @JsonInclude(NON_NULL), @JsonCreator, @JsonTypeInfo / @JsonSubTypes, @JsonFormat.

Trap: enableDefaultTyping() and @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS) on open types let incoming JSON name the class to instantiate, which reintroduces the gadget-chain problem. Use a closed list of logical names (Id.NAME + @JsonSubTypes), or configure a PolymorphicTypeValidator.

Records with Jackson. Since Jackson 2.12 records bind through the canonical constructor, with no setters or no-arg constructor needed, and validation in the compact constructor runs on every read.

@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)   // tolerate fields you did not ask for
public record MatchRule(String name, List<String> keys) {
    public MatchRule { keys = keys == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(keys); }
}

RefinePoint: ReconDefinition, stored as jsonb, nests records such as Control(name, type, side, severity, params), and the LlmClient types (LlmRequest, Message, LlmResponse) are records nested in the interface. ReconDraftSpec, the JSON the model returns when drafting a reconciliation, sets @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true), because a model may add a field nobody asked for and that should not fail the whole draft.

3.8 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is type erasure and why does Java use it?

The compiler checks generic types, then removes them: type parameters become their leftmost bound, and casts are inserted at use sites. Java chose it for migration compatibility, so generic and pre-Java-5 code could share the same class files and collection classes. The cost is that runtime code cannot ask for a type argument: no new T(), no new T[], no instanceof List<String>.

Q2. Can you get the generic type at runtime?

Not from an instance, but yes from declarations. A field's declared type, a method's signature and a class's generic superclass are stored in the Signature attribute, readable with getGenericType(), getGenericReturnType() and getGenericSuperclass(). An anonymous subclass such as new TypeReference<List<Foo>>() {} records its superclass's arguments, which is how Jackson and Spring recover them.

Q3. Predict the output.

List<String> a = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> b = new ArrayList<>();
System.out.println(a.getClass() == b.getClass());

true. Both are java.util.ArrayList at runtime; there is only one class.

Q4. Why does this not compile: void f(List<String> x) and void f(List<Integer> x)?

Both erase to f(List), so the class file would contain two methods with the same descriptor. The compiler reports "name clash: same erasure". Different return types do not help. Rename the methods, or give them different non-generic parameters.

Q5. What is a bridge method? When is it generated?

A synthetic method the compiler adds so that overriding still works after erasure, and for covariant return types. If IntNode extends Node<Integer> overrides set(Integer), the compiler adds set(Object), which casts and delegates. Reflection shows it with isBridge(), and frameworks that scan methods must skip it. Spring's BridgeMethodResolver exists to find the real method, so that annotations on it are seen.

Q6. Why can't you create a generic array?

Arrays check the element type on each store at runtime (ArrayStoreException), which needs a reified component type, and generics have erased theirs. If new List<String>[2] were legal, you could assign it to Object[], store a List<Integer>, and nothing would catch it until a confusing ClassCastException later. Use List<List<String>>, or do what ArrayList does internally: hold Object[] and cast on read.

Q7. Are arrays covariant? Are generics? Which is safer?

Arrays are covariant, since String[] is an Object[], and enforce safety at runtime with ArrayStoreException. Generics are invariant and enforce it at compile time, so the error surfaces earlier. Wildcards add controlled variance to generics when needed.

Q8. Explain PECS with a JDK example.

Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src): the source produces Ts for reading, the destination consumes them. Collection.addAll(Collection<? extends E>) reads from its argument, and removeIf(Predicate<? super E>) feeds elements to its predicate, so a Predicate<Object> works on a List<String>.

Q9. What can you add to a List<? extends Number>?

Only null. The actual list could be List<Integer> or List<Double>, and the compiler cannot prove any concrete value fits. You can read elements as Number. Conversely, a List<? super Integer> accepts Integers, but reads only give you Object.

Q10. List<?> vs List<Object> vs raw List?

List<Object> accepts any object but only a list declared with exactly Object. List<?> can refer to any list, is read-only in practice (except null), and stays type-checked. Raw List turns generics off for everything it touches, including unrelated generic methods on that type, and produces unchecked warnings. Use raw types only in class literals and instanceof.

Q11. What is wildcard capture?

The compiler gives a ? a temporary name so that it can type-check a call. You cannot write list.set(0, list.get(0)) on a List<?>, because the two ?s are not known to be the same. A private generic helper <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l) captures it and compiles, and Collections.swap uses this technique.

Q12. What does <T extends Comparable<? super T>> mean?

T must be comparable to itself or to some supertype. Without ? super, a type that inherits its compareTo from a parent, such as java.sql.Timestamp with Comparable<Date>, would be rejected. Collections.sort and max use this signature.

Q13. What is a recursive type bound? Why does Enum use one?

E extends Enum<E> means each enum is parameterised by itself, so compareTo(E) accepts only the same enum type, and valueOf returns it. Fluent builder hierarchies use the same pattern, Builder<T extends Builder<T>>, so that self() returns the subclass and chained calls keep their type.

Q14. What is heap pollution? Show one.

A variable of a parameterised type holds an object that is not that type. It usually comes from raw types or unchecked casts, and fails later with a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in sight.

static <T> T[] toArray(T... items) { return items; }
static <T> T[] twice(T a, T b) { return toArray(a, b); }   // creates Object[] at runtime
String[] s = twice("x", "y");                              // ClassCastException: Object[] to String[]

Q15. What are reifiable types? What does @SafeVarargs promise?

Reifiable types keep complete information at runtime: primitives, non-generic classes, raw types, List<?>, and arrays of those. @SafeVarargs asserts that a generic varargs method does not write to the array or let it escape, which silences the caller's warning. It is allowed only on final, static, private methods and constructors, because an override could break the promise.

Q16. Can a generic class have a static field of type T?

No. Statics belong to the single erased class, while T varies per use. class Box<T> { static T x; } does not compile. A static generic method declares its own parameter.

Q17. Can a generic class extend Exception? Can you catch T?

No to both. Exception handlers are matched at runtime by class, and the argument is gone by then. However, <T extends Throwable> void f() throws T is allowed, and it enables the "sneaky throw" trick to rethrow checked exceptions unchecked.

Q18. How would you implement a typesafe heterogeneous container?

Key the map by Class<T> and cast through Class.cast, so that one map holds many value types safely.

private final Map<Class<?>, Object> values = new HashMap<>();
<T> void put(Class<T> k, T v) { values.put(k, k.cast(v)); }
<T> T get(Class<T> k) { return k.cast(values.get(k)); }

Spring's ApplicationContext.getBean(Class<T>) has this shape. Note that a class token cannot express List<String>; a super type token can.

Q19. How does an enum compile? Can it extend a class or be subclassed?

To a final class extending java.lang.Enum, with public static final constants, a synthetic $VALUES array, values() and valueOf. It cannot extend another class but can implement interfaces. Constants with bodies are anonymous subclasses, and in that case the enum isn't marked final. Since Java 17 such enums are implicitly sealed.

Q20. Is == safe for enums?

Yes, and preferred. Each constant is a single instance per class loader, enforced by private constructors, class initialisation, the serialization mechanism and a reflection block. == is null-safe and checked at compile time: comparing different enum types is a compile error, whereas equals would just return false.

Q21. Why is an enum the best way to implement a singleton?

Three attacks that break hand-written singletons fail here. Reflection throws "Cannot reflectively create enum objects"; serialization writes only the name and resolves it back through valueOf; and class initialisation gives thread safety for free. The limits are that it cannot extend a class and initialises eagerly with the class. In a Spring application a singleton-scoped bean is the normal answer, since it can be replaced in tests.

Q22. EnumMap vs HashMap? How does EnumSet work?

EnumMap stores values in an array indexed by ordinal(): no hashing, no entry objects, iteration in declaration order. EnumSet holds a bit vector: one long up to 64 constants, long[] beyond. Operations like addAll and containsAll are single bitwise operations, so it replaces bit-flag ints with type safety. Both reject a null key or element.

Q23. Why should you never persist ordinal()?

It is a position, so inserting or reordering constants re-maps existing data with no error. JPA's @Enumerated default is ORDINAL, which makes this a default trap. Persist the name with EnumType.STRING, or a stable explicit code through an AttributeConverter if names may change.

Q24. How do you look up an enum from a value without a loop?

Build a static map in the enum, in a static field initialiser and not from the constructor, since constants are constructed before other statics are initialised.

private static final Map<String, IsoCurrency> BY_CODE =
    Arrays.stream(values()).collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(IsoCurrency::code, c -> c));
public static Optional<IsoCurrency> of(String code) { return Optional.ofNullable(BY_CODE.get(code)); }

Enum.valueOf throws IllegalArgumentException for an unknown name, which is awkward to use for parsing external input.

Q25. What happens if a new enum constant is added but a switch using it is not recompiled?

For an old-style switch statement with no default, no case runs and execution simply continues, and the mapping survives reordering thanks to the $SwitchMap array. For a switch expression without default, the compiler's synthetic default throws MatchException on Java 21 classes. This matters in shared libraries, and it is why services must be rebuilt together after an enum changes.

Q26. Can an enum have abstract methods, fields and constructors?

Yes, all three. Constructors are implicitly private, and each constant must implement any abstract method. Fields should be final, because constants are global singletons and mutable state on them is shared across the entire JVM.

Q27. Enum vs sealed interface with records?

An enum is a fixed set of instances, all with the same shape, so it fits statuses and strategies without per-instance data. A sealed hierarchy is a fixed set of types, each with its own data, so sealed interface Node permits Literal, Binary, Call fits an AST, and a pattern-matching switch handles it exhaustively.

Q28. What is an annotation really?

An interface extending java.lang.annotation.Annotation, with attribute values stored in the class file. At runtime getAnnotation returns a JDK dynamic proxy implementing that interface, which you can see by printing its class ($Proxy12). It has no behaviour; a processor, a framework or an aspect supplies the behaviour.

Q29. Explain each @Retention value with an example.

SOURCE: discarded by javac, as with @Override, @SuppressWarnings and Lombok's annotations. CLASS: in the class file but not loaded for reflection; it is the default, and bytecode tools use it. RUNTIME: available to reflection, as with @Transactional and @Entity. Forgetting RUNTIME is the classic reason a custom annotation "does nothing".

Q30. How does Spring find @Service when it is not literally @Component?

Component scanning reads class files with ASM without loading them, and uses metadata that includes annotations on annotations. @Service is meta-annotated with @Component, so it matches. MergedAnnotations follows the hierarchy and applies @AliasFor attribute overrides, which is how @GetMapping is a composed @RequestMapping(method = GET) and @SpringBootApplication bundles three annotations. Plain method.getAnnotation(Component.class) would not see it.

Q31. Why doesn't an annotation on an interface method always work?

Java does not inherit method annotations, and @Inherited only applies to class-level annotations from superclasses. Spring compensates by searching super-methods and interfaces with AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation, but mechanisms vary: a @Transactional on an interface works with JDK proxies and has had different rules with class proxies. The documented recommendation is to annotate concrete classes.

Q32. How do you write a custom annotation with an aspect? What are the ways it silently fails?

Define it with @Retention(RUNTIME), @Target(METHOD), and use an @Aspect bean with @Around("@annotation(x)"). It fails silently when: the retention is wrong; the call is self-invocation (this.foo()) that bypasses the proxy; the method is private, or final on a CGLIB proxy; the object was created with new rather than by Spring; or spring-boot-starter-aop is missing. The Spring chapters cover proxies in detail.

Q33. What is the difference between an annotation processor and runtime reflection?

A processor runs inside javac, sees source elements, and generates new source or reports compile errors. MapStruct, for example, has no runtime cost and fails at build time. Reflection reads annotations at runtime, which is flexible and allows conditional behaviour, but costs startup time and fails late. Spring AOT and Micronaut move framework work to build time for faster startup and native images.

Q34. How does Lombok work if processors cannot modify classes?

It uses the annotation-processing entry point, then casts to javac's internal classes and modifies the AST directly, adding getters, constructors and so on before bytecode generation. This is unsupported API use, which is why new JDK releases can break Lombok and it needs --add-opens style workarounds. Records replace much of what @Value gave you.

Q35. What is reflection and what are its downsides?

Runtime inspection and invocation of classes, without compile-time knowledge. Downsides: errors shift from compile time to runtime; invocation is slower with boxing; encapsulation is bypassed; and GraalVM native images need configuration for each reflective access. Refactoring tools also miss string names. Frameworks are its proper home, with application code rarely needing it.

Q36. getMethods() vs getDeclaredMethods()?

getMethods returns public methods including inherited ones. getDeclaredMethods returns every method declared in that class, of any access, but none inherited, and includes bridges and synthetics. getDeclaredFields follows the same rule, so to find a private inherited field you must walk getSuperclass(). Spring's ReflectionUtils does this. Order is not guaranteed.

Q37. Can reflection change a final field or a private field?

Private: yes, with setAccessible(true), subject to module encapsulation. Instance final: yes after setAccessible, but JIT-compiled code may have assumed it constant, and inlined constants never change, so results are unreliable. static final: always IllegalAccessException, and the old hack of clearing the modifiers field stopped working in Java 12. Record and hidden-class fields cannot be changed either.

Q38. What does InvocationTargetException mean?

Method.invoke wraps any exception the target threw. The real problem is in getCause(). A proxy handler that does not unwrap it makes callers see UndeclaredThrowableException, because InvocationTargetException is a checked exception the interface does not declare. That hides the real exception from catch blocks and from Spring's rollback rules.

Q39. What is InaccessibleObjectException, and how did you handle it when upgrading to Java 17?

Strong encapsulation (JEP 403) blocks reflective access to JDK internals, so old library versions fail with "module java.base does not opens java.lang to unnamed module". The right fix is upgrading the library (common offenders were old ByteBuddy, Lombok, Gson on JDK classes). The temporary one is --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED. jdeps --jdk-internals finds usage before upgrading.

Q40. MethodHandle vs reflection?

A method handle is a typed, directly executable reference, with access checked once at lookup. In a static final field the JIT can inline through it, and invokeExact avoids boxing. Reflection is easier and is built on method handles since Java 18. Use reflection for one-off framework work and handles in hot paths. invokedynamic, lambdas and string concatenation all link through them.

Q41. What is VarHandle and what did it replace?

A typed reference to a field or array element, with access modes: plain, getAcquire/setRelease, volatile, and atomics like compareAndSet. It replaced sun.misc.Unsafe and field updaters as the supported way to do low-level concurrency. The JDK's own AtomicBoolean and AtomicReference are built on it.

Q42. How does Proxy.newProxyInstance work internally?

It generates a class at runtime that implements the given interfaces and extends Proxy, with each method looked up once and held in a static Method field. A call forwards to handler.invoke(proxy, method, args). Generated classes are cached per class loader and interface list, so repeat calls reuse them. equals, hashCode and toString are routed through the handler too.

Q43. JDK proxy vs CGLIB: why does Spring Boot default to CGLIB?

The JDK proxy needs an interface and can only be injected as that interface; CGLIB subclasses the class, so injecting the concrete type also works. Boot set proxyTargetClass=true by default in 2.0 to avoid the confusing "bean is of type $Proxy" errors. CGLIB's limits are that final classes and methods cannot be advised; Spring repackages it inside spring-core.

Q44. Why does a @Transactional method fail silently when final, and what happens to fields?

A CGLIB subclass cannot override it, so the call runs directly on the proxy instance, not on the target. Because Objenesis created the proxy without running constructors, its fields are null, which gives a confusing NullPointerException on injected collaborators. Kotlin users hit this constantly, since classes are final by default, hence the kotlin-spring plugin.

Q45. How does Mockito create a mock?

With ByteBuddy. Older versions generated a subclass, so final classes could not be mocked. Since Mockito 5 the default is mock-maker-inline, which uses a Java agent to instrument the class's bytecode, so final classes, and with mockStatic, static methods work too. Objenesis skips constructors. It is the same family of techniques as Hibernate's proxies.

Q46. What is SPI? Give JDK examples, and how is it different from an API?

An API is the contract callers use, while an SPI is the contract implementers provide, and the framework calls them. Examples: JDBC Driver, java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider, javax.annotation.processing.Processor, logging bindings. ServiceLoader connects them by reading META-INF/services/<interface> files, or provides in module-info.

Q47. How does JDBC find the driver without Class.forName?

Since JDBC 4, DriverManager's initialisation uses ServiceLoader for java.sql.Driver. Each driver jar lists itself under META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver, and its static initialiser registers the driver. Dropping PostgreSQL's jar on the class path is enough. Old Class.forName("org.postgresql.Driver") code simply forced that registration by hand.

Q48. What are common ServiceLoader problems?

The provider needs a public no-arg constructor (or, in a named module, a static provider() method). The file name must be the fully qualified interface name, exactly. A provider failure surfaces as ServiceConfigurationError during iteration, so a single bad jar can break the loop unless caught around hasNext and next. Loaded providers are not reloaded unless reload(). The class loader matters: a shaded fat jar merging META-INF/services files badly loses providers, so use the Maven Shade ServicesResourceTransformer.

Q49. Describe the plugin system in your project.

"ryfn-plugin-api defines two extension points, DataConnector and FunctionPlugin, with no dependency on the services. Plugins.load runs ServiceLoader over a URLClassLoader that adds the jars in RYFN_PLUGINS_DIR, with the service's loader as parent. So a jar, with its META-INF/services file, adds a connector or a rule function after a restart, and core code never changes. A broken plugin is logged and left out, so it can't stop a service. Plugins are trusted code, so operators install them, not tenants. ryfn-plugin-example is the reference implementation."

Q50. Static nested vs inner class: when to use each?

Default to static nested. An inner class carries a hidden this$0 reference, costing memory and risking leaks, and is worth it only when each instance truly belongs to an outer instance and uses it, as ArrayList.Itr does with its list. Effective Java item 24: "favour static member classes over nonstatic."

Q51. Show how an inner class can leak memory. What is the fix?

class ReportBuilder {
    private final String name = "July close";
    private final List<Row> rows = loadMillions();
    Runnable notifier() {
        return new Runnable() { public void run() { log.info("done: " + name); } };  // reads this.name
    }
}
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(new ReportBuilder().notifier(), 0, 1, MINUTES);

The scheduler keeps the Runnable, which keeps the ReportBuilder through this$0, and with it all the rows, just to read one string. Fix: copy what is needed first, String n = name; return () -> log.info("done: " + n);, so the lambda captures only the string; or use a static nested class that takes only what it needs. In a heap dump this appears as a retained path through this$0.

Q52. Lambda vs anonymous class internally?

An anonymous class is a real class file (Outer$1), with a new object on each evaluation, and this means that object. A lambda compiles to a private synthetic method plus invokedynamic linked through LambdaMetafactory, with a hidden class created at first use. It captures only what it uses, and a non-capturing lambda is reused as one instance. this in a lambda means the enclosing object. Full details are in the functional programming chapter.

Q53. Can an inner class have static members? Can a local class capture variables?

Since Java 16 (the records JEP), inner classes may declare static members. Before that, only constants were allowed. Local and anonymous classes can capture effectively final locals, copied into synthetic fields as val$x. Local records, enums and interfaces are allowed and are implicitly static, so they cannot capture.

Q54. How does an inner class access the outer's private fields?

Before Java 11, javac generated package-private synthetic accessors (access$000), which widened the access surface and showed up in stack traces. Since Java 11 (JEP 181, nest-based access control), nestmates share private access directly at the JVM level, and no accessors are generated.

Q55. What exactly happens during Java deserialization?

ObjectInputStream reads the class descriptor, checks serialVersionUID, and allocates the object without running constructors of Serializable classes, running only the no-arg constructor of the first non-serialisable superclass. It then sets the fields via reflection, including final ones, and invokes readObject and readResolve if defined. Because this bypasses constructors, invariants are not checked unless readObject re-validates them.

Q56. What is serialVersionUID and what happens if you don't declare it?

It's the version number compared when reading. If undeclared, the JVM computes it by hashing the class's name, interfaces, fields and methods, so an innocent change such as adding a method causes InvalidClassException on old data. Declare it explicitly, and increment only for incompatible changes. Adding a field (default on read) or changing a field from transient to non-transient is compatible; deleting a field, changing its type, or making it transient is not.

Q57. transient vs static vs volatile for serialization?

transient and static fields are not written. transient restores to the default (or set it in readObject), and a static field just has whatever value is current in the reader's JVM. volatile has nothing to do with serialization. transient on a final field leaves it at default, and without custom hooks it can't be reassigned, so avoid that combination.

Q58. What if a parent is not Serializable but the child is? And the reverse?

Child serialisable, parent not: parent fields are not saved, and the parent's no-arg constructor runs on read, so it must exist and be accessible, or you get InvalidClassException. Parent serialisable: children inherit that, whether wanted or not. A non-serialisable field reference that is not transient throws NotSerializableException at write time.

Q59. Serializable vs Externalizable?

Serializable: the JVM writes the fields by reflection, and no constructor runs. Externalizable: you control all reading and writing, a public no-arg constructor is required and does run, and it can be more compact. Both are out of fashion: choose JSON, Protobuf or Avro for data that crosses a process boundary.

Q60. Why is Java deserialization a security risk, and how do you defend against it?

Reading bytes instantiates attacker-chosen classes from the class path, and readObject methods in common libraries can be chained into code execution, before your code ever looks at the object. Defences: never deserialise untrusted input; use data formats that bind to known types; apply ObjectInputFilter allow-lists (JEP 290, global filter factories in JEP 415); keep gadgets out with dependency updates. The same risk applies to Jackson default typing, as well as to old XML and YAML libraries (SnakeYAML's constructor).

Q61. How does Jackson work under the hood? Why reuse ObjectMapper?

It introspects a type once (properties, creators, annotations), builds a serialiser or deserialiser, and caches it per mapper. Reads stream through a JsonParser token by token, and the optional Afterburner and Blackbird modules generate accessors to replace reflection. A new mapper per request re-does the introspection every time, which is far slower. Once configured it is thread-safe. For custom settings, derive one with mapper.copy() or get an immutable ObjectReader/ObjectWriter.

Q62. How do records work with Jackson? What are the gotchas?

Since 2.12, records bind through the canonical constructor using the component names, so no extra annotations are needed, and compact constructor validation always runs. Gotchas: unknown properties still fail on a bare new ObjectMapper() unless you add @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) or disable FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, while Spring Boot's mapper disables it by default; versions before 2.15 had edge cases around @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore on components; and an extra accessor such as isActive() on a record can add a JSON property you did not intend.

Q63. How do you handle polymorphic JSON safely?

Use @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, property = "type") with @JsonSubTypes listing the allowed classes, or a sealed hierarchy with a custom deserialiser. Avoid Id.CLASS and default typing on broad types like Object. For versioned event payloads, also ignore unknown fields so that older consumers tolerate new ones.

Q64. How would you evolve a stored JSON format?

Add fields as optional with defaults, tolerate unknown ones, never rename or re-type without a migration, and keep a version number where the shape may change meaningfully. Enum values need care too: a removed constant fails on read unless READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL or a @JsonEnumDefaultValue is used. In RefinePoint, a process's definition is JSON in a jsonb column bound to ReconDefinition, so enum names and field names are effectively part of the database schema.

4. Collections Internals I: Lists, HashMap, HashSet

"How does HashMap work?" is the most-asked Java interview question in the world, so a one-paragraph answer will not stand out. A senior answer goes through hash spreading, the index mask, the resize split and treeification, and connects each detail to a production consequence. This chapter gives you that answer, along with the internals of the list family and the iteration rules that catch people out.

4.1 The collections hierarchy

Map is not a Collection: it has key-value pairs, and exposes three collection views (keySet, values, entrySet) backed by the map itself. Modifying a view modifies the map. SequencedCollection arrived in Java 21 and is covered in chapter 5.

4.2 ArrayList

ArrayList is a growable wrapper over Object[] elementData, with a size field separate from the array's capacity.

elementData (capacity 10)         size = 4
+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
| a  | b  | c  | d  |null|null|null|null|null|null|
+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
  0    1    2    3    add("e") writes index 4, size++ : O(1)

add(1, "x"): System.arraycopy shifts 1..3 one to the right : O(n)
remove(1):   System.arraycopy shifts left, last slot nulled for GC : O(n)

Growth. new ArrayList<>() shares an empty array and allocates capacity 10 on the first add (lazy since Java 8). When full, grow() computes newCapacity = old + (old >> 1), which is 1.5x, then Arrays.copyOf. Growth is amortised O(1): across n appends the total copying is bounded by about 3n element moves, since the geometric series converges.

Details interviewers probe:

  • System.arraycopy is a JVM intrinsic that uses bulk memory moves, so shifting is much faster than a Java loop, though still O(n).
  • RandomAccess is a marker interface. Algorithms such as Collections.binarySearch check instanceof RandomAccess to choose index-based or iterator-based paths.
  • trimToSize() shrinks the capacity, and ensureCapacity(n) or new ArrayList<>(n) avoids repeated copying. Removing elements never shrinks the array automatically, so a list that once held a million items keeps that array.
  • Why 1.5x and not 2x? It wastes less memory, and with a factor below the golden ratio the sum of freed blocks can eventually fit the next allocation. Overflow is handled by ArraysSupport.newLength, with OutOfMemoryError above the maximum array size.
  • elementData is transient. writeObject serialises only size elements, not the empty capacity.

4.3 LinkedList, Vector, Stack, ArrayDeque

LinkedList is a doubly linked list, with Node<E> { item, next, prev } and pointers to first and last. get(i) walks from the nearer end, so it is O(n). Each node costs roughly 24–32 bytes of overhead on top of the element reference, and the nodes are scattered over the heap, causing cache misses when traversing.

Big-O flatters LinkedList. add(0, x) is O(1), but you usually have to find the position first, which is O(n) with pointer chasing. An ArrayList arraycopy over contiguous memory beats it in nearly all real workloads. Even Joshua Bloch, who wrote it, has said he never uses it. For queue or stack behaviour, use ArrayDeque.

ArrayDeque is a circular buffer with head and tail indices. Both ends are O(1) without node allocation, and it doubles capacity (or grows by 50% once large) when full. null elements are not allowed, because null signals "empty" from poll.

capacity 8: head = 6, tail = 2 (wraps around)
index:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
value: [c] [d] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [a] [b]
        addFirst writes index 5; addLast writes index 2

Vector is a synchronised ArrayList from Java 1.0 that doubles when full. Each method locks, but compound actions like "check then add" still race. Stack extends Vector is a design mistake: it inherits add(int, E), which breaks LIFO. Use ArrayDeque for a stack, and CopyOnWriteArrayList or an explicit lock for concurrent lists.

Complexity table

Operation ArrayList LinkedList ArrayDeque HashMap/HashSet TreeMap/TreeSet
get by index O(1) O(n) n/a n/a n/a
add at end O(1) amortised O(1) O(1) amortised n/a n/a
add/remove at front O(n) O(1) O(1) n/a n/a
add/remove in middle O(n) O(n) to find, O(1) to link n/a n/a n/a
contains O(n) O(n) O(n) O(1) average O(log n)
put/remove by key n/a n/a n/a O(1) average, O(log n) worst O(log n)
Memory per element Lowest High Low High (entry object) High (entry with color and parent)

4.4 HashMap internals

The structure

transient Node<K,V>[] table;     // allocated lazily on the first put
transient int size;
int threshold;                   // capacity * loadFactor
final float loadFactor;          // default 0.75
transient int modCount;          // structural changes, for fail-fast iterators

static class Node<K,V> { final int hash; final K key; V value; Node<K,V> next; }

From key to bucket, step by step

static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
int index = (table.length - 1) & hash;

Why spread (h ^ h >>> 16)? The index uses only the low bits of the hash. Table sizes are small, so with 16 buckets only 4 bits matter. Hash codes that differ only in their high bits (such as Float keys, or sequences of multiples of 2^16) would all collide, so folding the high 16 bits into the low 16 gives them a say at negligible cost.

Why a power-of-two capacity? (n - 1) & hash is a very fast modulo, and it only works because n - 1 is all ones in binary. It is also what makes the resize split cheap. new HashMap<>(17) is rounded up to 32 by tableSizeFor.

hashCode          1011 0110 1101 0010  0001 1100 1010 0101
h >>> 16          0000 0000 0000 0000  1011 0110 1101 0010
hash = h ^ h>>>16 1011 0110 1101 0010  1010 1010 0111 0111
n - 1 = 15        0000 0000 0000 0000  0000 0000 0000 1111
index             .................................... 0111  = 7

put, the full flow

Note the comparison order: hash first, then ==, then equals. Comparing stored ints is cheap, and it means equals is only called on real hash matches. get follows the same path without the insert.

Replacing a value does not increment modCount, since it is not a structural change. That is why you can call map.put(existingKey, v) while iterating without getting ConcurrentModificationException.

Load factor and capacity

Threshold = capacity × load factor: 16 × 0.75 = 12, so the 13th entry triggers a resize to 32. The 0.75 default is a trade-off between memory and collisions. With random hashes, bin lengths follow a Poisson distribution with λ ≈ 0.5, giving P(bin has 8 entries) ≈ 0.00000006. That figure is why bins rarely treeify unless the hash function is poor or under attack.

Presizing: to hold n entries without resizing, use capacity n / 0.75 + 1. new HashMap<>(n) does not mean "n entries": new HashMap<>(1000) gets a table of 1024, with a threshold of 768, and resizes once. Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(int numMappings), which does the arithmetic for you.

Resize and the bucket split

Doubling the table means each entry either stays at index j or moves to j + oldCap, decided by a single bit: hash & oldCap. There is no rehash and no re-modulo.

oldCap = 16, entries in old bucket 5:
hash ...0 0101 : hash & 16 == 0  stays at  5      (lo list)
hash ...1 0101 : hash & 16 != 0  moves to  5 + 16 = 21  (hi list)

Each resize is O(n), and a large one is a visible allocation plus a copy pause on that one put. A resize of a many-million-entry map shows up as a latency spike, so presize when the size is known.

Treeification

Constant Value Meaning
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD 8 A bin at this length is converted to a red-black tree
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY 64 If the table is smaller than this, resize instead of treeifying
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD 6 During a resize split, a tree bin with 6 or fewer entries becomes a list again

Treeifying changes the worst case from O(n) to O(log n) per bin. The gap between 8 and 6 provides hysteresis, so a bin hovering around one value does not flip back and forth. TreeNode objects are about twice the size of Node.

How can a tree be ordered when keys may not be Comparable? It orders by hash first. If hashes are equal and the key implements Comparable, it uses compareTo. Otherwise tieBreakOrder uses class name and identity hash so that insertion can continue, but a lookup may need to search both subtrees. So a tree bin only reaches O(log n) lookup with distinct hashes or Comparable keys.

Why was this added? Hash-flooding denial of service: an attacker submits POST parameter names that all collide ("Aa" and "BB" have the same hashCode, and any concatenation of them does too), degrading a request-parsing map to O(n²) overall. Java 8's trees cap the damage, since String is Comparable.

Java 7 vs Java 8

Java 7 Java 8+
Bin insert At head At tail
Worst-case bin O(n) linked list O(log n) tree
Hash function Several shifts and XORs One h ^ h>>>16, since trees handle bad cases
Resize Rehash each entry; reverses bin order hash & oldCap split; keeps order
Concurrent resize Can create a cycle, causing an infinite loop No cycle, but still loses data
Null key Special-cased Hash 0, bucket 0
Table allocation Lazy since 7u40 Lazy

The Java 7 infinite loop. Two threads resize at once. Because Java 7 reverses each bin as it moves entries, the threads see opposite link directions, and one can write A.next = B while the other has B.next = A. A later get that walks that bin never terminates, showing up as a thread stuck at 100% CPU inside HashMap.get.

Java 8 preserves order with its lo and hi lists, so the cycle no longer forms, but HashMap remains unsafe for concurrent writes: updates can be lost, and size can be wrong. Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Null keys and iteration order

One null key is allowed (hash 0, bucket 0), and any number of null values. map.get(k) == null therefore does not distinguish "absent" from "maps to null", so use containsKey, or better, do not store nulls. Map.of, ConcurrentHashMap and Hashtable reject nulls.

Iteration order is not guaranteed and can change on resize or between JDK versions. Iteration scans the whole table, so its cost is O(capacity + size). A map with a large capacity and few entries iterates slowly even if it is almost empty, and clear() keeps the capacity.

Trap: code that "works" because it relied on HashMap order breaks when a key is added or the JDK changes, as when Java 8 changed String-keyed iteration order and broke many brittle tests. Use LinkedHashMap if order matters.

4.5 HashSet

HashSet is a thin wrapper around a HashMap, where each element is a key and the value is a shared dummy object:

private transient HashMap<E,Object> map;
private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();
public boolean add(E e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; }
public boolean contains(Object o) { return map.containsKey(o); }

That is why it allows one null, has the same complexity, and has the same memory overhead (about 32–48 bytes per element with entry plus header). add returns false for a duplicate, and the existing element is kept, not replaced. LinkedHashSet uses a LinkedHashMap, and TreeSet a TreeMap.

new HashSet<>(List.of("a", "b")).size();  // 2
Set<String> s = new HashSet<>(collection);  // capacity max(n / .75 + 1, 16), no resizing while copying

4.6 equals, hashCode and mutable keys

A bucket lookup first needs the same hashCode, and then equals. Break the contract and entries disappear.

Situation Effect in a HashMap
equals overridden, hashCode not Equal keys land in different buckets: duplicates, failed lookups
hashCode overridden, equals not Same bucket, but only the same instance matches
Constant hashCode Legal; everything in one bin, tree or O(n), very slow
Mutable field in hashCode, then mutated Entry stored under the old hash: unreachable by get, and still counted and iterated 
List<String> key = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
Map<List<String>, String> m = new HashMap<>();
m.put(key, "v");
key.add("b");                  // hashCode changes
m.get(key);                    // null: looks in the new bucket
m.containsKey(List.of("a"));   // false: right bucket, but stored key's equals now fails
m.size();                      // 1: the entry leaks, unreachable through lookups

Stored Node.hash is a final copy of the hash at insert time, so resizing also never re-reads hashCode(). Good keys are immutable: String, wrappers, enums, records of immutable values, and UUID.

RefinePoint: ConsumedEvents guards idempotency in the database, but in-memory keys follow the same rule. The gateway's rate-limit keys are plain strings ("ip:" + address, "user:" + subject, "key:" + digest), so the bucket map's keys cannot mutate.

4.7 Iterators and fail-fast behaviour

ArrayList, HashMap and most non-concurrent collections have fail-fast iterators. Each structural change increments modCount. The iterator saves it as expectedModCount on creation, and each next() compares the two.

This has nothing to do with threads, despite its name: one thread is enough. It is best-effort, and is not a concurrency guarantee, since the check is unsynchronised.

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : list) if (s.equals("a")) list.remove(s);   // CME on the next iteration

// The famous exception: removing the second-to-last element does NOT throw
List<String> two = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
for (String s : two) if (s.equals("a")) two.remove(s);     // no CME, and "b" is never visited

The second loop does not throw because after the removal size is 1, and the cursor is 1, so hasNext() returns false, and the check in next() never runs.

Ways to remove while iterating:

list.removeIf(s -> s.startsWith("x"));            // best: O(n), one bulk shift
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();            // explicit iterator
while (it.hasNext()) if (bad(it.next())) it.remove();    // syncs expectedModCount; O(n) each for ArrayList
for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) if (bad(list.get(i))) list.remove(i);  // backwards
map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == null);
Iterator type Collections Behaviour under modification
Fail-fast ArrayList, HashMap, TreeMap Throws CME on a best-effort basis
Weakly consistent ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue Never throws; may or may not show changes
Snapshot CopyOnWriteArrayList Never throws; sees the array at creation; remove unsupported

4.8 Comparable vs Comparator

Comparable<T> Comparator<T>
Package java.lang java.util
Method compareTo(T) compare(T, T)
Where defined In the class itself: the natural order External: any number of orders
Used by TreeMap, Collections.sort(list) list.sort(cmp), TreeMap(cmp), streams 
Comparator<Run> byOrg = Comparator.comparing(Run::orgCode)
    .thenComparing(Run::startedAt, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.reverseOrder()))
    .thenComparingInt(Run::matched);

Rules: be consistent with equals, or a TreeSet will drop elements that compareTo says are equal, as with BigDecimal 2.0 and 2.00. Never subtract to compare: a - b overflows, whereas Integer.compare does not. And a violated contract can make TimSort throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!".

List.sort and Arrays.sort(Object[]) use TimSort, which is stable and O(n log n) with O(n) for nearly sorted data. Arrays.sort(int[]) uses dual-pivot quicksort, which is not stable, because stability is meaningless for primitives.

4.9 Immutable and fixed-size collections

List.of Collections.unmodifiableList(x) Arrays.asList(a) List.copyOf(x) stream.toList()
Add/remove UOE UOE UOE UOE UOE
set UOE UOE Allowed, writes to the array UOE UOE
Reflects source changes n/a Yes, it is a view Yes, it wraps the array No, independent No
Nulls NPE Allowed if source does Allowed NPE Allowed
Truly immutable Yes No No Yes Unmodifiable

(UOE = UnsupportedOperationException.)

List<String> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
List<String> copy = List.copyOf(src);
src.add("b");
view.size();  // 2: the view sees it
copy.size();  // 1

int[] nums = {1, 2};
Arrays.asList(nums).size();   // 1: a List<int[]>, because int is not a reference type
String[] names = {"x"};
List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList(names);
fixed.set(0, "y");            // names[0] is now "y"
List.of("a").contains(null);  // NPE: List.of rejects even a null query

Implementation notes. List.of uses compact classes such as ImmutableCollections.List12 and ListN, with @Stable fields. Set.of and Map.of randomise iteration order with a per-JVM salt, deliberately, so nobody relies on it. They also throw IllegalArgumentException on duplicates, which surprises people who build a Set.of(a, b) from runtime values.

4.10 Collections utility methods

sort, reverse, shuffle, binarySearch (the list must be sorted), frequency, disjoint, nCopies, max, min, swap, rotate, addAll, emptyList, singletonList, unmodifiableX, synchronizedX, and checkedX. Collections.emptyList() returns a shared immutable singleton, so returning it costs no allocation. Prefer returning empty collections over null.

RefinePoint: the engine's SideProcessing presizes its row lists with new ArrayList<>((int) count) when the count is known, as large files would otherwise repeatedly copy a large array. removeIf on entrySet() is how RateLimitFilter and SlidingWindowLimiter evict idle buckets, with no iterator handling.

4.11 Interview questions and answers

Q1. How does HashMap work internally?

HashMap is an array of buckets, where each bucket holds a linked list or, past a threshold, a red-black tree. put spreads the key's hashCode with h ^ h >>> 16, finds the bucket with (n-1) & hash, then compares the stored hash and equals along the bin to replace or append. When size passes capacity × 0.75 the table doubles and entries split between j and j + oldCap. A bin of 8 or more converts to a tree if the table has at least 64 slots; otherwise the table resizes instead. Average get and put are O(1), with O(log n) as the worst case per bin.

Q2. Why is the HashMap capacity always a power of two?

So that hash & (n - 1) can replace the slower %, and so that a resize split can be decided by one bit. It requires the low bits of the hash to be good, which is exactly why the hash is spread with h ^ (h >>> 16). tableSizeFor rounds any requested capacity up to the next power of two.

Q3. Why XOR with the high 16 bits instead of just using hashCode()?

A small table uses only the low bits of the hash, so hash codes that differ only in their high bits would always collide. XOR mixes the high half into the low half, cheaply, so those bits affect the index. XOR is preferred over & and | because it keeps the bits balanced. It's only one shift because trees now handle pathological cases, so a complex hash function is no longer worth it.

Q4. Why is the default load factor 0.75?

A balance of memory against collisions. Higher values fill the table better, but lengthen bins and slow lookups; lower values waste space and resize more. At 0.75 the expected bin length stays well under 1, and the JDK comments give a Poisson estimate of about 0.00000006 for a bin of 8. It is rarely worth changing, and presizing is usually the better tuning.

Q5. What is the threshold? When does a resize happen, and what is the size after new HashMap<>(10)?

Threshold is capacity × loadFactor, and a resize happens when ++size > threshold after an insert. new HashMap<>(10) allocates nothing yet: it stores 16 in threshold, and on the first put allocates a table of 16 with a threshold of 12. The size is still 0, since size counts entries and not slots.

Q6. How many resizes does it take to insert 1,000 items into a default HashMap? How do you avoid them?

Seven: capacity grows 16 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256 → 512 → 1024 → 2048, since 1024 × 0.75 = 768 < 1000. To avoid them, use HashMap.newHashMap(1000) (Java 19+) or new HashMap<>((int) (1000 / 0.75f) + 1).

Q7. What happens on a hash collision?

Keys with the same bucket index chain in that bin: appended at the tail in Java 8+, with each lookup comparing stored hash, then ==, then equals. Note the difference between a hash collision (same hash) and a bucket collision (different hashes, same index). Comparing stored hashes filters out the second kind without calling equals.

Q8. When exactly does a bin convert to a tree? Back to a list?

On inserting into a bin that already has 8 nodes, making it the 9th (binCount >= TREEIFY_THRESHOLD - 1), treeifyBin runs. If the table is under 64, it resizes instead, as spreading entries is cheaper than building trees. It converts back at 6 or fewer during a resize split, and also on removal when the tree becomes very small (its root or close children are null). The 8/6 gap prevents flip-flopping.

Q9. How is a tree bin ordered if keys are not Comparable?

By hash, then by compareTo if the key's class implements Comparable<SameClass>, then by tieBreakOrder (class name and identityHashCode) so that inserts always have a place. On lookup, equal hashes with non-comparable keys force searching both subtrees, which degrades towards O(n). So keys with a poor hash but no Comparable get no real benefit.

Q10. What is a hash flooding attack and how did Java respond?

An attacker crafts many keys with identical hashCode, like form parameter names built from "Aa" and "BB", turning map operations O(n) and a request O(n²), which burns CPU with a tiny payload. Java 8's treeified bins cap it at O(log n), since String is Comparable. Servers also limit parameter counts, as Tomcat does with maxParameterCount.

Q11. Describe the resize in Java 8. Why doesn't it recompute hashes?

It allocates a table of double the size and walks each old bin. Each node's new position depends on one extra bit, so hash & oldCap == 0 keeps it at j, and otherwise it moves to j + oldCap. Stored hashes are reused, so hashCode() isn't called, and two sublists keep their relative order. Tree bins are split the same way, and they untreeify if a side has 6 or fewer.

Q12. Why could a Java 7 HashMap loop forever?

Its resize reversed bin order through head insertion. Two threads resizing at once could produce A.next = B and B.next = A. The next get on that bin spins forever at 100% CPU, which a thread dump shows as a thread stuck in HashMap.get. Java 8 keeps order and avoids this cycle, but concurrent writes still corrupt state.

Q13. Is Java 8 HashMap safe for concurrent use now that the loop is fixed?

No. Concurrent puts can overwrite each other's bucket head, resize can lose entries, size can be wrong (++size is not atomic), and tree bins can throw ClassCastException during concurrent treeify. Visibility is not guaranteed either. If you need concurrent access, use ConcurrentHashMap. A map published once and only read afterwards is safe, if safely published, and Map.copyOf makes that explicit.

Q14. Can HashMap have a null key? Where is it stored?

One null key, with hash 0, so bucket 0, and any number of null values. Because get returns null both for absent keys and null values, use containsKey or getOrDefault with care: getOrDefault returns the stored null, not the default, when the key maps to null.

Q15. Predict the output.

Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
System.out.println(m.put("a", 1));
System.out.println(m.put("a", 2));
System.out.println(m.get("a"));
System.out.println(m.putIfAbsent("a", 3));
System.out.println(m.computeIfPresent("a", (k, v) -> null));
System.out.println(m.size());

null, 1, 2, 2, null, 0. put returns the previous value, putIfAbsent returns the existing value and changes nothing, and a remapping function that returns null removes the entry.

Q16. What happens if two keys are equal but have different hashCodes?

They usually land in different buckets, so the map holds both, and a lookup with a third equal key finds at most one of them. Even in the same bucket, the stored-hash check fails first, so equals is not reached. The contract is violated, and the behaviour looks random, which is why IDE-generated methods and records are the safe default.

Q17. What if hashCode always returns 1?

It's legal, and every entry lands in one bin. Once it reaches 8 entries the table resizes up to 64, and then that bin treeifies. With Comparable keys, lookups are O(log n); without, ties force a search of both subtrees, near O(n). Inserts stay O(log n) only with Comparable keys, since an equality scan is needed otherwise. The map still works correctly, just slowly.

Q18. What happens if you mutate a key after inserting it?

Its stored hash is stale, so a get with the mutated object computes a new bucket and misses. A get with an object equal to the old state finds the bucket but equals fails against the mutated stored key. The entry can't be found but still occupies memory, counts in size, and appears in iteration, which is a real leak. Use immutable keys.

Q19. What makes a good HashMap key? Why is String ideal?

It should be immutable, with consistent equals and hashCode, and a well-distributed hash. String is final and immutable, caches its hash after the first computation, and implements Comparable, so tree bins work well. UUID, wrappers, enums and records of immutable values also fit. Avoid double-based keys, mutable objects, and JPA entities with generated IDs.

Q20. Why not use an enum as a HashMap key?

It works, but EnumMap is better: an array by ordinal, no hashing, smaller and iterating in declaration order. An enum's hashCode is the identity hash, which varies between JVM runs, so HashMap<Status, ...> iteration order can differ between runs, which can make output and tests non-deterministic.

Q21. HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs Collections.synchronizedMap?

HashMap Hashtable synchronizedMap ConcurrentHashMap
Thread safety None One lock on every method One lock, wrapper CAS and per-bin locks
Null key or value Allowed No As the wrapped map No
Iterator Fail-fast Fail-fast, plus legacy Enumeration Fail-fast; caller must lock Weakly consistent
Index hash & (n-1) (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % n, table size prime-ish Same as wrapped map spread & (n-1)
Use HashMap for local use and ConcurrentHashMap for shared use. Hashtable is legacy. Chapter 5 covers CHM.

Q22. HashSet internals: how does it guarantee uniqueness?

It delegates to HashMap, storing each element as a key with a shared PRESENT value. add calls map.put and returns true when the previous value was null. Uniqueness therefore means hashCode + equals, and a duplicate add does not replace the existing element, because put keeps the old key and only overwrites the value.

Q23. Predict the output.

record P(int x) {}
class Q { int x; Q(int x) { this.x = x; } }
Set<Object> s = new HashSet<>();
s.add(new P(1)); s.add(new P(1));
s.add(new Q(1)); s.add(new Q(1));
System.out.println(s.size());

3. Records implement value-based equals and hashCode, so the second P is a duplicate. Q inherits identity equality from Object, so both instances stay.

Q24. How would you find duplicates in a list in O(n)?

Set<T> seen = new HashSet<>(); list.stream().filter(x -> !seen.add(x)).toList(), using the boolean from add. For counts, use Collectors.groupingBy(identity(), counting()), or map.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum). A stateful lambda like that is fine in a sequential stream, but not in a parallel one.

Q25. ArrayList vs LinkedList: which do you use and why?

ArrayList, almost always. Indexing is O(1), iteration is cache-friendly, and memory overhead is low. LinkedList theoretically wins at inserts in the middle, but finding the position is O(n) pointer chasing. In practice it loses benchmarks even in many "insert heavy" scenarios. It's only useful with a long-held ListIterator, and for queue or stack use ArrayDeque is faster.

Q26. How does ArrayList grow? What is its amortised cost?

On overflow, it allocates old + old >> 1 (1.5x) and copies with Arrays.copyOf. The first add to a default list allocates capacity 10. Appends are amortised O(1), since doubling-style growth keeps total copying linear in n. For a known size, presize to skip the copies: a list growing to 1 million elements from the default makes about 28 copies and much garbage.

Q27. Is the default capacity of ArrayList allocated when it is created?

No. Since Java 8 new ArrayList<>() points at a shared empty array and allocates 10 on the first add. new ArrayList<>(0) uses a different empty array, and grows 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 6 and so on, which is worse if the list does get filled. This matters for classes that create many mostly empty lists.

Q28. How is an ArrayList serialised? Why is elementData transient?

The array usually has unused capacity. writeObject writes size and only the live elements, and readObject allocates exactly that many. It avoids serialising nulls. The same reasoning applies to HashMap, whose table is transient too, and which writes pairs and rebuilds on read, as hash codes may differ between JVMs.

Q29. Does removing elements shrink an ArrayList?

No. remove shifts and nulls the last slot, but capacity stays. A list that peaked at 1M elements holds that array until trimToSize() or until the list is discarded. In a long-lived cache or buffer, that shows up in heap dumps as a huge Object[] that is mostly nulls. Replace the list, or call trimToSize after large removals.

Q30. Predict the output.

List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
a.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));
a.remove(0);
a.add(0, 5);
System.out.println(a);

[5, 30]. Removing the value 10 leaves [20, 30], removing index 0 leaves [30], and inserting at 0 gives [5, 30].

Q31. What is RandomAccess?

A marker interface saying that indexed access is fast. Generic algorithms use it to pick a strategy: Collections.shuffle, binarySearch and others use get(i) on RandomAccess lists, and iterators otherwise. Calling list.get(i) in a loop on a LinkedList is O(n²), which is the kind of hidden cost this avoids.

Q32. What is Arrays.asList and what are its traps?

It returns a fixed-size list backed by the array, a private nested class named Arrays.ArrayList, not java.util.ArrayList. set writes through, while add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. With an int[], you get a single-element List<int[]>. For a growable list use new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(a)), and for an immutable one use List.of(a).

Q33. List.of vs Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf?

List.of creates a new immutable list and rejects nulls. unmodifiableList is a read-only view, so changes to the source show through. List.copyOf makes an immutable copy, and returns the same instance if the input is already an immutable list, so it is cheap to use defensively. A public API should take List.copyOf of input it stores.

Q34. What does list.subList return? What is the trap?

A view on the parent, so list.subList(0, 10).clear() removes from the parent efficiently. Trap one: structurally modifying the parent afterwards makes the view throw ConcurrentModificationException. Trap two: holding a small sublist of a huge list keeps the whole list reachable. Copy it with new ArrayList<>(sub) if it outlives the operation.

Q35. What is a ConcurrentModificationException? Does it need multiple threads?

It is thrown when a fail-fast iterator sees modCount differ from its saved copy. No threads are needed: modifying a list inside a for-each over it is the common cause. It is best-effort and may not fire at all, so never rely on it for correctness.

Q36. Why doesn't removing the second-last element throw CME?
