For-each calls hasNext() before next(), and hasNext() is simply cursor != size. After the removal size is one smaller and equals cursor, so the loop ends without calling next(), where the check lives, and the last element is silently skipped. It is a good demonstration that fail-fast is not guaranteed.

Q37. How do you safely remove while iterating?

Best is collection.removeIf(predicate), which is one O(n) pass for ArrayList. Other options: Iterator.remove, which updates expectedModCount but shifts each time and is O(n²) overall for many removals in a large list; an index loop running backward; or building a new list using a stream filter. For maps, entrySet().removeIf(...), or keySet().removeAll(...).

Q38. Does a concurrent read during HashMap.put cause CME?

No. CME comes only from iterators, not from get. A concurrent get may simply miss an entry or read stale data. Without synchronisation there's no guarantee it sees the latest value at all, which is why races can pass tests but fail in production.

Q39. Why does map.put(existingKey, newValue) during iteration not throw?

Replacing a value is not a structural change, so modCount doesn't change. Adding a new key does. Map.Entry.setValue is also safe, and is the proper way to update values while iterating. compute and merge on HashMap detect changes: a mapping function that modifies the map throws CME on Java 9+.

Q40. What do fail-fast, fail-safe and weakly consistent mean?

Fail-fast iterators throw on detecting a change (ArrayList, HashMap). "Fail-safe" is an informal term for iterators that never throw, working on a copy or tolerating changes. Javadoc distinguishes snapshot (CopyOnWriteArrayList, frozen at creation) from weakly consistent (ConcurrentHashMap: reflects some changes, each element returned at most once).

Q41. Comparable vs Comparator: how do you choose?

Comparable defines the type's single natural order, when one obvious ordering exists (dates, money), and compareTo should be consistent with equals. Comparator is for alternative orders, chained with comparing and thenComparing. Comparators can also order types you don't own. Null handling should be explicit with nullsFirst and nullsLast.

Q42. Why is return a.x - b.x a bug in a comparator?

Integer subtraction overflows for values of large magnitude: Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1 becomes positive, inverting the order, and also breaking transitivity. Use Integer.compare, Long.compare, or Comparator.comparingInt. For doubles, use Double.compare, since it handles NaN and -0.0.

Q43. What does "Comparison method violates its general contract" mean?

TimSort detected an inconsistent comparator while merging: for example, a non-transitive one, or one that returns random values or reads mutable state. It only fails on some inputs, usually with 32 or more elements, so it surfaces in production and not in small tests. Fix the comparator, using Comparator.comparing chains and consistent null handling.

Q44. Why does a TreeSet drop elements that equals says are different?

TreeSet uses compareTo or the comparator for identity, not equals. A comparator on name alone treats two people with the same name as duplicates. new TreeSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("2.0"), new BigDecimal("2.00"))) has one element, while a HashSet of the same keeps two. Keep the comparator consistent with equals, or understand that consequence.

Q45. Which sorting algorithm does Java use?

Arrays.sort(Object[]), List.sort and Collections.sort use TimSort, a stable merge and insertion hybrid that takes advantage of existing runs. Primitive arrays use dual-pivot quicksort, with fallbacks such as heap sort on bad input since Java 14; stability doesn't matter there. parallelSort splits work over the common fork-join pool. ArrayList.sort sorts its array in place and bumps modCount.

Q46. ArrayDeque vs Stack vs LinkedList as a stack or queue?

ArrayDeque: a circular array with no per-element allocation, usually the fastest, but no nulls. Stack: synchronised and legacy, and inherits Vector's index methods, breaking LIFO. LinkedList: allocates a node per element, but allows nulls. Note that Deque.push adds at the front, so iteration runs LIFO, the reverse of Stack's iteration order.

Q47. Why was Vector replaced?

Every method synchronises, so uncontended calls still pay, while compound actions like if (!v.contains(x)) v.add(x) still race. It also doubles rather than growing 1.5x. Modern alternatives are ArrayList with explicit locking, CopyOnWriteArrayList, or a concurrent queue.

Q48. What is the difference between size() and capacity? Can you read a list's capacity?

Size counts elements and capacity is the array's length. ArrayList has no public capacity accessor. get(i) with i >= size throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, even when capacity is sufficient.

Q49. Iterator vs ListIterator vs Spliterator?

Iterator moves forward and removes. ListIterator moves both ways, with indices, set and add. Spliterator (Java 8) supports trySplit for parallel streams, plus characteristics like SIZED, ORDERED and DISTINCT that let streams skip work. ArrayList's splitter divides the array range in half, which is why it parallelises much better than LinkedList.

Q50. Are keySet(), values() and entrySet() copies?

No. They are live views created lazily and cached in the map. map.keySet().remove(k) removes from the map, while add throws UnsupportedOperationException. To keep a stable snapshot, copy with List.copyOf(map.keySet()).

Q51. How do you iterate a map efficiently?

Use entrySet() or map.forEach((k, v) -> ...). Iterating keySet() and calling get per key hashes each key a second time, wasting CPU. All iteration is O(capacity + size), so a HashMap that once grew huge and then shrank iterates slowly even when nearly empty, as remove never shrinks the table. Create a new map to compact.

Q52. What does computeIfAbsent do, and why does it beat get-then-put?

It returns the existing value, or computes, stores and returns a new one, with one hash lookup. map.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(v) is the idiomatic multimap. On a HashMap, the function must not modify the map, or it throws ConcurrentModificationException since Java 9. A function that returns null stores nothing.

Q53. merge vs compute?

merge(key, value, fn) puts value when absent, and otherwise applies fn(old, value), removing if it returns null. It suits counters: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum). compute(key, fn) always runs with the key and its possibly null value, for more general updates.

Q54. How do you create an unmodifiable map from an existing map? Why might Map.of fail at runtime?

Map.copyOf(m) for an independent copy, or Collections.unmodifiableMap(m) for a view. Map.of takes up to 10 pairs, with Map.ofEntries for more. It throws IllegalArgumentException on duplicate keys and NullPointerException on nulls, which can break at runtime when the keys come from variables rather than literals.

Q55. Why does HashMap's iteration order change between runs with enum or object keys, but stay stable with String keys?

Order depends on hash codes and table size. String.hashCode is defined by a stable formula. Object.hashCode and hence enum hash codes are identity-based and vary per JVM. Even so, never rely on the order with String keys, since it changes with table size and across JDK releases.

Q56. How much memory does a HashMap use, and how would you reduce it?

Each entry costs a Node of about 32 bytes with compressed oops, plus a table slot of 4 bytes (roughly 5–8 with unused capacity), plus the key and value objects. A HashMap<Long, Long> costs on the order of 80–100 bytes per entry to hold 16 bytes of real data. For huge maps use primitive collections (fastutil, Eclipse Collections, Agrona), arrays with sorted keys, or off-heap storage. Or, as RefinePoint does for large files, process the data in DuckDB instead of on the Java heap.

Q57. A service's p99 latency spikes periodically. How could a HashMap be involved?

Resizing a very large map copies and reallocates on a single put, so an ever-growing cache causes spikes and growing GC pressure from a huge table array, which may be a humongous allocation in G1. A map with poor hashing may show slow lookups, visible in a profiler as TreeNode.find or equals. Check with JFR or async-profiler, then presize, bound the cache, or use a concurrent one like Caffeine.

Q58. A thread dump shows threads stuck in HashMap.get at 100% CPU. What is happening?

On Java 7 or earlier, a concurrent resize created a cycle. On Java 8+, unsynchronised concurrent use can still produce a corrupted tree bin that loops in TreeNode methods such as balanceInsertion or root(). Either way the cause is a shared HashMap written by several threads. Restart to recover, then replace it with ConcurrentHashMap and find the sharing, commonly a singleton Spring bean with a map field.

Q59. You see OutOfMemoryError, and a heap dump shows one huge HashMap. What do you check?

Whether it's an unbounded cache with no eviction, a key that does not implement equals/hashCode so that "same" keys accumulate, or mutable keys leaking entries. Look at its retained size in Eclipse MAT, and the actual key values, then cap it with TtlCache-style limits, Caffeine, or a LinkedHashMap LRU. Static collections and singleton beans are the typical holders.

Q60. How does Collections.synchronizedList handle iteration?

Individual methods lock a mutex, but iteration doesn't, so the caller must wrap it: synchronized (list) { for (var x : list) ... }, or else it can throw CME. The same goes for compound actions. This is the core reason concurrent collections exist.

Q61. How did you use these collections in your project?

"In FxRates we build a HashMap<String, TreeMap<LocalDate, BigDecimal>> keyed by currency pair, using computeIfAbsent to create the inner map. In the engine, row lists are presized to the known count. The gateway's rate limiter uses a ConcurrentHashMap of string keys, evicting idle entries with entrySet().removeIf, and the rule parser's cache is a bounded LinkedHashMap. The general rule I follow is that key types are immutable, sizes are known up front where possible, and each cache has a bound."

5. Collections Internals II: Sorted, Linked, Concurrent & Specialised

Chapter 4 covered the collections everybody uses. This chapter covers the ones that separate a senior engineer: the sorted maps, the linked and reference-based maps, the heap behind PriorityQueue, the blocking queues behind every thread pool, and ConcurrentHashMap, whose Java 8 rewrite is one of the most-asked internals questions after HashMap itself. It ends with a decision table and with the concurrent structures RefinePoint actually runs: rate-limit buckets, a TTL cache, a sliding-window limiter and LRU caches.

5.1 TreeMap and the red-black tree

TreeMap is a red-black tree, a self-balancing binary search tree. Each Entry holds key, value, left, right, parent and a color boolean. Keys are ordered by compareTo or by the comparator passed to the constructor, and the comparator defines equality: equals is never called.

The red-black rules keep the tree balanced:

  1. Every node is red or black, and the root is black.
  2. A red node has no red child.
  3. Every path from a node down to its null leaves passes the same number of black nodes (the black height).

Together these guarantee that the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log2(n + 1), and get, put and remove are O(log n) in the worst case, not just on average.

Insertion: insert as in a plain binary search tree, colour the new node red, then repair. If the parent is red, either recolour (the uncle is red: push the blackness down from the grandparent) or rotate (the uncle is black: at most two rotations). Deletion needs at most three rotations. Rotations change a few pointers, so they are O(1); recolouring can walk up the tree, which is O(log n).

Operation TreeMap HashMap
get / put / remove O(log n) worst case O(1) average
Ordered iteration Yes, in key order No
Range queries, floor and ceiling Yes No
Memory per entry ~40 bytes plus key and value ~32 bytes plus table slot
Null key No with natural order (NPE); a comparator may allow it One allowed
Key needs Comparable or a comparator equals and hashCode

Since Java 7, the first put into an empty TreeMap calls compare(key, key), so a non-comparable or null key fails immediately instead of on the second insert.

NavigableMap

TreeMap implements NavigableMap (Java 6), which adds the operations that make sorted maps worth their cost:

NavigableMap<LocalDate, BigDecimal> rates = new TreeMap<>();
rates.floorEntry(date);        // greatest key <= date ("rate on or before")
rates.ceilingKey(date);        // least key >= date
rates.lowerKey(date);          // strictly less
rates.higherKey(date);         // strictly greater
rates.headMap(date, true);     // view of keys <= date
rates.tailMap(date, false);    // view of keys > date
rates.subMap(from, true, to, false);
rates.descendingMap();         // reverse-order view
rates.pollFirstEntry();        // remove and return the smallest

Range views are live: they write through to the map, and inserting a key outside a view's range through that view throws IllegalArgumentException.

RefinePoint: FxRates.of(quotes) builds a HashMap<String, TreeMap<LocalDate, BigDecimal>>, one tree per currency pair, and answers "the rate on or before this date" with floorEntry(date). A rate published on Friday is the right rate for a Sunday transaction, and the lookup is O(log n) without any scanning. Elsewhere, RowChecker uses new TreeMap<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER) so that field names match regardless of case, and JobRegistry keeps handlers in a TreeMap so that the job list always appears in the same order.

TreeSet is backed by a TreeMap exactly as HashSet is backed by a HashMap.

5.2 LinkedHashMap and the LRU cache

LinkedHashMap extends HashMap and threads a doubly linked list through all its entries. Its Entry extends HashMap.Node with before and after pointers, and the map keeps head and tail. Buckets still give O(1) lookup, and the list gives predictable iteration order.

Mode Constructor Order Use
Insertion order (default) new LinkedHashMap<>() Order keys were first inserted; re-putting a key does not move it Predictable JSON, reports, stable output
Access order new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) Least recently accessed first; get, put, getOrDefault, compute move the entry to the tail LRU caches

HashMap calls three hooks that LinkedHashMap overrides: afterNodeAccess (move to tail in access order), afterNodeInsertion (offer eviction) and afterNodeRemoval (unlink). After each insertion it calls removeEldestEntry(head), which returns false by default. Override it and you have an LRU cache:

// Real, from ryfn-expression's ExpressionEngine: parsed rules cached by rule text
private final Map<String, Parsed> cache = Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<>(256, 0.75f, true) {
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, Parsed> eldest) {
        return size() > CACHE;      // CACHE = 2000
    }
});

RefinePoint: parsing a rule (lexer, parser, AST, compile) is far more expensive than looking it up, and a run evaluates the same few rules millions of times. The access-ordered LinkedHashMap keeps the 2,000 most recently used parsed rules, and ai-service's SchemaInsightService uses the same pattern for schema insights. Both are wrapped in Collections.synchronizedMap because they are singleton beans called from many request threads.

Trap: in access-order mode get is a structural modification: it relinks the list and increments modCount. Iterating over the map while calling get throws ConcurrentModificationException, and two threads calling get on an unsynchronised access-ordered map can corrupt the list. That is why the wrapper above is not optional. For a heavily concurrent cache, use Caffeine, which approximates LRU (W-TinyLFU) without a global lock.

5.3 IdentityHashMap, WeakHashMap and EnumMap

IdentityHashMap compares keys with == and hashes with System.identityHashCode, deliberately breaking the Map contract. Internally it uses open addressing with linear probing in a single Object[] in which keys and values alternate (table[i] is a key, table[i + 1] its value), so there are no entry objects. Uses: graph algorithms that must track visited objects (serialisers, deep-copy, proxies), where two equal-but-distinct objects must count separately, and where calling equals on every node would be slow or wrong.

RefinePoint: the engine's Controls deduplicates matched groups with Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()). A group is a List<Rec> shared by every record in it, so "have I seen this group?" is an identity question. A HashSet<List<Rec>> would hash and compare whole lists, element by element, for every record.

WeakHashMap holds its keys through WeakReferences registered with a ReferenceQueue. When a key is no longer strongly reachable, the GC clears the reference, and the next map operation calls expungeStaleEntries(), which removes the entry.

Traps: values are held strongly, so a value that refers to its own key keeps the key alive forever; String literals and small boxed integers are always reachable (the pool and caches hold them), so they never disappear; and it is not thread-safe. ThreadLocal's internal ThreadLocalMap uses the same weak-key idea, with the same trap for values, which is the root of the classic thread-pool ThreadLocal leak. For caches, weak keys are rarely what you want; use Caffeine with size and expiry bounds.

EnumMap (covered in chapter 3) is an array indexed by ordinal(): no hashing, no entries, iteration in declaration order, no null keys. Use it whenever the keys are an enum.

5.4 PriorityQueue: a binary heap in an array

PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap stored in Object[] queue. The smallest element (by natural order or comparator) is at index 0, and each parent is no greater than its children. No pointers are needed:

parent(i) = (i - 1) >>> 1       left(i) = 2i + 1       right(i) = 2i + 2

array:  [ 2 | 5 | 3 | 9 | 7 | 4 ]
index:    0   1   2   3   4   5
Operation Cost How
offer / add O(log n) Append at the end, sift up while smaller than the parent
poll O(log n) Take index 0, move the last element there, sift down by swapping with the smaller child
peek O(1) Index 0
remove(Object), contains O(n) Linear scan
Build from a collection O(n) Floyd's heapify, sifting down from the middle

Iteration is not sorted: the iterator walks the array, which is only partially ordered. Printing a PriorityQueue shows heap order, a favourite output-prediction trick. To consume in order, poll repeatedly. Nulls are rejected, and the queue is not thread-safe; PriorityBlockingQueue is the concurrent version. Capacity starts at 11 and grows by doubling while small (under 64), then by 50%.

Top-K pattern: to keep the k largest of n items, use a min-heap of size k. Offer each item, and when the size exceeds k, poll the smallest. That is O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, instead of sorting everything.

PriorityQueue<Break> top = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(Break::absAmount));
for (Break b : breaks) {
    top.offer(b);
    if (top.size() > 10) top.poll();          // drop the smallest of the 11
}

5.5 The BlockingQueue family

A BlockingQueue adds operations that wait for space or for an element, which makes it the standard way to connect producers and consumers, and the work queue inside every ThreadPoolExecutor.

Throws Returns special value Blocks Times out
Insert add(e) offer(e) returns false put(e) offer(e, time, unit)
Remove remove() poll() returns null take() poll(time, unit)
Examine element() peek() n/a n/a

No BlockingQueue accepts null, because null is the "nothing there" value of poll.

Implementation Bounded Internals Notes
ArrayBlockingQueue Yes, fixed at creation Circular array, one ReentrantLock, conditions notEmpty and notFull Optional fairness; predictable memory; producers and consumers contend on one lock
LinkedBlockingQueue Optional, default Integer.MAX_VALUE Linked nodes, two locks (putLock, takeLock), AtomicInteger count Producers and consumers rarely block each other, so higher throughput; one node allocated per element
SynchronousQueue Capacity zero Direct hand-off; each put waits for a take Used by Executors.newCachedThreadPool
PriorityBlockingQueue No Array heap under one lock take returns the smallest; put never blocks
DelayQueue No PriorityQueue of Delayed elements plus a leader thread take returns an element only once its delay has expired
LinkedTransferQueue No Lock-free dual queue transfer(e) waits until a consumer receives it
LinkedBlockingDeque Optional Linked, one lock Blocking at both ends; work stealing designs

The DelayQueue leader pattern: only one thread (the leader) waits with a timed awaitNanos for the head's delay; other takers wait indefinitely. When the head expires, the leader takes it and signals the next waiter to become leader. That avoids every waiting thread waking up for the same deadline.

How the queue shapes a ThreadPoolExecutor: the pool grows to corePoolSize, then queues, and only creates threads beyond the core (up to maximumPoolSize) when offer to the queue fails. Consequences:

  • With an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue (what Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses), maximumPoolSize is never used, and a slow consumer lets the queue grow until OutOfMemoryError.
  • With a SynchronousQueue (what newCachedThreadPool uses), every task that finds no idle thread creates a new one, which is unbounded threads instead.
  • In production, use a bounded queue with an explicit rejection policy (CallerRunsPolicy gives natural back-pressure).

RefinePoint: the durable work queues (runs, jobs, exports, data-source refreshes) are PostgreSQL tables claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, not in-memory BlockingQueues. A queue in the heap disappears on restart and cannot be shared by several instances; a table survives both, and adding instances adds consumers. In memory, each worker only tracks what it is running, in a ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() of run IDs, checked against its slot count before it claims more.

5.6 ConcurrentHashMap internals

Java 7: segments

Java 7's map was an array of Segments, each a small hash table that extended ReentrantLock. A write locked one segment, so up to concurrencyLevel (default 16) writers could proceed in parallel; reads were mostly lock-free through volatile fields. size() summed the segments twice without locking, compared their modCounts, and on disagreement locked every segment. The concurrency level was fixed at creation, and each segment cost memory even when empty.

Java 8: CAS plus per-bin locks

Java 8 rewrote it on the same table-of-bins layout as HashMap, with the lock granularity reduced to one bin:

  • Empty bin: insert with a single CAS (casTabAt), with no lock at all.
  • Non-empty bin: synchronized on the bin's first node, then walk the list or tree as HashMap does. Two writers conflict only if they hit the same bin.
  • Reads take no lock. table is volatile, each Node's val and next are volatile, and bins are read with acquire semantics (tabAt). A get sees a fully constructed node or none.
  • Negative hashes are reserved for special nodes: MOVED = -1 (a ForwardingNode during resize), TREEBIN = -2 (the head of a treeified bin), RESERVED = -3 (a placeholder used by computeIfAbsent and compute). spread(h) is (h ^ (h >>> 16)) & 0x7fffffff, so user hashes are never negative.
  • Tree bins use the same 8 and 64 thresholds as HashMap, but are wrapped in a TreeBin with its own small read-write lock, so that readers can fall back to walking the next links while a writer is rebalancing.

sizeCtl

One volatile int coordinates initialisation and resizing:

Value Meaning
0 Table not created yet; use the default capacity of 16
Positive, before initialisation The initial capacity to use
Positive, after initialisation The next resize threshold, n - (n >>> 2), which is 0.75n
-1 A thread is initialising the table
Other negative A resize is in progress: the high bits hold a resize stamp for this table size, the low bits one more than the number of resizing threads

Resize: transfer and helping

Resizing is done cooperatively. The thread that crosses the threshold allocates nextTable (double size) and starts moving bins from the highest index downwards, claiming a stride of bins at a time through a CAS on transferIndex (at least 16 bins per claim). Every moved bin is replaced with a ForwardingNode pointing at the new table.

Each bin is split into a low and a high list exactly as in HashMap (hash & n), with a lastRun optimisation that reuses the unchanged tail of the list. Readers are never blocked: a get that hits a ForwardingNode simply continues its search in the new table. Writers that hit one help with the transfer instead of waiting, so a resize under heavy write load is finished by all writers together.

Counting: baseCount and CounterCells

A single AtomicLong size would make every insert contend on one memory location. addCount first tries a CAS on baseCount; if that fails because of contention, it adds to one of an array of CounterCells (padded with @Contended against false sharing), chosen by a per-thread probe value. That is the same design as LongAdder. size() and mappingCount() return baseCount plus the sum of all cells, which is an estimate under concurrent updates. mappingCount() returns a long and is preferred; size() caps at Integer.MAX_VALUE.

Why no nulls?

In a concurrent map, get(k) == null could mean "absent" or "mapped to null", and the usual way to tell, containsKey(k), is a second call that can race with another thread's change. Banning nulls makes null an unambiguous "absent", which is what putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent and getOrDefault rely on. Doug Lea has also said that allowing nulls even in non-concurrent maps was a mistake.

Atomic compound operations

Individual operations are thread-safe, but a sequence of them is not:

if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);           // race: two threads both put
map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1);                       // race: lost updates

map.putIfAbsent(k, v);                             // atomic
map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum);                     // atomic increment
map.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new LongAdder()).increment();   // best for hot counters
map.replace(k, expectedOld, newValue);             // compare-and-set per key

computeIfAbsent pitfalls

computeIfAbsent guarantees that the function runs at most once per absent key. It does that by holding the bin lock (or a ReservationNode in an empty bin) while the function runs. Consequences:

  1. A slow function blocks other keys. Every other write that hashes to the same bin waits, and so does any thread computing the same key. Never do network I/O or database calls inside it.
  2. No recursive updates. A function that modifies the same map (for example, a memoised recursive Fibonacci) can deadlock or corrupt the map. Java 8 could spin forever (JDK-8062841); Java 9+ detects most cases and throws IllegalStateException("Recursive update").
  3. Java 8 locked even on a hit. It took the bin lock when the key was already present. Java 9 checks the first node of the bin without locking, and a get first is still a cheap fast path for hot keys on Java 8.
  4. Returning null stores nothing, so the function will run again on the next call.

Weakly consistent iteration and bulk operations

Iterators and the keySet, values and entrySet views are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException, they traverse elements as they existed at some point since the iterator was created, they may or may not reflect later updates, and they return each element at most once. putAll and clear are not atomic. Java 8 added parallel bulk operations, forEach, search, reduce and their typed variants, which take a parallelismThreshold and run on the common fork-join pool. ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() gives a concurrent Set.

5.7 CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentSkipListMap and the other concurrent collections

CopyOnWriteArrayList holds a volatile Object[]. Every write takes a lock, copies the whole array, modifies the copy and publishes it with one volatile write. Reads and iteration take no lock and work on whatever array they started with, so the iterator is a snapshot: it never throws CME, never sees later changes, and does not support remove.

Reads Writes Iteration Best for
CopyOnWriteArrayList Lock-free, O(1) O(n) copy under a lock Snapshot Listener lists, configuration: read very often, written rarely
Collections.synchronizedList Locked Locked, O(1) amortised Must lock manually Moderate, balanced access

A list of 100,000 elements written 1,000 times a second copies 100 million references a second: it is the wrong tool for write-heavy lists. CopyOnWriteArraySet is backed by a CopyOnWriteArrayList, so contains is O(n).

ConcurrentSkipListMap is a concurrent, sorted NavigableMap, built as a skip list: a sorted linked list of nodes, plus layers of index lists that skip over progressively more nodes. Each level is chosen randomly, giving expected O(log n) search, and all updates use CAS, with no locks. Nothing equivalent can be built from a red-black tree without locking, because a rebalancing rotation touches several nodes at once.

level 3:  head ------------------------------> 50 ---------------------> null
level 2:  head ---------> 20 ----------------> 50 --------> 80 --------> null
level 1:  head -> 10 ---> 20 ---> 30 -------> 50 -> 60 --> 80 -> 90 --> null
search 60: level 3 to 50, level 2 to 50 (80 too far), level 1 to 60

Use it for concurrent ordered data: leaderboards, time-ordered indexes, "next deadline" maps. ConcurrentSkipListSet is the set version. Its size() is only an estimate while other threads update it, and nulls are not allowed.

Others: ConcurrentLinkedQueue (lock-free Michael-Scott queue; size() is O(n)), ConcurrentLinkedDeque, and the blocking queues of section 5.5.

Collections.synchronizedX vs concurrent collections

Collections.synchronizedMap(m) ConcurrentHashMap
Locking One mutex for every call CAS and per-bin locks; reads lock-free
Read scalability Readers block each other Readers never block
Iteration Fail-fast; caller must hold synchronized (map) Weakly consistent; no lock needed
Compound actions Caller holds the mutex around them Atomic methods (compute, merge, …)
Nulls As the wrapped map Not allowed
Wraps any map Yes, for example a LinkedHashMap LRU No, it is its own structure

The wrapper is still the right choice when you need the behaviour of a specific map, like the LRU ordering of LinkedHashMap, and contention is modest.

5.8 Java 21 sequenced collections

Before Java 21, getting the last element was different for each type: list.get(list.size() - 1), deque.getLast(), sortedSet.last(), and for a LinkedHashSet there was no direct way at all. JEP 431 added three interfaces that give every collection with a defined encounter order one API:

Interface Methods
SequencedCollection<E> addFirst, addLast, getFirst, getLast, removeFirst, removeLast, reversed()
SequencedSet<E> Same, with reversed() returning a SequencedSet
SequencedMap<K,V> firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, putFirst, putLast, sequencedKeySet, sequencedValues, sequencedEntrySet, reversed()

Facts that interviewers check:

  • reversed() returns a view, not a copy, so writes through it reach the original.
  • getFirst() on an empty collection throws NoSuchElementException, unlike peekFirst().
  • Sorted collections reject addFirst, addLast, putFirst and putLast with UnsupportedOperationException, because the comparator decides the position.
  • LinkedHashMap.putFirst and putLast move an existing key; LinkedHashSet.addFirst moves an existing element to the front.
  • HashMap, HashSet and PriorityQueue are not sequenced, because they have no defined order.
  • Collections.unmodifiableSequencedCollection, unmodifiableSequencedSet and unmodifiableSequencedMap were added too.
LinkedHashMap<String, Integer> steps = new LinkedHashMap<>();
steps.put("load", 1); steps.put("match", 2); steps.put("report", 3);
steps.firstEntry();            // load=1
steps.pollLastEntry();         // removes report=3
steps.putFirst("validate", 0); // validate now comes first
steps.reversed().keySet();     // [match, load, validate]

5.9 Choosing the right collection

Need Single thread Shared between threads
Fast lookup by key HashMap ConcurrentHashMap
Sorted keys, ranges, floor and ceiling TreeMap ConcurrentSkipListMap
Insertion order LinkedHashMap / LinkedHashSet Collections.synchronizedMap(new LinkedHashMap<>())
LRU cache LinkedHashMap with access order Caffeine, or a synchronised LinkedHashMap at low contention
Enum keys or elements EnumMap / EnumSet Wrap with synchronizedMap, or a ConcurrentHashMap
Unique elements HashSet ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()
List read often, written rarely ArrayList CopyOnWriteArrayList
Stack or queue ArrayDeque ConcurrentLinkedQueue / ConcurrentLinkedDeque
Producer-consumer with back-pressure n/a ArrayBlockingQueue / bounded LinkedBlockingQueue
Priority order PriorityQueue PriorityBlockingQueue
Run at a later time n/a DelayQueue, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor
Identity semantics IdentityHashMap Rarely needed
Entries that vanish with their key WeakHashMap Caffeine weakKeys()

5.10 RefinePoint: concurrent collections in production code

Gateway rate limiting: token buckets in a ConcurrentHashMap

api-gateway's RateLimitFilter limits each caller per minute: an API key (300 by default), a signed-in user identified by the token's subject (900), and every IP address (1,800). Each limit is a token bucket that holds a minute's requests and refills continuously.

private final Map<String, Bucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Bucket byAddress = buckets.computeIfAbsent("ip:" + address, k -> new Bucket(perAddress, now));
Bucket own = caller == null ? byAddress : buckets.computeIfAbsent(caller, k -> new Bucket(limit, now));
long wait = Math.max(own.take(now), own == byAddress ? 0 : byAddress.take(now));

static final class Bucket {
    private double tokens; private long last;           // guarded by the bucket's monitor
    synchronized long take(long now) {
        refill(now);                                     // tokens += elapsed * perNano, capped
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return 0; }
        return (long) Math.ceil((1 - tokens) / perNano); // nanoseconds until a token is due
    }
}

Why it is built this way:

  • Two levels of concurrency. The map only finds or creates the bucket, and computeIfAbsent guarantees one bucket per key even when the first requests arrive together. The arithmetic on the bucket is guarded by the bucket's own monitor, so callers with different keys never contend with each other, and the critical section is a few floating-point operations.
  • The construction is cheap, so holding the bin lock inside computeIfAbsent is harmless here.
  • Bounded memory. Every 10,000 calls, buckets.entrySet().removeIf(...) drops buckets idle for over 10 minutes. Weakly consistent iteration means it never throws, even with requests arriving during the sweep.
  • A known, accepted race. A sweep can remove a bucket that a concurrent request has just fetched. That request takes from a detached bucket, and the next one creates a fresh full bucket, so the limit is briefly lenient for one caller who had been idle for ten minutes. Making it exact would need a lock around every lookup, which isn't worth it.
  • Per instance. The buckets live in one gateway's heap, so with several gateways each limits what passes through it. A shared limit would need Redis or similar.

TtlCache: why it does not use computeIfAbsent

ryfn-platform's TtlCache caches answers fetched from other services (access decisions, plan limits, API keys) with an expiry time:

public V get(K key, Supplier<V> loader) {
    long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
    Entry<V> entry = entries.get(key);
    if (entry != null && entry.expiresAt() > now) return entry.value();
    V value = loader.get();                                   // remote call, outside any lock
    if (ttlMillis > 0) {
        if (entries.size() >= maxEntries) entries.clear();    // crude but safe bound
        entries.put(key, new Entry<>(value, now + ttlMillis));
    }
    return value;
}

The loader is an HTTP call to another service. Inside computeIfAbsent it would run while holding a bin lock, so one slow call would block every other key in that bin. The trade-off is explicit: two threads that miss at the same moment may both call the loader, which is harmless because the loads are idempotent reads. Clearing the whole map when it is full is cruder than LRU eviction, but it can never grow without bound, and the cost of a clear is only a few extra calls.

SlidingWindowLimiter: a Deque per key

For limits like AI requests per user per hour and per workspace per day (UsageLimits in ryfn-platform), SSO lookups, and the public try-it import and confirmation pages, SlidingWindowLimiter keeps the timestamps of recent calls per key:

private final Map<String, Deque<Long>> calls = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Deque<Long> window = calls.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayDeque<>());
synchronized (window) {
    while (!window.isEmpty() && now - window.peekFirst() >= windowMillis) window.pollFirst();
    if (window.size() >= max) throw new RateLimitExceededException(..., retryAfterSeconds);
    window.addLast(now);
}
if (calls.size() > 10_000) evictIdle(now);

ArrayDeque fits exactly: new timestamps go on the tail and expired ones leave from the head, both O(1), with no node allocation. ArrayDeque is not thread-safe, so each deque is used only under its own monitor, which again limits contention to one key. Compared with a token bucket, a sliding log is exact (never more than max calls in any window), at the cost of storing up to max timestamps per key, which is fine for small limits like hourly AI quotas. The same idea appears in PublicContactController, which keeps a Deque<Instant> per sender to throttle the public contact form.

Other small patterns from the codebase

Code Collection Why
RunWorker, ExportWorker, RefreshWorker ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() of IDs Track in-flight work on this instance; compare with slot count before claiming more
InboxStream ConcurrentHashMap<String, Set<SseEmitter>>, inner sets from newKeySet() One user can have several open browser tabs; emitters are added and removed from different threads
BankFeedService locks.computeIfAbsent(consentId, k -> new Object()) with synchronized Per-key locking: refreshes of the same bank consent are serialised, different consents run in parallel
ExpressionEngine, SchemaInsightService Synchronised access-order LinkedHashMap Bounded LRU caches
FxRates TreeMap.floorEntry Rate on or before a date
Controls newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()) Visit each shared group object once

5.11 Interview questions and answers

Q1. How does TreeMap work internally?

It is a red-black tree: a binary search tree ordered by compareTo or a comparator, where node colours and three rules keep the height at most 2 log2(n + 1). get, put and remove are O(log n) in the worst case. Inserts add a red leaf, then fix any red-red violation by recolouring or by at most two rotations. Equality is decided by the comparator returning 0, never by equals.

Q2. Why a red-black tree and not an AVL tree?

AVL trees are more strictly balanced (height about 1.44 log n), so lookups are slightly faster, but inserts and deletes rotate more often. Red-black trees need at most two rotations per insert and three per delete, which suits a general-purpose map with mixed reads and writes. HashMap's tree bins use red-black trees for the same reason.

Q3. HashMap vs TreeMap vs LinkedHashMap?

HashMap: O(1) average, no order. LinkedHashMap: O(1) average plus insertion or access order, at the cost of two extra pointers per entry. TreeMap: O(log n), sorted, with range and nearest-key queries, requires comparable keys and forbids null keys under natural ordering. Choose by the ordering you need, not by habit.

Q4. Can a TreeMap hold a null key?

Not with natural ordering: compareTo on null throws NullPointerException, and since Java 7 even the first put checks this. With a comparator such as Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()), null keys work. null values are always allowed.

Q5. What happens if a TreeMap comparator is inconsistent with equals?

The map follows the comparator. Two keys that compare as 0 are the same key, so the second put replaces the first's value and keeps the original key. A TreeMap with String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER treats "USD" and "usd" as one key, which is useful when intended and a lost-data bug when not.

Q6. What do floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey and higherKey return?

The greatest key less than or equal to the argument, the least key greater than or equal, the greatest strictly less, and the least strictly greater, each null if none exists. They are O(log n). Typical uses: the rate in effect on a date (floorEntry), the next scheduled slot (ceilingKey), and IP-range lookups.

Q7. Are headMap, tailMap and subMap copies?

No, they are live views backed by the map. Changes in either direction show up in the other, and putting a key outside the view's range through the view throws IllegalArgumentException. Copy with new TreeMap<>(map.headMap(k)) if you need a snapshot.

Q8. How would you implement "find the rate in effect on a date"?

Keep a TreeMap<LocalDate, BigDecimal> per currency pair and call floorEntry(date). That is what RefinePoint's FxRates does, and it also falls back to the inverse pair, dividing with an explicit scale and RoundingMode when only the other direction is quoted. For concurrent updates, ConcurrentSkipListMap offers the same floorEntry.

Q9. How does LinkedHashMap maintain order?

Each entry has before and after pointers in a doubly linked list with head and tail. HashMap's hooks keep the list in step: afterNodeInsertion appends, afterNodeRemoval unlinks, and in access-order mode afterNodeAccess moves the accessed entry to the tail. Iteration walks the list, so it costs O(size), not O(capacity) as in HashMap.

Q10. Does re-inserting an existing key change LinkedHashMap's order?

Not in insertion-order mode: the key keeps its original position. In access-order mode, the put counts as an access and moves it to the tail. Java 21's putLast and putFirst move it explicitly in either mode.

Q11. Implement an LRU cache in Java.

Extend LinkedHashMap with access order and override removeEldestEntry:

class Lru<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int max;
    Lru(int max) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.max = max; }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) { return size() > max; }
}

Every operation is O(1). It is not thread-safe, so wrap it with Collections.synchronizedMap for modest concurrency, as RefinePoint's ExpressionEngine does for its 2,000 parsed rules, or use Caffeine for high concurrency. Interviewers sometimes ask for it from scratch: a HashMap<K, Node> plus a hand-written doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail nodes.

Q12. Why can iterating an access-ordered LinkedHashMap throw CME even without any put?

In access-order mode get moves the entry and increments modCount, so it is a structural modification. Calling get inside a loop over the map, or a second thread calling get, invalidates the iterator. It is also why such a map needs locking even for "read-only" use from several threads.

Q13. What is IdentityHashMap and when would you use it?

A map that compares keys with == and hashes with System.identityHashCode, stored with linear probing in one array of alternating keys and values. Use it when identity matters more than equality: tracking visited objects in graph traversal, serialisation or deep copy, or proxies. It intentionally violates the general Map contract, so never expose it as an ordinary Map to code that expects equals semantics.

Q14. How does WeakHashMap remove entries?

Each entry is a WeakReference to its key, registered with a ReferenceQueue. When the GC finds the key only weakly reachable, it clears the reference and queues the entry. The next get, put or size calls expungeStaleEntries, which polls the queue and unlinks those entries. Removal is lazy, so stale entries can sit there until the map is touched.

Q15. Why might entries in a WeakHashMap never disappear?

The value strongly references the key (directly, or through an object graph), so the key stays reachable from the map itself. Or the keys are always reachable anyway: string literals held by the pool, cached Integers, enum constants, or Class objects. Or the map is never touched, so expunging never runs.

Q16. Weak vs soft vs phantom references?

Weak: cleared at the next GC that finds the object only weakly reachable, which suits canonicalising maps and metadata. Soft: cleared only under memory pressure, which looks like a cache but makes heap usage and GC behaviour unpredictable, so explicit size-bounded caches are preferred. Phantom: never returns the referent, and is enqueued after the object is finalised, for cleanup actions; java.lang.ref.Cleaner is built on it.

Q17. How is a PriorityQueue implemented?

A binary min-heap in an Object[]: the element at index i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and is no greater than them. offer appends and sifts up, poll moves the last element to the root and sifts down, both O(log n). peek is O(1), contains and remove(Object) are O(n), and building from a collection is O(n) heapify.

Q18. Predict the output.

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(List.of(5, 1, 4, 2, 3));
System.out.println(pq);
while (!pq.isEmpty()) System.out.print(pq.poll() + " ");

The first line prints the heap array, such as [1, 2, 4, 5, 3], which is not sorted. The loop prints 1 2 3 4 5. Only poll returns elements in priority order; toString, iterators and streams follow the array.

Q19. How do you make a max-heap? How do you find the top K elements?

new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()) gives a max-heap. For the top K of N, keep a min-heap of size K and poll whenever it exceeds K, which leaves the K largest: O(N log K) time and O(K) memory. Sorting everything is O(N log N), and a max-heap of all N elements uses O(N) memory.

Q20. What does each BlockingQueue method do when the queue is full or empty?

add and remove throw; offer returns false and poll returns null; put and take block; offer and poll with a timeout wait up to that long. peek and element examine the head without removing it. None of them accept null.

Q21. ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue?

ArrayBlockingQueue: bounded, fixed array, one lock shared by producers and consumers, no allocation per element, optional fairness. LinkedBlockingQueue: optionally bounded, but unbounded (Integer.MAX_VALUE) by default; one node per element, but separate put and take locks, so producers and consumers do not contend, which usually gives higher throughput. Always give LinkedBlockingQueue a capacity in production code.

Q22. Why does LinkedBlockingQueue use two locks but ArrayBlockingQueue only one?

In a linked queue, producers touch only the tail and consumers only the head, and an AtomicInteger count keeps them in step, so the two ends can be locked separately (the two-lock queue algorithm). In a circular array, both ends share one array and index arithmetic that depends on the count, so a single lock is simpler. Benchmarks show the array version often competes well at moderate contention because it avoids allocation.

Q23. What is a SynchronousQueue? Where is it used?

A queue with no capacity: every put waits until a take receives the element, which makes it a direct hand-off. Executors.newCachedThreadPool uses it, so a task submitted when no thread is idle makes the pool create a new thread rather than queue it. That is why a cached pool can create thousands of threads under load.

Q24. How does DelayQueue work?

It is an unbounded queue of Delayed elements kept in a PriorityQueue ordered by remaining delay. take returns the head only when its delay has expired. A single leader thread waits with a timeout for the head, while other takers wait indefinitely, which avoids every waiting thread waking for the same deadline. It suits simple timeouts or retry-after-delay in a single JVM; for durable scheduling use a database table or a scheduler.

Q25. How does the work queue affect ThreadPoolExecutor behaviour?

Up to corePoolSize threads are created first; then tasks are queued; only when the queue rejects an offer are threads added up to maximumPoolSize; after that the rejection policy runs. With an unbounded queue the pool never exceeds the core size and the queue can grow until OOM. With a SynchronousQueue, every task without an idle thread gets a new thread. A bounded queue with CallerRunsPolicy gives back-pressure.

Q26. Why is Executors.newFixedThreadPool considered risky in production?

It uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. When producers outpace the threads, tasks pile up in memory until OutOfMemoryError, with nothing to slow the producers and nothing in the logs until it is too late. Build a ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue, a rejection policy, named threads and metrics. In Java 21, I/O-bound tasks may suit virtual threads with a Semaphore to bound concurrency instead.

Q27. How did ConcurrentHashMap work in Java 7?

It was an array of Segments, each a small hash table extending ReentrantLock. A write locked only its segment, so up to concurrencyLevel (16 by default) writes could run in parallel; reads were mostly lock-free through volatile fields. size() summed segments without locking twice and compared modification counts, locking all segments if they differed. The concurrency level was fixed at creation.

Q28. How does ConcurrentHashMap work in Java 8 and later?

It uses one table of bins like HashMap. Inserting into an empty bin is a single CAS; otherwise the writer synchronises on the bin's first node. Reads take no lock, relying on volatile table slots and node fields. Resizing is cooperative, with threads claiming ranges of bins and leaving ForwardingNodes behind. Size is tracked with baseCount plus striped CounterCells. Long bins treeify into a TreeBin, as in HashMap.

Q29. Why did Java 8 replace segments?

Segments fixed the maximum write concurrency at creation, cost memory even for small maps, and locked a whole segment for a write that touched one bin. Per-bin locking scales with the table size, the empty-bin CAS needs no lock at all, and synchronized on an uncontended object is cheap. The rewrite also added tree bins, cooperative resizing, scalable counting and the functional methods compute, merge and the bulk operations.

Q30. Is ConcurrentHashMap.get ever blocked?

No. get reads the table slot with volatile (acquire) semantics and walks nodes whose val and next are volatile. During a resize, a ForwardingNode redirects the search to the new table, and in a tree bin under modification the reader walks the linked next pointers instead. Readers never take the bin lock.

Q31. What are MOVED, TREEBIN and RESERVED?

Reserved negative hash values marking special nodes. MOVED (-1) is a ForwardingNode: this bin has been transferred to the new table. TREEBIN (-2) is the head of a treeified bin. RESERVED (-3) is a placeholder that holds an empty bin while computeIfAbsent or compute runs the function. User hashes are masked with 0x7fffffff so they can never collide with these.

Q32. What is sizeCtl?

A volatile int that controls initialisation and resizing. 0 means use the default capacity; a positive value before initialisation is the requested capacity, and after it the next resize threshold (0.75n); -1 means a thread is initialising; other negative values mean a resize is running, encoding a resize stamp and the number of helping threads. Threads CAS it to coordinate who initialises and who joins a resize.

Q33. How does a ConcurrentHashMap resize without stopping everything?

The thread that crosses the threshold creates a table twice the size and starts moving bins from the top index down, claiming strides of at least 16 bins through a CAS on transferIndex. Each bin is locked only while it is split into low and high lists, then replaced with a ForwardingNode. Writers that hit a forwarding node help with the transfer; readers follow it into the new table. The last thread to finish installs the new table and sets the new threshold.

Q34. How does ConcurrentHashMap count its size?

addCount tries to CAS baseCount; under contention it adds to a CounterCell chosen by the thread's probe hash, and the cell array grows when contention persists, as in LongAdder. size() and mappingCount() add baseCount and all cells. Under concurrent updates the result is a moment-in-time estimate, not a linearisable count. Prefer mappingCount(), which returns a long.

Q35. Why doesn't ConcurrentHashMap allow null keys or values?

Because null must mean "absent". In a concurrent map, distinguishing "absent" from "mapped to null" would need containsKey after get, and another thread could change the map between the two calls. Without nulls, get, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent and getOrDefault have unambiguous single-call semantics. Use Optional or a sentinel value object if you need to represent "known to be empty".

Q36. Is this code thread-safe with a ConcurrentHashMap?

if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, load(k));
map.put(word, map.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1);

No. Each call is atomic, but the check-then-act and read-modify-write sequences are not, so two threads can both load, or both read 5 and both write 6. Use computeIfAbsent(k, this::load) (if load is quick) and merge(word, 1, Integer::sum). For very hot counters, computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new LongAdder()).increment().

Q37. What are the pitfalls of ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent?

The function runs while the bin is locked, so a slow function blocks writes to every key in that bin, and other threads asking for the same key wait. The function must not modify the map: Java 8 could hang (JDK-8062841), and Java 9+ throws IllegalStateException("Recursive update"). On Java 8 it locked even when the key was present, so hot paths often call get first. A function returning null stores nothing, so it runs again next time. Never put network or database calls inside it.

Q38. Why does RefinePoint's TtlCache call get and put instead of computeIfAbsent?

Its loader is a remote call to another service. Inside computeIfAbsent that call would hold a bin lock for the length of a network round trip, blocking unrelated keys in the same bin. The chosen trade-off is that two threads missing at the same moment may both load the value, which is harmless because the loads are idempotent reads, and the second put just overwrites the first with an equal value.

Q39. What does "weakly consistent iterator" mean?

It never throws ConcurrentModificationException, it returns each element at most once, it reflects the map as it was at some point at or after the iterator was created, and it may or may not reflect later changes. So the gateway can sweep idle rate-limit buckets with entrySet().removeIf(...) while requests keep adding new buckets.

Q40. Are ConcurrentHashMap.putAll and clear atomic?

No. They apply entry by entry, so a concurrent reader can see some of the new entries and not others, or a partly cleared map. If you need an atomic swap of the whole content, build a new map and publish it through a volatile field or an AtomicReference.

Q41. What are the ConcurrentHashMap bulk operations?

forEach, search, reduce and typed variants such as reduceValuesToLong, each taking a parallelismThreshold. If the map has more elements than the threshold, the work is split across the common fork-join pool. Long.MAX_VALUE forces sequential execution and 1 maximises parallelism. They run on weakly consistent snapshots, so results reflect concurrent changes only partly.

Q42. How do you create a concurrent Set?

ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(), or map.keySet(defaultValue) to get a view that adds entries with that value. For a sorted concurrent set use ConcurrentSkipListSet, and for a rarely changing one, CopyOnWriteArraySet. RefinePoint's workers track their in-flight run, export and refresh IDs in ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().

Q43. Hashtable vs Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap?

Hashtable and synchronizedMap lock one monitor for every operation, so readers block each other, iteration needs manual locking, and compound actions need external synchronisation. ConcurrentHashMap has lock-free reads, per-bin writes, weakly consistent iteration and atomic compound methods. Use synchronizedMap only to add thread safety to a map whose specific behaviour you need, such as an access-ordered LinkedHashMap.

Q44. How does CopyOnWriteArrayList work, and when should you avoid it?

It holds a volatile array; every write locks, copies the whole array, applies the change and publishes the copy, while reads and iterators use whichever array they saw, without locking. Iterators are snapshots that never throw and do not support remove. Avoid it for large or frequently written lists: each write is O(n) in time and allocation. It is ideal for listener and observer lists, and configuration read on every request but changed rarely.

Q45. What is a skip list, and why does ConcurrentSkipListMap use one?

A sorted linked list plus randomly built index levels that skip ahead, giving expected O(log n) search, insert and delete. Each update changes only a few pointers that can each be CASed independently, so the whole structure is lock-free. A balanced tree's rotations change several nodes atomically, which is hard to do without locks. That makes it the standard concurrent sorted map.

Q46. ConcurrentSkipListMap vs TreeMap wrapped in synchronizedSortedMap?

The skip list scales with concurrent readers and writers and has weakly consistent iterators, at the cost of more memory per entry and somewhat slower single-threaded operations. The synchronised TreeMap serialises every access, and iterating or using views needs the caller to hold the lock. Choose the skip list when several threads read or write a sorted map at the same time.

Q47. Which concurrent collections have an O(n) size()?

ConcurrentLinkedQueue and ConcurrentLinkedDeque traverse the nodes to count them, and the result can be stale. ConcurrentHashMap's size is a fast sum of counters but only an estimate under change. Do not use size() of a concurrent queue as a loop condition or a capacity check; use isEmpty() or a separate counter.

Q48. What are sequenced collections in Java 21?

JEP 431 added SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap, giving every collection with a defined encounter order uniform first, last and reverse operations: getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast, reversed(), and for maps firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, putFirst and sequenced views. List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet, LinkedHashMap and SortedMap implement them; HashMap, HashSet and PriorityQueue do not.

Q49. Predict the output.

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
List<Integer> rev = list.reversed();
rev.add(0);
System.out.println(list + " " + rev + " " + list.getLast());

[0, 1, 2, 3] [3, 2, 1, 0] 3. reversed() is a view, so adding at the end of the reversed view adds at the front of the original.

Q50. Why does TreeSet.addFirst throw?

A sorted set's comparator decides every element's position, so "put this first" has no meaning. addFirst, addLast, and on sorted maps putFirst and putLast, throw UnsupportedOperationException. getFirst and removeFirst work, and mean the smallest element.

Q51. Which collection would you use for each: unique visitor IDs per day; a leaderboard updated by many threads; the latest N events; tasks due at a time; a per-request list of DTOs?

Unique IDs: HashSet, or ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() if shared. Concurrent leaderboard: ConcurrentSkipListMap keyed by score and ID. Latest N events: ArrayDeque with pollFirst when over N, guarded if shared, or a ring buffer. Tasks due at a time: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor or DelayQueue in one JVM, and a database table with next_run_at across instances. Per-request DTOs: ArrayList, presized if the count is known.

Q52. Describe the rate limiter in your gateway.

"RateLimitFilter is a Spring Cloud Gateway global filter with a token bucket per caller: per API key, per user from the token's subject, and per IP address. Buckets live in a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Bucket>, created with computeIfAbsent so each key gets exactly one, and each Bucket guards its token arithmetic with its own synchronized methods, so different callers never contend. Over the limit we return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers. Every 10,000 calls we drop buckets idle for ten minutes with entrySet().removeIf, which is safe during traffic because the iteration is weakly consistent. It's per gateway instance; a shared limit across instances would need Redis."

Q53. What race exists in that design, and why accept it?

The idle sweep can remove a bucket that a concurrent request has just fetched with computeIfAbsent. That request then takes a token from a bucket no longer in the map, and the caller's next request gets a fresh, full bucket. The effect is a brief, slightly lenient limit for a caller who had been idle for ten minutes. Eliminating it would require locking around every lookup, slowing every request to fix a harmless edge case.

Q54. Token bucket vs sliding window log vs fixed window?

Fixed window: one counter per period, cheap, but allows twice the limit around a window boundary. Sliding log: stores a timestamp per call and is exact, but memory grows with the limit. Token bucket: two numbers per key, allows controlled bursts and smooth refill. RefinePoint uses token buckets for high-volume gateway limits (hundreds per minute) and SlidingWindowLimiter's exact sliding log for small quotas like AI calls per user per hour, where storing up to max timestamps per key is cheap.

Q55. Why does SlidingWindowLimiter use ArrayDeque with synchronized instead of a concurrent queue?

The check and the add must be atomic together: drop expired timestamps, compare the size with the limit, then append. A ConcurrentLinkedDeque makes each step thread-safe but not the sequence, and its size() is O(n). An ArrayDeque under the deque's own monitor makes the whole sequence atomic per key, with O(1) operations at both ends and no node allocation, while different keys use different monitors.

Q56. How do you lock per key in Java?

The simplest is a map of lock objects: synchronized (locks.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> new Object())) { ... }, which RefinePoint's BankFeedService uses so that refreshes of one bank consent are serialised while different consents run in parallel. Watch growth, since the map holds one object per key, and is fine when keys are bounded, such as consents. Alternatives are lock striping (a fixed array of locks indexed by hash, as Guava's Striped offers), or ConcurrentHashMap.compute itself when the critical section only updates that entry. Across instances, use a database row lock or advisory lock.

Q57. Your service's ConcurrentHashMap cache keeps growing until OOM. How do you fix it?

ConcurrentHashMap has no eviction. Bound it: by size (Caffeine's maximumSize, or TtlCache-style clear-when-full), by time (expireAfterWrite), or both, and record hit rates and evictions as metrics. Also check the keys: unbounded key spaces like full URLs, query strings or user input need normalising or should not be cached. A heap dump in Eclipse MAT shows the map's retained size and sample keys.

Q58. A ConcurrentHashMap shows high contention in a profiler. What could cause it?

Several threads writing the same few keys, which all land in the same bins and serialise on the same bin lock; a slow compute or computeIfAbsent function holding a bin lock; a poor hashCode sending many keys to few bins; or many threads incrementing one entry with merge. Fixes: LongAdder values for hot counters, moving slow work outside the lock, a better hash, or sharding the hot key.

Q59. Why is the RateLimitFilter.Bucket using synchronized acceptable with virtual threads and reactive code?

The gateway runs on Netty event-loop threads, not virtual threads, and the critical section is a few arithmetic operations with no I/O, so a monitor is held for nanoseconds. Pinning a virtual thread (an issue in Java 21, fixed in Java 24 by JEP 491) only matters when a thread blocks inside synchronized, which never happens here. A ReentrantLock would add allocation and code for no benefit.

Q60. What is false sharing and how do concurrent collections avoid it?

Two variables written by different threads that sit on the same 64-byte cache line make the cores invalidate each other's caches on every write, even though they are logically independent. ConcurrentHashMap's CounterCell and LongAdder's cells are annotated with @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, which pads them onto separate cache lines. Application code can use -XX:-RestrictContended with the annotation, or pad manually, but rarely needs to.

Q61. Tell me how you chose collections in your project.

"The rule was: pick the structure by access pattern, and know who else touches it. Single-threaded engine code uses ArrayList, HashMap and TreeMap: the FX rate lookup is a TreeMap.floorEntry, case-insensitive field matching uses a TreeMap with CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER, and matched groups are deduplicated with an identity set. Shared state in singleton beans is concurrent and bounded: ConcurrentHashMap for rate-limit buckets and short-lived caches, with per-key monitors for compound updates; newKeySet() for in-flight work; synchronised access-order LinkedHashMaps for LRU caches. Work that must survive restarts or be shared across instances is not in a Java collection at all, but in PostgreSQL with SKIP LOCKED."

6. Functional Java: Lambdas, Streams & Optional

Every Java interview since 2016 includes a stream question, and at 12 years of experience the bar is higher than "I can write filter().map().collect()". Interviewers want to know how a lambda becomes an object without a class file, why a stream does nothing until the terminal operation, when a parallel stream makes things slower, and whether you can write a groupingBy with a downstream collector on a whiteboard without hesitation. This chapter covers the machinery first, then a long set of questions including the classic "write this stream" coding problems.

6.1 Functional interfaces: the types behind every lambda

A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM — single abstract method). A lambda or method reference has no type of its own; it takes the type of the functional interface it is assigned to (its target type).

@FunctionalInterface                       // optional, but the compiler then enforces "exactly one abstract method"
public interface MatchRule {
    boolean matches(Txn bank, Txn ledger);
    default MatchRule and(MatchRule other) {          // default methods do not count
        return (b, l) -> matches(b, l) && other.matches(b, l);
    }
    String toString();                                // public Object methods do not count either
}

Rules worth saying out loud: default and static methods do not count; abstract methods that re-declare public Object methods (equals, toString) do not count; @FunctionalInterface is optional but documents intent and turns accidental breakage into a compile error. Comparator has two abstract-looking methods (compare and equals) and is still functional for that reason.

The java.util.function catalog

Interface Method Shape Typical use
Function<T,R> R apply(T) T → R map
BiFunction<T,U,R> R apply(T,U) (T,U) → R Map.merge, replaceAll
UnaryOperator<T> T apply(T) T → T List.replaceAll, Stream.iterate
BinaryOperator<T> T apply(T,T) (T,T) → T reduce, toMap merge
Supplier<T> T get() () → T orElseGet, lazy init, collect supplier
Consumer<T> void accept(T) T → void forEach, ifPresent
BiConsumer<T,U> void accept(T,U) (T,U) → void Map.forEach, collector accumulator
Predicate<T> boolean test(T) T → boolean filter, removeIf
BiPredicate<T,U> boolean test(T,U) (T,U) → boolean Files.find
IntFunction<R>, ToIntFunction<T>, IntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperator, IntPredicate, IntSupplier, IntConsumer, ObjIntConsumer<T>, IntToLongFunction … primitive specialisations avoid boxing in IntStream etc.

There are 43 interfaces in java.util.function. You do not memorise them all; you memorise the pattern: Function/Supplier/Consumer/Predicate/Operator, the Bi prefix for two arguments, Int/Long/Double prefixes for primitive inputs, To<Prim> for primitive outputs, and Obj<Prim>Consumer for mixed.

Composition methods you should be able to use fluently:

Function<String, String> trim = String::trim;
Function<String, Integer> length = trim.andThen(String::length);     // trim first, then length
Function<String, Integer> same   = String::length.compose(trim);     // does NOT compile: a method ref needs a target type
Function<String, Integer> ok     = ((Function<String, Integer>) String::length).compose(trim);

Predicate<Break> open = b -> b.status() == BreakStatus.OPEN;
Predicate<Break> big  = b -> b.amount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0;
breaks.stream().filter(open.and(big.negate())).toList();
breaks.stream().filter(Predicate.not(Break::isResolved)).toList();    // Predicate.not — Java 11
Comparator<Break> order = Comparator.comparing(Break::status).thenComparing(Break::amount, Comparator.reverseOrder());

Function.identity() returns t -> t; UnaryOperator.identity() is the same with the narrower type.

6.2 Lambda internals: no class file, one invokedynamic

An anonymous class compiles to a separate Outer$1.class file, loaded like any other class. A lambda does not. Compile this:

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String prefix = "ORG-";
        Function<String, String> f = code -> prefix + code;
        System.out.println(f.apply("42"));
    }
}

javac does two things:

  1. Desugars the body into a private synthetic method in the same class: private static String lambda$main$0(String prefix, String code). Captured variables become leading parameters. If the body uses this (or an instance field), the method is an instance method instead of static.
  2. Emits one invokedynamic instruction at the place the lambda is evaluated. Its bootstrap method is LambdaMetafactory.metafactory, and its static arguments describe the target interface method (Function.apply), the implementation method handle (lambda$main$0) and the instantiated signature.
javap -c -p Demo.class (abridged)
  0: ldc           #7      // String ORG-
  2: astore_1
  3: aload_1
  4: invokedynamic #9,  0  // InvokeDynamic #0:apply:(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/util/function/Function;
  9: astore_2
 ...
private static java.lang.String lambda$main$0(java.lang.String, java.lang.String);

BootstrapMethods:
  0: #40 REF_invokeStatic java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory
     Method arguments: (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;
                       REF_invokeStatic Demo.lambda$main$0:(Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
                       (Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;

At runtime, the first time that invokedynamic executes, the JVM calls the bootstrap method. LambdaMetafactory spins a tiny class in memory that implements Function, has one field per captured value and an apply that calls lambda$main$0. Since JDK 15 it is defined as a hidden class (Lookup.defineHiddenClass), so it is not discoverable by name and can be unloaded with its defining class. The bootstrap returns a CallSite bound to a factory; the call site is linked once and every later execution goes straight to the factory.

Capturing vs non-capturing:

Non-capturing s -> s.trim() Capturing s -> prefix + s
Instance per evaluation The same singleton every time A new object each evaluation (holds captured values)
Allocation None after linkage One small object (often removed by escape analysis)
f1 == f2 for two evaluations true (implementation detail, never rely on it) false

Why this design beat inner classes: no class file bloat (a codebase with 5,000 lambdas would otherwise ship 5,000 classes), the translation strategy can change in a future JDK without recompiling your code, and the JIT sees through the linked call site and inlines the body. The same invokedynamic trick is used for string concatenation since Java 9 (StringConcatFactory) and for record equals/hashCode/toString (ObjectMethods).

To see the generated classes: java -Djdk.internal.lambda.dumpProxyClasses=/tmp/lambdas Demo.

Capture and "effectively final"

A lambda may read local variables of the enclosing method only if they are final or effectively final (never reassigned after initialisation).

int count = 0;
runs.forEach(r -> count++);          // compile error: local variables referenced from a lambda must be final or effectively final

Why: the lambda captures the value, copied into a field of the lambda object (look at the leading parameters of lambda$main$0). The local variable lives in a stack frame that may be gone when the lambda runs — on another thread, after the method returned. If Java allowed mutation, you would have two copies that silently diverge, or would need to move locals to the heap and synchronise them. Java chose "capture by value, and forbid anything that would make the copy observable".

Instance and static fields are not restricted: the lambda captures this (for instance fields) and reads the field through it, so mutation is visible — and racy if the lambda runs on another thread.

int[] counter = {0};                 // compiles: the array reference is effectively final
runs.forEach(r -> counter[0]++);     // works sequentially, data race in parallel — a code smell
long n = runs.stream().filter(Run::failed).count();   // the functional answer

this in a lambda vs an anonymous class

public class Outer {
    String name = "outer";
    void test() {
        Runnable lambda = () -> System.out.println(this.name);          // "outer": lexical this
        Runnable anon = new Runnable() {
            String name = "anon";
            public void run() { System.out.println(this.name); }        // "anon": the anonymous instance
        };
    }
}

A lambda is lexically scoped: this, super and variable names mean exactly what they mean in the enclosing method. It cannot declare a parameter or local with the same name as an enclosing local (compile error), whereas an anonymous class introduces a new scope and can shadow.

6.3 Method references: four kinds

Kind Syntax Equivalent lambda Example
Static method Class::staticMethod (a, b) -> Class.staticMethod(a, b) Integer::parseInt, Math::max, Objects::nonNull
Bound instance (specific object) obj::method x -> obj.method(x) System.out::println, cache::get
Unbound instance (arbitrary object of a type) Class::instanceMethod (obj, x) -> obj.method(x) String::length, BigDecimal::add, String::compareToIgnoreCase
Constructor Class::new x -> new Class(x) ArrayList::new, int[]::new, TreeMap::new

BigDecimal::add is the unbound kind: add is an instance method, the first lambda parameter becomes the receiver, so it fits BinaryOperator<BigDecimal> as (a, b) -> a.add(b). That is why reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add) works.

Two subtle differences from the equivalent lambda:

String s = null;
Supplier<Integer> lambda = () -> s.length();   // fine now, NPE only when get() is called
Supplier<Integer> ref    = s::length;          // NPE immediately: the receiver is evaluated (and null-checked) at creation

Supplier<Run> eager = repo.findLatest()::copy; // findLatest() runs ONCE, when the reference is created
Supplier<Run> lazy  = () -> repo.findLatest().copy();   // runs on every get()

The bound receiver is evaluated when the method reference expression is evaluated, not when the function is called. That matters for side effects and for nulls.

Overload ambiguity is the other trap: Integer::toString can mean the static toString(int) or the instance toString(), so Function<Integer,String> f = Integer::toString; fails to compile ("ambiguous"). Use String::valueOf or a lambda.

6.4 Stream pipeline internals

A stream is not a data structure. It is a description of a computation over a source, executed once by a terminal operation. Three parts:

  1. Source — a Spliterator (collection, array, Files.lines, generator, IntStream.range).
  2. Intermediate operations — filter, map, sorted… each returns a new stream stage; nothing executes.
  3. Terminal operation — collect, forEach, reduce, findFirst, count… triggers execution and consumes the stream.

The stage linked list

Internally each stage is an AbstractPipeline node (ReferencePipeline.Head, StatelessOp, StatefulOp) holding a link to its upstream stage, the op flags and the source. Building a pipeline only allocates these nodes.

When the terminal operation runs, it calls wrapSink, which walks from the last stage back to the head, wrapping each stage's logic around the next one as a Sink (a Consumer with begin(size), accept(t), end() and cancellationRequested()). Then it calls spliterator.forEachRemaining(sinkChain) — the source pushes elements one at a time through the whole chain.

Vertical execution (loop fusion)

Because of the sink chain, a stream processes element 1 through all stateless stages, then element 2, and so on. It does not filter the whole list, then map the whole list. This is effectively loop fusion: one pass, no intermediate collections.

Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return s.length() > 1; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
      .forEach(s -> System.out.println("forEach " + s));
filter a
filter bb
map bb
forEach BB
filter ccc
map ccc
forEach CCC

Stateless vs stateful operations

Category Operations Behaviour
Stateless intermediate filter, map, flatMap, mapMulti, peek, mapToInt, boxed, unordered Handle each element independently; fully fused
Stateful intermediate sorted, distinct, limit, skip, takeWhile, dropWhile Need to remember previous elements; sorted is a full barrier
Short-circuiting intermediate limit, takeWhile Can finish without consuming the whole source
Terminal forEach, forEachOrdered, collect, reduce, toList, count, min, max, toArray Consume everything
Short-circuiting terminal findFirst, findAny, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch Stop at the first decisive element

sorted() cannot emit anything until it has seen everything: its sink buffers all elements in accept, sorts in end(), then pushes them downstream. That changes the printed order in peek-based puzzles:

Stream.of(3, 1, 2)
      .peek(x -> System.out.println("peek " + x))
      .sorted()
      .forEach(x -> System.out.println("each " + x));
// peek 3, peek 1, peek 2, each 1, each 2, each 3

Short-circuiting

When a pipeline contains a short-circuit op, the terminal switches from forEachRemaining to a loop of tryAdvance calls that checks sink.cancellationRequested() before each element:

Optional<String> first = Stream.of("x", "yy", "zzz", "wwww")
        .filter(s -> { System.out.println("check " + s); return s.length() > 1; })
        .findFirst();
// check x, check yy   — "zzz" and "wwww" are never examined
