That is why Stream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2).filter(i -> i > 1000).findFirst() terminates on an infinite source, while Stream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2).sorted().findFirst() never does (sorted must consume everything first).

Spliterator and characteristics

Spliterator = splittable iterator. Two jobs: traverse (tryAdvance, forEachRemaining) and split (trySplit returns a spliterator covering a prefix, used by parallel streams). It reports characteristics that the pipeline uses to optimise:

Flag Meaning Optimisation it enables
SIZED / SUBSIZED Exact size known (and after splits) toArray allocates exactly once; count() can skip traversal
ORDERED Encounter order is meaningful (List, arrays) Must preserve order; unordered() drops it
DISTINCT No duplicates (Set) distinct() becomes a no-op
SORTED Already sorted (TreeSet) sorted() with natural order becomes a no-op
NONNULL, IMMUTABLE, CONCURRENT Source guarantees Fewer checks; safe concurrent modification

The famous consequence (Java 9+):

List.of(1, 2, 3).stream().peek(System.out::println).count();   // prints NOTHING, returns 3
List.of(1, 2, 3).stream().filter(x -> true).peek(System.out::println).count();  // prints 1 2 3

With a SIZED source and no stage that can change the count, count() returns the size directly. peek is a debugging aid, not a place for logic.

Streams are single-use and lazy

Stream<Run> s = runs.stream().filter(Run::failed);
s.count();
s.toList();           // IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed

A stream also binds lazily to its source: for most JDK collections, the spliterator is created when the terminal operation starts, so modifications made before the terminal operation are visible, and structural modification during it throws ConcurrentModificationException (fail-fast spliterator) — or, worse, produces undefined results for non-interfering requirements.

6.5 Collectors in depth

collect(Collector) is a mutable reduction: create a container, fold elements into it, merge containers (in parallel), optionally transform at the end.

toList variants

Call Mutable? Nulls Since
collect(Collectors.toList()) Unspecified, in practice ArrayList (mutable) Allowed 8
collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()) Unmodifiable NPE on null 10
stream.toList() Unmodifiable Allowed 16

toMap: duplicates, merge, nulls, map type

Map<String, Run> byCode = runs.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Run::code, r -> r));
// IllegalStateException: Duplicate key RUN-7 (attempted merging values ...) if two runs share a code

Map<String, Run> latest = runs.stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Run::code, Function.identity(),
                 (a, b) -> a.startedAt().isAfter(b.startedAt()) ? a : b,   // merge function
                 LinkedHashMap::new));                                       // map supplier keeps order

Trap: toMap throws NullPointerException if any value is null, because it uses HashMap.merge, which rejects null values — even though HashMap itself allows them. Either filter nulls, map them to a sentinel, or collect with collect(HashMap::new, (m, r) -> m.put(k(r), v(r)), Map::putAll).

groupingBy and downstream collectors

groupingBy(classifier) = groupingBy(classifier, HashMap::new, toList()). The power is the downstream collector applied per group.

Map<BreakStatus, List<Break>> byStatus     = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::status));
Map<BreakStatus, Long> countByStatus       = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::status, counting()));
Map<String, Set<String>> accountsByOrg     = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::orgCode, mapping(Break::account, toSet())));
Map<BreakStatus, Optional<Break>> biggest  = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::status, maxBy(comparing(Break::amount))));
Map<BreakStatus, Break> biggestNoOptional  = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::status,
        collectingAndThen(maxBy(comparing(Break::amount)), Optional::get)));
Map<String, Map<BreakStatus, Long>> nested = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::orgCode, groupingBy(Break::status, counting())));
TreeMap<LocalDate, List<Break>> sorted     = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::valueDate, TreeMap::new, toList()));
Map<BreakStatus, List<Break>> bigOnly      = breaks.stream().collect(groupingBy(Break::status,
        filtering(b -> b.amount().compareTo(LIMIT) > 0, toList())));   // Java 9: keeps empty groups

filtering inside groupingBy differs from filter before it: filtering first drops groups that end up empty; the filtering downstream keeps the key with an empty list. flatMapping (Java 9) is the flat equivalent of mapping.

groupingBy throws NPE when the classifier returns null ("element cannot be mapped to a null key"). groupingByConcurrent builds a ConcurrentHashMap and is the right choice only in unordered parallel streams.

partitioningBy, teeing, collectingAndThen

Map<Boolean, List<Break>> split = breaks.stream().collect(partitioningBy(b -> b.ageDays() > 30));
// ALWAYS has both keys true and false, even if one list is empty (groupingBy would omit the missing key)

record Totals(BigDecimal debit, BigDecimal credit) {}
Totals t = txns.stream().collect(teeing(                                 // Java 12: two collectors, one pass
        filtering(Txn::isDebit,  reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Txn::amount, BigDecimal::add)),
        filtering(Txn::isCredit, reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Txn::amount, BigDecimal::add)),
        Totals::new));

List<String> names = users.stream().map(User::name)
        .collect(collectingAndThen(toList(), Collections::unmodifiableList));

Other collectors you should name: joining(", ", "[", "]"), summingInt/Long/Double, averagingDouble, summarizingLong (count, sum, min, max, average in one pass), minBy/maxBy, reducing, toCollection(TreeSet::new).

Writing a custom Collector

public static Collector<Txn, ?, Map<String, BigDecimal>> sumByCurrency() {
    return Collector.of(
        HashMap::new,                                                     // supplier
        (Map<String, BigDecimal> m, Txn t) -> m.merge(t.currency(), t.amount(), BigDecimal::add),  // accumulator
        (m1, m2) -> { m2.forEach((k, v) -> m1.merge(k, v, BigDecimal::add)); return m1; },        // combiner
        Collector.Characteristics.UNORDERED);                            // identity finisher implied
}

Characteristics: IDENTITY_FINISH (finisher is a cast, skip it), UNORDERED (result does not depend on encounter order), CONCURRENT (one shared container may be accumulated from many threads — only honoured if also UNORDERED or the stream is unordered).

6.6 flatMap, mapMulti, reduce vs collect

map is one-to-one; flatMap is one-to-many: each element maps to a stream and the streams are concatenated.

List<Txn> all = statements.stream().flatMap(st -> st.lines().stream()).toList();
Optional<Account> acct = findUser(id).flatMap(User::primaryAccount);      // Optional.flatMap avoids Optional<Optional<…>>
Stream.of("a,b", "c").flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(","))).toList();  // [a, b, c]

// Java 16 mapMulti: push zero or more results without creating a stream per element
statements.stream().<Txn>mapMulti((st, sink) -> st.lines().forEach(sink)).toList();

flatMap was not lazy over the inner stream until JDK 10 (it pushed the whole inner stream even after findFirst); since then it respects short-circuiting.

reduce vs collect:

reduce collect
Kind Immutable reduction: combine values into a new value Mutable reduction: accumulate into a container
Good for Sums, max, combining immutable values (BigDecimal, String concatenation of few elements) Lists, maps, StringBuilder, anything with a container
Parallel rule Identity must be a true identity; accumulator must be associative and stateless Supplier must create a fresh container per call 
int sum = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).reduce(0, Integer::sum);           // 15
Optional<Integer> max = Stream.of(4, 9, 2).reduce(Integer::max);          // no identity -> Optional
int totalLength = words.stream().reduce(0, (acc, w) -> acc + w.length(), Integer::sum);  // 3-arg: identity, accumulator, combiner

// Wrong: a mutable container passed as identity is SHARED across threads in parallel
List<String> bad = words.parallelStream().reduce(new ArrayList<>(), (l, w) -> { l.add(w); return l; }, (a, b) -> { a.addAll(b); return a; });

The broken last example corrupts the list in parallel (and duplicates elements) because every split uses the same ArrayList identity. Use collect.

Trap: reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b) or reduce(1, ...) as a sum identity gives different answers sequentially and in parallel, because subtraction is not associative and 1 is not the identity for +. Parallel reduction applies the identity once per chunk.

6.7 Parallel streams

collection.parallelStream() (or .parallel()) splits the source with trySplit, processes chunks as ForkJoinTasks on the ForkJoinPool common pool, and merges results. The common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 worker threads (the calling thread also works, so all cores are used), configurable with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N.

Each worker has its own deque; it pushes and pops its own subtasks LIFO and steals from the tail of another worker's deque when idle (work stealing), so uneven chunks balance out.

Splitting quality decides the speed-up

Source Splits Parallel suitability
ArrayList, arrays, IntStream.range Exact halves in O(1), SIZED+SUBSIZED Excellent
HashSet, HashMap.keySet By bucket ranges, sizes estimated Good
TreeSet/TreeMap By subtree Fair
LinkedList Must walk the list Poor
Stream.iterate, BufferedReader.lines, Files.lines (pre-JDK 9) Sequential by nature, batches of growing size Poor

When NOT to use parallel streams

  1. Inside a web server request. The common pool is shared by every parallel stream and every CompletableFuture.*Async without an executor in the JVM. Ten concurrent requests each running a parallel stream compete for the same N-1 threads; you gain nothing and add contention.
  2. Blocking I/O in the lambda (HTTP calls, JDBC). Workers block, the pool starves, unrelated code stalls. Use an explicit executor (or virtual threads).
  3. Small data or cheap operations. The NQ rule of thumb: N elements × Q cost per element should exceed roughly 10,000 before parallelism pays for splitting, task creation and merging.
  4. Order-dependent operations. findFirst, limit, skip, sorted, forEachOrdered and distinct on ordered streams must preserve encounter order and buffer a lot. Use findAny, call .unordered() when order does not matter.
  5. Side effects or shared mutable state. parallelStream().forEach(list::add) on an ArrayList loses elements or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
  6. Contended merges. groupingBy in parallel merges maps (expensive); groupingByConcurrent avoids it but loses order.
List<Integer> unsafe = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 10_000).parallel().forEach(unsafe::add);   // size < 10000, or an exception
List<Integer> safe = IntStream.range(0, 10_000).parallel().boxed().toList();  // ordered, correct

forEach on a parallel stream does not respect encounter order; forEachOrdered does, at the cost of buffering.

Running a parallel stream in a custom pool (customPool.submit(() -> list.parallelStream()...).get()) works because tasks forked from inside a ForkJoinPool run in that pool. It is an implementation behaviour, not a documented contract — prefer explicit executors for anything that blocks.

RefinePoint: we never use parallel streams in request handling. The heavy matching of millions of rows does not happen in Java collections at all: ryfn-engine loads files into DuckDB in-process and SqlCompiler turns match rules into SQL, so DuckDB's own vectorised, multi-threaded executor does the work. Streams are used for the in-memory glue — grouping breaks, building summaries, mapping DTOs — where sequential streams are fast enough and predictable.

6.8 Primitive streams and boxing cost

Stream<Integer> stores Integer objects: 16 bytes each plus a 4–8 byte reference, a pointer chase per element, and allocation for values outside the -128..127 cache. IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream work on primitives and add numeric terminals.

int total = runs.stream().mapToInt(Run::matchedCount).sum();         // no boxing
OptionalDouble avg = runs.stream().mapToLong(Run::durationMs).average();   // OptionalDouble, empty for no elements
IntSummaryStatistics st = runs.stream().mapToInt(Run::breakCount).summaryStatistics();
List<Integer> boxed = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).boxed().toList();    // back to objects
IntStream.range(0, 5);        // 0..4
IntStream.rangeClosed(0, 5);  // 0..5
"hello".chars();              // IntStream of UTF-16 code units; use codePoints() for emoji/supplementary chars

Stream<Integer>.reduce(0, Integer::sum) unboxes and re-boxes at every step. On a few million elements the primitive version is several times faster and allocates nothing. There is no CharStream, ByteStream or FloatStream.

6.9 Stream vs loop performance

  • For small collections (tens to hundreds of elements) a plain for loop is usually faster: no pipeline objects, no lambda dispatch, simpler for the JIT. The difference is microseconds and almost never matters.
  • For large data with stateless stages, JIT-compiled streams come close to loops because the sink chain inlines; boxing is the real cost, not the stream framework.
  • Streams win on readability of transformations (group, partition, aggregate) and on optional parallelism; loops win for complex control flow (early return from the method, break out of nested loops, checked exceptions, mutating several locals).
  • Measure with JMH, not System.currentTimeMillis() in main — warm-up and dead-code elimination make naive benchmarks meaningless.

Senior answer: "I default to streams for transformations and loops for control flow, and I only optimise after a profiler shows the pipeline is hot."

6.10 Optional

Optional<T> is a container for zero or one value, designed (by its authors' own statement) as a method return type that forces the caller to think about absence.

Correct usage

public Optional<Workspace> findByCode(String code) { ... }

String plan = workspaces.findByCode(code)
        .filter(Workspace::active)
        .map(Workspace::plan)
        .map(Plan::name)
        .orElse("FREE");

Workspace ws = workspaces.findByCode(code)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("Workspace " + code));     // Java 8 with supplier
Workspace ws2 = workspaces.findByCode(code).orElseThrow();               // Java 10: NoSuchElementException

opt.ifPresentOrElse(this::notify, () -> log.warn("none"));                // Java 9
Optional<Run> any = primary().or(this::fallback);                        // Java 9: lazy alternative Optional
long present = ids.stream().map(repo::findById).flatMap(Optional::stream).count();   // Java 9
if (opt.isEmpty()) { ... }                                                // Java 11

orElse vs orElseGet

String v = Optional.of("cached").orElse(loadFromDb());        // loadFromDb() ALWAYS runs — argument evaluated first
String w = Optional.of("cached").orElseGet(() -> loadFromDb()); // loadFromDb() runs only when empty

orElse(x) is fine for constants and already-computed values. For anything with a cost or side effect (DB call, creating an entity, logging) use orElseGet. This is the single most-asked Optional question, and it causes real bugs: an orElse(repository.save(new Default())) inserts a row on every call.

Incorrect usage

Anti-pattern Why Better
opt.get() without check Same NPE risk with a different exception orElseThrow() (explicit intent)
if (opt.isPresent()) { x = opt.get(); } Null-check with more ceremony map / ifPresent / orElse
Optional field in an entity/DTO Not Serializable, Jackson/JPA friction, extra allocation Nullable field
Optional parameter Callers must wrap; three states (null, empty, present) Overloads
Optional<List<T>> Empty list already means "none" Return List.of()
Optional.of(maybeNull) NPE when null Optional.ofNullable
Returning null from an Optional method Defeats the purpose Always Optional.empty()
Optional for identity-sensitive ops (==, synchronized) It is a value-based class Compare with equals

Spring Data repositories return Optional<T> from findById; Spring MVC accepts Optional request params; Jackson needs the jdk8 module (included by Spring Boot) to serialise it — another reason to keep it off DTOs.

6.11 Checked exceptions in lambdas

The java.util.function interfaces declare no checked exceptions, so this fails to compile:

List<String> contents = paths.stream().map(Files::readString).toList();   // unhandled IOException

Options, in order of preference:

// 1. Wrap into the JDK's unchecked equivalent, inside a small helper method
private static String read(Path p) {
    try { return Files.readString(p); }
    catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
}
paths.stream().map(Loader::read).toList();

// 2. A throwing functional interface plus an adapter
@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws Exception; }
static <T, R> Function<T, R> unchecked(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) {
    return t -> {
        try { return f.apply(t); }
        catch (RuntimeException e) { throw e; }
        catch (Exception e) { throw new CompletionException(e); }
    };
}
paths.stream().map(unchecked(Files::readString)).toList();

// 3. Return a result type instead of throwing (keeps going on errors)
sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Failed {}
record Ok(Txn txn) implements Parsed {}
record Failed(int line, String error) implements Parsed {}

"Sneaky throw" (using generic type erasure to rethrow a checked exception without declaring it) works but hides exceptions from the compiler and from catch clauses callers would write; avoid it in application code. When a loop needs checked exceptions and early exit, a plain for loop is often the clearest answer.

Remember resource-backed streams: Files.lines, Files.list, Files.walk hold an open file handle and must be closed — try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path)) { ... }. A stream's onClose handlers run on close(), not after the terminal operation.

6.12 RefinePoint patterns with streams

Grouping breaks for the dashboard tiles:

record Totals(long count, BigDecimal amount) {}
public record BreakSummary(BreakStatus status, long count, BigDecimal total) {}

public List<BreakSummary> summarise(List<Break> breaks) {
    Map<BreakStatus, Totals> byStatus = breaks.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Break::status,
                 () -> new EnumMap<>(BreakStatus.class),                 // iterates in enum declaration order
                 teeing(counting(),
                        reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Break::amount, BigDecimal::add),
                        Totals::new)));                                  // one pass: count and sum together
    return byStatus.entrySet().stream()
        .map(e -> new BreakSummary(e.getKey(), e.getValue().count(), e.getValue().amount()))
        .toList();
}

Summing money correctly:

BigDecimal total = lines.stream().map(Txn::amount).reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);

Map<String, BigDecimal> byCurrency = lines.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Txn::currency, TreeMap::new,
                 reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Txn::amount, BigDecimal::add)));

RefinePoint: money is always BigDecimal and always summed with reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add), for example the total(items) helper in the month-end certification code (CertificationService) and the report builder's SUM aggregate. summingDouble(t -> t.amount().doubleValue()) is the tempting shortcut and it is banned: double cannot represent 0.10 exactly, so errors accumulate over a month of lines. In a reconciliation product, "off by 3 cents against the bank total" is a visible defect that destroys trust.

RefinePoint: the real pipelines are short and readable. RecordService groups result items per run with groupingBy(Item::runId, LinkedHashMap::new, toList()), so runs stay in the order they arrived, and DataQualityService indexes error records by row number with toMap(ErrorRecord::getRowNumber, r -> r, (a, b) -> a), where the explicit merge function documents that the first record for a row wins. MatchStrategy is a plain enum (EXACT, NUMERIC_TOLERANCE, JARO_WINKLER…), which the engine's configuration selects, so no stream is needed there.

6.13 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is a functional interface? Is Comparator one even though it declares two methods?

An interface with exactly one abstract method, which lambdas and method references can implement. Comparator declares compare and equals, but equals re-declares a public Object method and does not count, so Comparator is functional. Default and static methods never count. @FunctionalInterface is optional; it makes the compiler reject a second abstract method.

Q2. What is the type of a lambda expression?

It has no type of its own; its type is the target type inferred from the context (assignment, method argument, return, cast). The same lambda s -> s.isEmpty() can be a Predicate<String> or a Function<String, Boolean>. That is why var f = s -> s.isEmpty(); does not compile — there is no target type to infer from.

Q3. How is a lambda compiled and executed? Does it create an inner class?

No class file is generated. javac moves the body into a private synthetic method (lambda$main$0) and puts an invokedynamic instruction where the lambda is evaluated, with LambdaMetafactory.metafactory as bootstrap. On the first execution the JVM runs the bootstrap, which spins a hidden class implementing the interface and returns a call site; later executions reuse the linked call site. Non-capturing lambdas yield a cached singleton, capturing lambdas allocate a small object holding the captured values.

Q4. Why did Java choose invokedynamic instead of anonymous inner classes for lambdas?

Four reasons: no class-file explosion (each anonymous class is a .class file to load and verify), no forced allocation for non-capturing lambdas, the JVM can change the translation strategy in a later release without recompilation (the bytecode only says "give me a Function"), and the JIT optimises linked invokedynamic call sites as well as ordinary calls. Lambdas also do not capture this unless they use it, so they do not accidentally retain the outer object the way inner classes do.

Q5. Why must captured local variables be effectively final?

Because the lambda captures the value, copied into the lambda object, while the local variable lives in a stack frame that may disappear before the lambda runs (possibly on another thread). Allowing reassignment would create two copies that silently diverge, or require moving locals to the heap with synchronisation. Fields are not restricted because the lambda reads them through the captured this reference. Workarounds like a one-element array or AtomicInteger compile but are usually a sign the code should use a reduction.

Q6. What does this refer to inside a lambda vs an anonymous class?

In a lambda, this is the enclosing instance (lexical scoping); in an anonymous class, this is the anonymous-class instance. Likewise a lambda cannot declare a parameter with the same name as an enclosing local variable, while an anonymous class can shadow it.

Q7. Name the four kinds of method references with examples.

Static (Integer::parseInt), bound instance on a specific object (System.out::println, cache::get), unbound instance on an arbitrary object of a type where the first argument becomes the receiver (String::length, BigDecimal::add), and constructor (ArrayList::new, int[]::new).

Q8. Is obj::method exactly equivalent to x -> obj.method(x)?

No. In the method reference, obj is evaluated once when the reference is created and null-checked immediately; in the lambda, obj is evaluated on every call. So String s = null; Supplier<Integer> r = s::length; throws NPE at creation, the lambda only when invoked. Also repo.load()::process calls load() once, while () -> repo.load().process() calls it each time.

Q9. Why does Function<Integer, String> f = Integer::toString; fail to compile?

It is ambiguous: it could refer to the static Integer.toString(int) (with unboxing) or the instance method Integer.toString() on the argument. Use String::valueOf or i -> i.toString().

Q10. What are intermediate and terminal operations? What is laziness?

Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) return a new stream and only record the step. Terminal operations (collect, forEach, count, findFirst) trigger execution by building the sink chain and pulling the source. Without a terminal operation nothing runs:

Stream.of(1, 2, 3).peek(System.out::println).map(x -> x * 2);   // prints nothing

Laziness enables fusion (one pass), short-circuiting on infinite streams and avoiding work for elements nobody consumes.

Q11. Explain the internal structure of a stream pipeline.

Each stage is an AbstractPipeline node linked to its upstream; the head holds the source Spliterator. The terminal operation calls wrapSink, which wraps each stage's operation around the downstream Sink, then calls spliterator.forEachRemaining(sink) (or a tryAdvance loop when short-circuiting). Elements are pushed one by one through all stateless stages; stateful stages like sorted buffer elements and release them in end().

Q12. Predict the output.

Stream.of("one", "two", "three", "four")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("F:" + s); return s.length() > 3; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("M:" + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
      .findFirst();

F:one, F:two, F:three, M:three. Execution is vertical (element by element) and findFirst stops after the first element that reaches it, so four is never touched.

Q13. Predict the output.

List<Integer> list = Stream.of(5, 3, 1).peek(System.out::print).sorted().peek(System.out::print).toList();

531135. The first peek sees each element as it enters sorted, which buffers all three before emitting 1, 3, 5 to the second peek.

Q14. Why does List.of(1,2,3).stream().peek(System.out::println).count() print nothing?

Since Java 9, count() checks whether the source is SIZED and no stage can change the number of elements; if so it returns the size without traversing. peek does not change the count, so it is skipped. Add a filter and it prints. Lesson: never put required logic in peek.

Q15. Can you reuse a stream?

No. A stream can be consumed once; a second terminal (or intermediate) operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. If you need to run several pipelines, keep a Supplier<Stream<T>> (() -> list.stream()) or collect once and reuse the collection.

Q16. Stateless vs stateful intermediate operations — why does it matter?

Stateless ops (filter, map, flatMap, peek) handle each element independently and fuse perfectly, including in parallel. Stateful ops (sorted, distinct, limit, skip) must see other elements; sorted is a full barrier that buffers the whole stream, distinct keeps a set, and limit/skip in ordered parallel streams must coordinate chunks. They decide memory use, whether infinite streams can terminate, and how well parallel streams scale.

Q17. What is a Spliterator? What are its characteristics used for?

A splittable iterator: it traverses (tryAdvance, forEachRemaining) and splits itself for parallelism (trySplit). Characteristics (SIZED, SUBSIZED, ORDERED, SORTED, DISTINCT, NONNULL, IMMUTABLE, CONCURRENT) let the framework skip work: exact-size arrays for toArray, no-op distinct() on a Set, no-op sorted() on a TreeSet, shortcut count(). Custom data sources (e.g., a paged API reader) can expose a stream through StreamSupport.stream(spliterator, false).

Q18. What does short-circuiting mean? Give examples.

An operation that can complete without processing all elements: findFirst, findAny, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch (terminal), limit, takeWhile (intermediate). allMatch stops at the first false, anyMatch at the first true. On an empty stream allMatch returns true and anyMatch returns false (vacuous truth).

Q19. Will this terminate?

Stream.iterate(1, i -> i + 1).filter(i -> i % 2 == 0).limit(3).forEach(System.out::println);   // A
Stream.iterate(1, i -> i + 1).sorted().limit(3).forEach(System.out::println);                  // B
IntStream.iterate(0, i -> (i + 1) % 2).distinct().limit(10).forEach(System.out::println);       // C

A prints 2, 4, 6 and stops. B never terminates (sorted must consume the infinite stream; eventually OutOfMemoryError). C prints 0 and 1 and then hangs: distinct never finds a third distinct value, so limit(10) is never satisfied. Use Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) (Java 9) or takeWhile to bound infinite streams.

Q20. map vs flatMap?

map transforms each element into exactly one element (Stream<List<T>> stays nested). flatMap transforms each element into a stream and concatenates them (Stream<T>). Same idea for Optional.flatMap, which avoids Optional<Optional<T>> when the mapper itself returns an Optional.

Q21. What is mapMulti and when would you use it over flatMap?

Java 16. The mapper receives the element and a Consumer and pushes zero or more outputs. It avoids creating a Stream per element, which helps when most elements map to zero or one results, and it makes type-filtering easy: objects.stream().<Txn>mapMulti((o, sink) -> { if (o instanceof Txn t) sink.accept(t); }).

Q22. reduce vs collect?

reduce is an immutable reduction: combine values into a new value (sum, max, BigDecimal totals). collect is a mutable reduction: accumulate into a container (lists, maps, StringBuilder). Using reduce to build a list either copies the list at every step (O(n²)) or, with a shared mutable identity, breaks in parallel.

Q23. What are the three overloads of reduce?

reduce(BinaryOperator) returns Optional<T> (no identity, empty stream → empty). reduce(identity, BinaryOperator) returns T. reduce(identity, BiFunction accumulator, BinaryOperator combiner) lets the result type differ from the element type; the combiner merges partial results in parallel. Requirements: identity must satisfy combiner(identity, x) == x, operations must be associative and stateless.

Q24. What is wrong here?

int sum = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).parallelStream().reduce(10, Integer::sum);

Sequentially it returns 20; in parallel it typically returns something like 50, because 10 is not an identity for addition and is applied once per chunk. Add the offset outside: 10 + list.stream().mapToInt(i -> i).sum().

Q25. Collectors.toList() vs Stream.toList() vs toUnmodifiableList()?

Collectors.toList() returns an unspecified list, in practice a mutable ArrayList, nulls allowed. toUnmodifiableList() (Java 10) is unmodifiable and throws NPE on null elements. Stream.toList() (Java 16) is unmodifiable and allows nulls. Switching collect(toList()) to .toList() in old code breaks callers that later call add on the result — the most common surprise when modernising.

Q26. What happens with duplicate keys in Collectors.toMap? With null values?

Duplicate keys throw IllegalStateException: Duplicate key … unless you pass a merge function (a, b) -> …. Null values throw NullPointerException because the implementation uses Map.merge. The four-argument form also takes a map supplier (LinkedHashMap::new, TreeMap::new, () -> new EnumMap<>(X.class)).

Q27. groupingBy vs partitioningBy?

groupingBy groups by any key and contains only keys that occurred. partitioningBy takes a Predicate, the map always has exactly two keys (true and false), even when one side is empty, and its implementation is a specialised two-slot map. Both accept downstream collectors.

Q28. What is a downstream collector? Give five examples.

The collector applied to each group's elements inside groupingBy/partitioningBy: counting(), summingLong(...), mapping(f, toSet()), maxBy(comparator), reducing(identity, mapper, op), filtering(pred, toList()), flatMapping(...), collectingAndThen(...), averagingDouble(...), joining(", "), or another groupingBy for nested maps.

Q29. filter before groupingBy vs filtering as downstream — any difference?

Yes. filter first removes elements, so a group whose elements were all removed disappears from the map. filtering keeps every key and gives it an empty list. If the UI must show every status even with zero items, use filtering (or start from an EnumMap pre-filled with zeros).

Q30. What is Collectors.teeing?

Java 12. Sends each element to two collectors and merges both results with a BiFunction, all in one pass: average = teeing(summingDouble(x), counting(), (sum, n) -> sum / n), or min and max together, or debit and credit totals.

Q31. What does collectingAndThen do?

Applies a finishing function to a collector's result: make a list unmodifiable, unwrap the Optional from maxBy inside a groupingBy (safe because a group is never empty), or convert a list to a custom type.

Q32. How do you write a custom Collector?

Implement Collector<T, A, R> or use Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, [finisher], characteristics…). The supplier must return a fresh container each time; the combiner must merge two partial containers correctly (it is only called in parallel, so bugs there hide until someone adds .parallel()); characteristics IDENTITY_FINISH, UNORDERED, CONCURRENT tell the framework what it may optimise.

Q33. How does a parallel stream work internally?

The source spliterator is split recursively via trySplit into chunks, each processed as a ForkJoinTask on the common ForkJoinPool (parallelism = cores − 1, plus the calling thread). Idle workers steal tasks from the tail of busy workers' deques. Partial results are combined up the task tree (combiner for collect/reduce). Ordered terminals must also stitch results in encounter order.

Q34. When should you not use parallel streams?

Small data or cheap per-element work, sources that split badly (LinkedList, Stream.iterate, I/O-backed streams), blocking I/O in the lambdas, code running in request threads of a server (shared common pool), order-sensitive operations (findFirst, limit, sorted), and any lambda with side effects on shared state. Measure before and after; most business code gets no benefit.

Q35. Why is blocking I/O in a parallel stream dangerous in a Spring Boot app?

All parallel streams and all CompletableFuture.supplyAsync calls without an explicit executor share the one common pool, sized to CPU count. A parallel stream that makes HTTP calls parks those few workers on I/O; every other part of the application that relies on the common pool stalls. Use a dedicated executor (or virtual threads in Java 21) for I/O fan-out.

Q36. Predict the result.

List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel().forEach(out::add);
System.out.println(out.size());

Unpredictable: a number below 1000, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when two threads resize the array concurrently. ArrayList is not thread-safe. Correct: IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel().boxed().toList().

Q37. findFirst vs findAny? forEach vs forEachOrdered?

findFirst returns the first element in encounter order (expensive to guarantee in parallel); findAny may return any element (cheaper in parallel; sequentially it usually returns the first, but do not rely on it). forEach in parallel processes elements in arbitrary order on many threads; forEachOrdered respects encounter order, losing much of the parallel benefit.

Q38. Is a parallel stream's result order guaranteed?

For an ordered source, operations like collect(toList()), toList(), toArray, reduce and findFirst preserve encounter order even in parallel; the framework merges partial results in order. Execution order (which element is processed when, by which thread) is not deterministic, and forEach/findAny/groupingByConcurrent give up ordering.

Q39. Why use IntStream instead of Stream<Integer>?

To avoid boxing: each Integer is a heap object with a header and a pointer indirection. Primitive streams also give numeric terminals (sum, average, summaryStatistics) and range/rangeClosed. Convert with mapToInt, mapToObj, boxed(), asLongStream().

Q40. Is a stream faster than a for loop?

Usually not for small collections — a loop has less overhead. For large data, sequential streams with primitive specialisations come close to loops after JIT inlining. Streams are chosen for clarity of transformation logic and easy (but rarely useful) parallelism. A senior answer mentions JMH, boxing as the real cost, and that I/O dominates in business code anyway.

Q41. Why does Optional exist and where should it be used?

To make "might be absent" explicit in method return types so callers must handle it, replacing null returns. Not designed for fields, parameters, collections or serialisation. Repository finders, cache lookups, "find first matching rule" are good uses.

Q42. orElse vs orElseGet — predict the side effect.

Optional.of("x").orElse(create());       // create() runs
Optional.of("x").orElseGet(this::create); // create() does not run

orElse takes a value, so its argument is evaluated before the call, even when the Optional is full. orElseGet takes a Supplier and calls it only when empty. Use orElseGet for anything expensive or with side effects.

Q43. Optional.of vs Optional.ofNullable vs Optional.empty?

of(x) throws NPE when x is null — use it when null would be a bug. ofNullable(x) returns empty for null. empty() is the singleton empty instance. orElseThrow() (Java 10) is the readable replacement for get().

Q44. Why shouldn't you use Optional as a field or method parameter?

As a field: Optional is not Serializable, JPA cannot map it, Jackson needs a module, and it costs an extra object per instance. As a parameter: the caller must wrap values, and the parameter now has three states (null, empty, present), which is worse than an overload or a nullable parameter. Use a nullable field with an Optional-returning getter if you want the API benefit.

Q45. What does Optional.map return when the mapper returns null?

Optional.empty(). map wraps the result with ofNullable, so a getter returning null safely ends the chain: user.map(User::address).map(Address::city).orElse("unknown").

Q46. How do you handle checked exceptions inside a stream lambda?

Wrap them: a helper method that catches IOException and throws UncheckedIOException, or an adapter unchecked(ThrowingFunction) that converts any checked exception to a runtime one. If the pipeline must continue past errors, map each element to a result type (Ok/Failed records in a sealed interface) and partition at the end. Sneaky throws hide the exception from the compiler and should be avoided in application code. For complex error handling a loop is often clearer.

Q47. Do you need to close a stream?

Only resource-backed streams: Files.lines, Files.list, Files.walk, BufferedReader.lines over a file, JdbcTemplate.queryForStream, Spring Data Stream<T> repository methods (which also need an open transaction). Use try-with-resources. Collection-backed streams hold nothing to release.

Q48. Write: find the second highest salary.

Optional<BigDecimal> second = employees.stream()
        .map(Employee::salary)
        .distinct()
        .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
        .skip(1)
        .findFirst();

distinct() handles ties (two people earning the top salary). Without it, skip(1) returns the top salary again. For the employee(s) with the second highest salary, group by salary into a TreeMap and take the second key's list. An O(n) alternative without sorting tracks the top two values in a single loop.

Q49. Write: group employees by department, count them, and find the highest-paid per department.

Map<String, Long> count = employees.stream().collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept, counting()));

Map<String, Optional<Employee>> top = employees.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept, maxBy(comparing(Employee::salary))));

Map<String, String> topName = employees.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept,
                 collectingAndThen(maxBy(comparing(Employee::salary)), o -> o.get().name())));

Map<String, Double> avg = employees.stream().collect(groupingBy(Employee::dept, averagingDouble(e -> e.salary().doubleValue())));

Q50. Write: frequency of each character in a string, in order of first appearance.

Map<Character, Long> freq = "programming".chars()
        .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
        .collect(groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, counting()));
// {p=1, r=2, o=1, g=2, a=1, m=2, i=1, n=1}

chars() gives an IntStream of UTF-16 code units; for text with emoji use codePoints() and Character.toString(int).

Q51. Write: first non-repeating character.

Optional<Character> first = input.chars()
        .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
        .collect(groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, counting()))
        .entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .findFirst();
// "swiss" -> 'w'

The LinkedHashMap supplier is the whole trick: a plain HashMap loses insertion order, so "first" becomes arbitrary. For the first repeating character, use a HashSet and filter(c -> !seen.add(c)) — a stateful lambda, acceptable only in a sequential stream.

Q52. Write: find duplicates in a list of integers.

Set<Integer> dups = nums.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Function.identity(), counting()))
        .entrySet().stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .collect(toSet());

// or, sequential only:
Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
Set<Integer> dups2 = nums.stream().filter(n -> !seen.add(n)).collect(toSet());

Q53. Write: join names of active users, sorted, comma-separated; and the longest word in a sentence.

String csv = users.stream().filter(User::active).map(User::name).sorted().collect(joining(", "));

String longest = Arrays.stream(sentence.split("\\s+"))
        .max(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length))
        .orElse("");

Q54. Write: flatten a list of lists and sum all numbers; and convert a list to a map of id → object, keeping the last on duplicates.

int sum = listOfLists.stream().flatMap(List::stream).mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();

Map<Long, Order> byId = orders.stream()
        .collect(toMap(Order::id, Function.identity(), (first, second) -> second));

Q55. Write: partition numbers into even and odd; sum squares of odd numbers.

Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> parts = nums.stream().collect(partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));
int sumSquaresOdd = nums.stream().filter(n -> n % 2 != 0).mapToInt(n -> n * n).sum();

Watch negative numbers: -3 % 2 is -1, so test n % 2 != 0, not n % 2 == 1.

Q56. Write: top 3 most frequent words in a text.

List<String> top3 = Arrays.stream(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+"))
        .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())
        .collect(groupingBy(Function.identity(), counting()))
        .entrySet().stream()
        .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()
                .thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))
        .limit(3)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
        .toList();

The explicit type witness Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue() is needed because .reversed() breaks the target-type inference chain — a detail interviewers like to probe.

Q57. Write: check whether a string is a palindrome, and reverse each word in a sentence, using streams.

boolean palindrome = IntStream.range(0, s.length() / 2)
        .allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(s.length() - 1 - i));

String reversedWords = Arrays.stream(sentence.split(" "))
        .map(w -> new StringBuilder(w).reverse().toString())
        .collect(joining(" "));

Q58. Write: sort a list of employees by department, then salary descending, then name.

List<Employee> sorted = employees.stream()
        .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
                .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
                .thenComparing(Employee::name))
        .toList();

comparing(Employee::salary).reversed().thenComparing(...) is a common bug when reversed() is applied to the whole chain after more comparators were added — it reverses everything before it.

Q59. Write: sum transaction amounts per currency with BigDecimal, and explain why not double.

Map<String, BigDecimal> totals = txns.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Txn::currency, TreeMap::new,
                 reducing(BigDecimal.ZERO, Txn::amount, BigDecimal::add)));

double is binary floating point; values like 0.1 have no exact representation, and errors accumulate over thousands of additions. In finance a 0.01 discrepancy is a defect. BigDecimal is exact for decimal values; just remember equals compares scale (2.0 ≠ 2.00), so compare amounts with compareTo.

Q60. How did you use streams in your project?

In RefinePoint we use streams for in-memory shaping, not for bulk data: grouping result items per run with groupingBy(Item::runId, LinkedHashMap::new, toList()), totalling amounts with reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add) in the certification and report code, indexing records with toMap and an explicit merge function, and mapping entities to record DTOs. There is no parallelStream anywhere in the services. Bulk matching of millions of rows goes to DuckDB via SQL compiled from match rules, because no Java stream beats a vectorised columnar engine on that workload.

Q61. What is wrong with this code from a code review?

List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
orders.stream().filter(Order::paid).forEach(o -> result.add(o.id()));

It uses a stream for iteration with side effects into an external mutable list — correct only sequentially, and it reads like a loop wearing a costume. Write List<String> result = orders.stream().filter(Order::paid).map(Order::id).toList();. Side effects belong in forEach only at the very end of a pipeline (logging, sending), never as a way of collecting.

Q62. Can a lambda throw an exception? What happens to an exception inside a parallel stream?

A lambda may throw unchecked exceptions freely and checked exceptions only if the functional interface declares them. In a parallel stream an exception in any worker is propagated to the caller of the terminal operation (wrapped/re-thrown by the ForkJoin framework); other tasks may still be running briefly, and there is no guarantee which element's exception you see if several fail.

Q63. What is the difference between Stream.of(array) and Arrays.stream(array) for a primitive array?

Stream.of(intArray) produces a Stream<int[]> with one element (the array itself), because of(T... values) cannot take primitives as T. Arrays.stream(intArray) produces an IntStream of the elements. Classic output-prediction trap: Stream.of(new int[]{1,2,3}).count() is 1.

Q64. Is a lambda serializable? Can a lambda be a Spring bean?

Only if its target type is serializable, e.g., an intersection cast (Runnable & Serializable) () -> …; then the compiler generates a $deserializeLambda$ method and serialises a SerializedLambda. It is fragile across recompilations, so avoid it. A lambda can absolutely be a Spring bean: @Bean Function<String, String> normaliser() { return String::trim; } — Spring Cloud Function is built on that.

7. Java 9 to 21: Every Feature an Interviewer Asks About

"Which Java version do you use, and what did you actually use from it?" is now a standard opener. A candidate who says "Java 17" and then cannot explain a sealed interface or a record's compact constructor loses credibility in the first five minutes. This chapter walks the releases from 9 to 21 (with a short look beyond), explains the features that changed how we write code — records, sealed types, pattern matching — at the level of why they exist and how they compile, and ends with the migration story every senior engineer should be able to tell: Java 8/11 + Spring Boot 2 to Java 21 + Spring Boot 3.

7.1 The release model and the LTS line

Since Java 9 (2017) a new feature release ships every six months (March and September). Every few releases is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release that vendors (Oracle, Eclipse Adoptium/Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul, Microsoft, Red Hat) patch for years. Since Java 17 the LTS cadence is every two years.

Features move through stages: incubator (a separate jdk.incubator.* module, API may change completely), preview (in the language/JVM but needs --enable-preview at compile and run time, may change or be withdrawn), then final (standard). Interviewers like asking "is X final in 21?" — the table below is the cheat sheet.

Version Type Features you must know
9 (2017) JPMS modules, JShell, private interface methods, List.of/Set.of/Map.of, Stream.takeWhile/dropWhile/ofNullable, iterate with predicate, Optional.or/stream/ifPresentOrElse, compact strings, G1 default GC, indy string concatenation, ProcessHandle, Flow (reactive streams), try-with-resources on effectively final variables, CompletableFuture.orTimeout
10 (2018) var for local variables, List.copyOf, Collectors.toUnmodifiableList, Optional.orElseThrow(), parallel full GC in G1, application class-data sharing, better container awareness
11 (2018) LTS Standard HttpClient, String.isBlank/strip/lines/repeat, Files.readString/writeString, var in lambda parameters, java Hello.java single-file launch, Predicate.not, Optional.isEmpty, Epsilon GC, ZGC (experimental), Flight Recorder open-sourced, Java EE and CORBA modules removed
12 Switch expressions (preview), Collectors.teeing, String.indent/transform, Shenandoah (experimental)
13 Text blocks (preview), yield
14 Switch expressions final, helpful NullPointerExceptions, records (preview), instanceof patterns (preview), CMS GC removed
15 Text blocks final, sealed classes (preview), hidden classes, ZGC and Shenandoah production-ready, Nashorn removed, biased locking disabled
16 Records final, instanceof pattern matching final, Stream.toList(), mapMulti, strong encapsulation by default, jpackage, Unix-domain sockets
17 (2021) LTS Sealed classes final, strong encapsulation of JDK internals (--illegal-access gone), pattern matching for switch (preview), RandomGenerator API, SecurityManager deprecated for removal, Applet API deprecated for removal, RMI activation removed
18–20 UTF-8 by default (18), simple web server jwebserver (18), finalize deprecated for removal (18), virtual threads / record patterns / structured concurrency previews (19–20)
21 (2023) LTS Virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections, generational ZGC, Key Encapsulation Mechanism API; previews: string templates, unnamed patterns and variables, unnamed classes and instance main, structured concurrency, scoped values

For awareness beyond 21: Java 22 finalised unnamed variables _ and the Foreign Function & Memory API; Java 23 withdrew string templates; Java 24 made synchronized no longer pin virtual threads and finalised stream gatherers; Java 25 (LTS, September 2025) finalised scoped values, flexible constructor bodies (statements before super(...)), compact source files with instance main methods, and module import declarations.

Interview tip: when asked "what's new in Java 21", lead with the story, not a list: "21 completes the data-oriented programming features that started in 14 — records, sealed types and pattern matching now work together with exhaustive switches — and it brings virtual threads, which change how we write blocking I/O code." Then give examples.

7.2 Java 9: modules (JPMS) and the small things

The module system

Before 9, the classpath was one flat list of JARs: any public class was visible to everyone, two JARs with the same package silently merged (or shadowed each other — "JAR hell"), and missing dependencies surfaced as NoClassDefFoundError at runtime. JPMS (Project Jigsaw) adds a module: a named set of packages with an explicit descriptor.

// module-info.java at the root of the source tree (illustrative: RefinePoint itself runs on the classpath)
module com.refinepoint.engine {
    requires java.sql;                        // read dependency
    requires transitive com.refinepoint.expression;  // our consumers also read it
    exports com.refinepoint.engine.api;       // only this package is accessible to other modules
    exports com.refinepoint.engine.spi to com.refinepoint.plugins;   // qualified export
    opens com.refinepoint.engine.model to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind;  // deep reflection at runtime only
    uses com.refinepoint.plugin.DataConnector;            // ServiceLoader consumer
    provides com.refinepoint.plugin.DataConnector with com.refinepoint.engine.CsvConnector;
}

Key ideas:

  • Strong encapsulation: public is no longer enough — a public class in a non-exported package is inaccessible from other modules, even with reflection (unless opens).
  • Reliable configuration: the module graph is resolved at startup; a missing module or two modules exporting the same package (split package) fails fast.
  • exports gives compile-time and runtime access to public types; opens gives runtime deep reflection (private members) — what Jackson, Hibernate and Spring need. open module opens every package.
  • Code on the classpath lives in the unnamed module (reads everything, exports everything). A plain JAR placed on the module path becomes an automatic module (name from the Automatic-Module-Name manifest entry or the file name), exports all packages and reads all modules — the bridge for migration.
  • jlink builds a custom runtime image containing only the modules you use (a 40–60 MB JRE instead of 300 MB); jdeps analyses dependencies, including use of JDK internals.

Do Spring Boot applications use modules? Almost never. Spring relies on classpath scanning, reflection and runtime proxies; frameworks and most libraries run happily in the unnamed module. The JDK itself is modular, which is the part that matters to everyone: it is why sun.misc.*/com.sun.* internals became inaccessible and why Java EE modules could be removed in 11.

The smaller Java 9 features

// Collection factories — immutable, null-hostile, randomised iteration order for Set/Map
List<String> roles = List.of("ADMIN", "APPROVER");
Map<String, Integer> limits = Map.of("FREE", 3, "PRO", 50);          // up to 10 pairs
Map<String, Integer> big = Map.ofEntries(Map.entry("A", 1), Map.entry("B", 2));
Set.of("a", "a");      // IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element
List.of("a", null);    // NullPointerException
roles.contains(null);  // NullPointerException too!

// Private interface methods — share code between default methods
interface Exporter {
    default byte[] csv(List<Row> rows)  { return encode(rows, ','); }
    default byte[] tsv(List<Row> rows)  { return encode(rows, '\t'); }
    private byte[] encode(List<Row> rows, char sep) { ... }
}

// try-with-resources on an effectively final variable
BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path);
try (reader) { ... }

// Diamond with anonymous classes
Comparator<Run> c = new Comparator<>() { public int compare(Run a, Run b) { ... } };

JShell is the REPL (jshell), handy for trying an API ("a,b".split(",").length) or a regex during an interview. Compact strings (JEP 254) store Latin-1 strings as one byte per char, roughly halving String memory in typical apps — internal, no API change.

7.3 Java 10: var

var is local variable type inference: the compiler infers the static type from the initializer. It is still static typing — the type is fixed at compile time and appears in the bytecode exactly as if you wrote it.

var runs = new ArrayList<ReconRun>();          // ArrayList<ReconRun>, not List<ReconRun>
for (var entry : totals.entrySet()) { ... }    // Map.Entry<String, BigDecimal>
try (var in = Files.newInputStream(p)) { ... }
var counter = new Object() { int hits; };      // non-denotable anonymous type: counter.hits works
Allowed Not allowed
Local variables with an initializer Fields, method parameters, return types
Enhanced for and classic for index var x; (no initializer)
try-with-resources resources var x = null; (no type to infer)
Lambda parameters (Java 11), to add annotations: (@NonNull var s) -> … var a = {1, 2}; (array initializer needs a type)
var f = s -> s.length(); (lambda needs a target type)
var mixed with explicit types in one lambda's params

Traps:

var list = new ArrayList<>();      // ArrayList<Object> — diamond with no target infers Object
var n = 10;  n = 10L;              // compile error: n is int
var id = 1_000_000_000_0L;         // long — the literal decides
var ids = List.of(1, 2L);          // List<Number & Comparable<...>> — an intersection type

var is a reserved type name, not a keyword: int var = 5; still compiles, but a class named var does not. Use it where the type is obvious from the right-hand side (new, factory with a clear name); avoid it when the type carries meaning the reader needs (var result = service.process(x);).

7.4 Java 11: HttpClient and String methods

HttpClient

java.net.http.HttpClient replaced HttpURLConnection (incubated in 9, standard in 11). It supports HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, synchronous and asynchronous calls, WebSocket, and is immutable and thread-safe — create one and reuse it.

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .executor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor())      // Java 21
        .build();

HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.example.com/rates?ccy=EUR"))
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))                            // per-request (response) timeout
        .header("Accept", "application/json")
        .GET()
        .build();

HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());          // blocking
CompletableFuture<String> body = client.sendAsync(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body);                                                   // async

In Spring Boot 3 you rarely call it directly, but Spring 6.1's RestClient can use it underneath (JdkClientHttpRequestFactory), which removes the need for Apache HttpClient in many services. Note it does not throw on 4xx/5xx — check statusCode() yourself.

New String methods

Method Since Note
isBlank() 11 true for empty or only whitespace (Character.isWhitespace)
strip(), stripLeading(), stripTrailing() 11 Unicode-aware whitespace; trim() only removes chars ≤ U+0020
lines() 11 Lazy Stream<String> split on \n, \r, \r\n
repeat(n) 11 "-".repeat(20)
indent(n), transform(f) 12 transform applies any function: s.transform(String::strip)
stripIndent(), translateEscapes(), formatted(args) 15 "%s-%d".formatted(code, n)
splitWithDelimiters, indexOf(ch, from, to) 21 Also StringBuilder.repeat in 21 
" hello ".trim();    // unchanged: EM SPACE (U+2003) is above U+0020
" hello ".strip();   // "hello"
"   ".isEmpty();               // false
"   ".isBlank();               // true

Java 11 also removed the Java EE modules (java.xml.bind JAXB, java.xml.ws JAX-WS, java.activation, java.corba, java.transaction). Upgrading from 8 to 11 classically fails with ClassNotFoundException: javax.xml.bind.JAXBException — fix by adding the libraries as normal dependencies (today the jakarta.xml.bind artifacts).

7.5 Switch expressions (14) and text blocks (15)

Switch expressions

// Old statement: fall-through, break noise, no value
String label;
switch (status) {
    case OPEN: case REOPENED: label = "Needs action"; break;
    case RESOLVED: label = "Done"; break;
    default: label = "Unknown";
}

// Switch expression: arrow labels, no fall-through, yields a value, exhaustive
String label = switch (status) {
    case OPEN, REOPENED -> "Needs action";
    case RESOLVED -> "Done";
    case IN_REVIEW -> {
        log.debug("review pending");
        yield "Waiting for approver";      // yield returns a value from a block
    }
};

Rules: a switch expression must be exhaustive — for an enum, cover every constant or add default. If you cover every constant without default, the compiler inserts a hidden default that throws (MatchException in Java 21; IncompatibleClassChangeError before) when a new constant appears at runtime from a recompiled enum. That is the desired behaviour: add a constant, and every switch without default fails to compile on the next build, showing you every place to update. Arrow-form case never falls through; yield is a contextual keyword used only inside switch expressions. Arrow labels can also be used in switch statements.

Text blocks

String sql = """
        SELECT r.id, r.status, count(b.id) AS breaks
        FROM recon_run r
        LEFT JOIN recon_break b ON b.run_id = r.id
        WHERE r.org_id = ?
        GROUP BY r.id, r.status
        """;

How the compiler processes a text block: (1) line terminators normalised to \n; (2) incidental indentation removed — the minimum indentation across all non-blank lines and the closing delimiter is stripped (so moving the closing """ left adds indentation to the content); (3) trailing spaces on each line removed; (4) escape sequences interpreted. The opening """ must be followed by a line break. New escapes: \<newline> joins lines (no \n), \s is a space that survives trailing-space stripping. A text block is an ordinary String constant, interned like any literal. Combine with formatted() for parameters — never build SQL with values via formatting; use bind parameters.

7.6 Records (16)

A record is a transparent, shallowly immutable carrier for a fixed set of values. The compiler generates the private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors named after the components (amount(), not getAmount()), and equals, hashCode, toString based on all components.

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {

    public Money {                                       // compact canonical constructor
        Objects.requireNonNull(amount, "amount");
        if (currency == null || currency.length() != 3) throw new IllegalArgumentException("ISO currency required");
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);  // reassign the PARAMETER; fields are assigned after the body
        currency = currency.toUpperCase();
    }

    public Money(String amount, String currency) {      // extra constructor must delegate to the canonical one
        this(new BigDecimal(amount), currency);
    }

    public static Money zero(String ccy) { return new Money(BigDecimal.ZERO, ccy); }   // static factory
    public Money plus(Money o) {                                                         // instance methods are fine
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
}

What the compiler generates and enforces:

  • The class is implicitly final and extends java.lang.Record — no extends allowed, but implements is.
  • Each component becomes a private final field; you cannot declare other instance fields (static fields are fine).
  • The canonical constructor takes all components in order. The compact form omits the parameter list and the field assignments; the body runs first and assigns the (possibly reassigned) parameters to fields at the end. You cannot assign this.amount in a compact constructor.
  • Accessors can be overridden (e.g., to return a defensive copy) but must be public with the exact return type.
  • equals/hashCode/toString are generated through invokedynamic with ObjectMethods as bootstrap — the same trick as lambdas.
  • Records can be nested (implicitly static), local (declared inside a method — great for intermediate stream results), generic, and can implement interfaces including sealed ones.
  • Serialization of a record always goes through the canonical constructor, so validation cannot be bypassed by a crafted byte stream — a security improvement over normal classes.

Limits: shallow immutability only — a List component can still be mutated unless you copy it (items = List.copyOf(items)); arrays as components have identity-based equals; no inheritance; no lazy or derived fields (compute in a method or in the constructor and make it a component).

Records as DTOs, with Jackson and JPA

public record CreateReconRequest(
        @NotBlank String name,
        @NotNull UUID leftSourceId,
        @NotNull UUID rightSourceId,
        @Size(max = 20) List<@Valid MatchRuleDto> rules) {}

@PostMapping("/orgs/{orgCode}/recons")
public ApiResponse<ReconDto> create(@PathVariable String orgCode, @Valid @RequestBody CreateReconRequest req) { ... }
  • Jackson 2.12+ deserialises records through the canonical constructor using component names — no @JsonCreator needed; Spring Boot 3 ships a compatible version. Bean Validation annotations on components work with @Valid.
  • JPA entities cannot be records: JPA needs a no-arg constructor, mutable state for dirty checking, and non-final classes for lazy-loading proxies. Records are excellent for projections: SELECT new com.x.RunSummary(r.id, r.status, r.startedAt) FROM ReconRun r, Spring Data class-based projections (List<RunSummary> findByOrgId(UUID orgId)), and JdbcTemplate row mappers ((rs, i) -> new RunSummary(...)). Hibernate 6.2+ also supports records as @Embeddable value objects.
  • Spring Boot @ConfigurationProperties binds to records via constructor binding (no @ConstructorBinding needed since Boot 3 when there is a single constructor).

RefinePoint: the AI service models its whole provider contract with records — LlmRequest, LlmResponse, Message, Attachment — so AnthropicClient and OpenAiCompatibleClient exchange immutable values and the structured JSON returned by the model is mapped straight onto records by Jackson. Entities stay classes extending BaseOrgEntity; everything crossing an API or service boundary is a record.

7.7 Sealed classes (17)

A sealed class or interface restricts which classes may extend or implement it.

public sealed interface MatchOutcome permits Matched, Break, Ignored {}

public record Matched(UUID leftId, UUID rightId, String rule) implements MatchOutcome {}
public record Break(UUID id, BreakReason reason, BigDecimal difference) implements MatchOutcome {}
public non-sealed class Ignored implements MatchOutcome { ... }       // reopened for extension

Rules:

  • Every permitted subclass must be final, sealed (with its own permits), or non-sealed. Records and enums are implicitly final.
  • Permitted subclasses must be in the same module, or in the same package if the code is in the unnamed module (normal classpath apps).
  • permits can be omitted when all subclasses are declared in the same source file.
  • Class.isSealed() and getPermittedSubclasses() expose the hierarchy reflectively; the JVM enforces it at class load (PermittedSubclasses attribute), so it is not merely a compiler check.

Why: sealed types make a hierarchy a closed set of alternatives (an algebraic sum type). The compiler then knows every case, so a switch over a sealed type can be exhaustive without default, and adding a new permitted subtype breaks compilation in every switch that does not handle it. That is safer than a default branch that silently swallows the new case.

7.8 Pattern matching: instanceof, switch, record patterns

Pattern matching for instanceof (16)

// Before
if (obj instanceof Break) { Break b = (Break) obj; total = total.add(b.difference()); }

// After: test, cast and bind in one step
if (obj instanceof Break b && b.difference().signum() != 0) { total = total.add(b.difference()); }

// Flow scoping: the binding is in scope where the compiler knows the match succeeded
if (!(obj instanceof Break b)) return;
log.info("break {}", b.id());          // b in scope here

// equals() becomes one line
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return o instanceof Money m && amount.compareTo(m.amount) == 0 && currency.equals(m.currency);
}

if (obj instanceof Break b || b.id() != null) does not compile — with || the binding is not definitely matched on the right side.

Pattern matching for switch (21)

static String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case null -> "null";                                  // explicit null handling (otherwise NPE)
        case Integer i when i > 1_000 -> "large int " + i;   // guard
        case Integer i -> "int " + i;
        case String s when s.isBlank() -> "blank string";
        case String s -> "string of " + s.length();
        case int[] arr -> "int array of " + arr.length;
        default -> "other " + o.getClass().getSimpleName();
    };
}

Rules interviewers test:

  1. Dominance: a label must not be unreachable because an earlier one already matches everything it matches. case CharSequence cs -> …; case String s -> …; is a compile error. Guarded patterns go before the unguarded pattern of the same type.
  2. Exhaustiveness: pattern switches (expression or statement) must be exhaustive — via default, a total pattern (case Object o), or covering all permitted subtypes of a sealed type.
  3. null: old switches throw NPE on null; a pattern switch does too unless it has case null (which can combine: case null, default -> …).
  4. Guards use when (the && guard syntax of the previews was dropped).
  5. Selector can be any reference type; case constants of enums can be qualified (case Status.OPEN) and mixed with patterns in Java 21.

Record patterns and nested deconstruction (21)

A record pattern matches a record and extracts its components in one step, and it nests:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect {}
record Point(double x, double y) {}
record Circle(Point centre, double r) implements Shape {}
record Rect(Point topLeft, Point bottomRight) implements Shape {}

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {                                                   // exhaustive: no default needed
        case Circle(Point c, double r) -> Math.PI * r * r;
        case Rect(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) -> Math.abs(x2 - x1) * Math.abs(y2 - y1);
    };
}

if (obj instanceof Circle(Point(var x, var y), var r) && r > 0) { ... }   // works with instanceof too

Record patterns call the accessor methods; var infers each component's type; generic records infer type arguments (case Box(String s) against Box<String>). In Java 21, _ as an unnamed pattern was preview (case Circle(_, var r)), final in Java 22.

Data-oriented programming

The three features together give a style Brian Goetz calls data-oriented programming: model data as immutable records, model alternatives as sealed interfaces, and write operations as exhaustive pattern switches outside the data types.

public sealed interface MatchOutcome permits Matched, Break, Ignored {}
public record Matched(UUID leftId, UUID rightId, String rule) implements MatchOutcome {}
public record Break(UUID id, BreakReason reason, BigDecimal difference) implements MatchOutcome {}
public record Ignored(UUID id, String why) implements MatchOutcome {}

String auditLine(MatchOutcome o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Matched(var l, var r, var rule)            -> "matched %s with %s by %s".formatted(l, r, rule);
        case Break(var id, var reason, var diff) when diff.signum() == 0 -> "break %s: %s".formatted(id, reason);
        case Break(var id, var reason, var diff)        -> "break %s: %s, diff %s".formatted(id, reason, diff);
        case Ignored(var id, var why)                   -> "ignored %s: %s".formatted(id, why);
    };
}

Compare with the classic OOP approach (an abstract describe() method on each type). OOP makes adding new types cheap; data-oriented makes adding new operations cheap and keeps the data types free of presentation or persistence logic. With a closed, stable set of outcomes and many operations (audit, export, UI, metrics), the sealed-switch style wins — the expression problem from chapter 1.

RefinePoint: the expression language ryfn-expression is a natural fit: the AST Node types (literals, field references, binary operators, function calls) are a closed set, and two very different operations walk the same tree — the evaluator and SqlCompiler, which turns a rule into DuckDB SQL. An exhaustive switch over a sealed node hierarchy means adding a node type is a compile error in both walkers until both handle it, instead of a runtime "unsupported node" in production.

7.9 Helpful NullPointerExceptions (14)

Before:  java.lang.NullPointerException
             at com.x.InvoiceService.total(InvoiceService.java:42)

After:   java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.math.BigDecimal.add(java.math.BigDecimal)"
             because the return value of "com.x.Line.amount()" is null

JEP 358: the JVM analyses the bytecode at the failing instruction and describes which expression was null — the array, the field, the method's return value. On by default since Java 15 (-XX:+ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages). Local variable names appear only when the class was compiled with -g (otherwise "<local4>"); Maven and Gradle compile with debug info by default. The message is computed lazily, only when getMessage() is called, so there is no cost for NPEs that are never inspected.

7.10 Sequenced collections (21)

Before 21, "get the first/last element" had a different API for every type: list.get(0), deque.getFirst(), sortedSet.first(), linkedHashSet.iterator().next() and no direct way at all for the last element of a LinkedHashSet. JEP 431 adds three interfaces into the existing hierarchy.

List<Run> runs = repo.recent();
Run newest = runs.getFirst();                // instead of runs.get(0)
Run oldest = runs.getLast();                 // instead of runs.get(runs.size() - 1)
for (Run r : runs.reversed()) { ... }        // a reversed VIEW, no copy

LinkedHashMap<String, Instant> seen = new LinkedHashMap<>();
Map.Entry<String, Instant> eldest = seen.firstEntry();
seen.putLast("RUN-9", Instant.now());        // moves to the end if present

reversed() returns a live view; writes through it affect the original. On unmodifiable lists addFirst throws UnsupportedOperationException; on a SortedSet, addFirst/addLast throw because position is determined by the comparator. getFirst() on an empty list throws NoSuchElementException (not IndexOutOfBoundsException).

7.11 Virtual threads, generational ZGC and other runtime changes

Virtual threads (JEP 444, final in 21) are lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM on a small pool of carrier platform threads. Blocking a virtual thread on I/O unmounts it from its carrier instead of blocking an OS thread, so thread-per-request code scales to hundreds of thousands of concurrent requests. In Spring Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs Tomcat request handling, @Async and scheduling on virtual threads. In Java 21, a virtual thread blocking inside synchronized pins its carrier (fixed in Java 24). Chapter 10 covers the internals.

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<Rate>> rates = currencies.stream().map(c -> executor.submit(() -> fxClient.rate(c))).toList();
}
Thread.ofVirtual().name("ingest-", 0).start(task);

Generational ZGC (JEP 439): ZGC (sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size) gains young and old generations, collecting short-lived objects more often and cheaply. In Java 21 enable with -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational; it became the default ZGC mode in 23 and the only mode in 24. G1 remains the default collector.

Strong encapsulation of JDK internals (JEP 403, Java 17): internal packages (sun.*, jdk.internal.*, private members of java.* classes) are closed to reflection by default and the --illegal-access escape hatch is gone. Java 9–15 merely warned ("An illegal reflective access operation has occurred"); 16 denied by default with a flag to relax; 17 removed the flag. Old libraries (Lombok < 1.18.22, old Mockito/ByteBuddy, old Groovy, some serialization libraries) fail with InaccessibleObjectException. Fixes: upgrade the library (the real fix), or --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED as a temporary bridge. sun.misc.Unsafe remained accessible through the jdk.unsupported module.

Do not confuse this with the Key Encapsulation Mechanism API (JEP 452, Java 21): a cryptography API (javax.crypto.KEM) for key-encapsulation schemes such as RSA-KEM and ECIES-style hybrid encryption, and a building block for post-quantum algorithms. Same word, unrelated feature — interviewers occasionally mix them up, and a calm clarification scores points.

Other runtime items worth naming: UTF-8 by default (Java 18: new FileReader(f) no longer depends on the OS locale, a source of mojibake on Windows servers), container awareness (heap sized from cgroup memory limits; use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 in Docker), CDS/AppCDS for faster startup, JFR as a free low-overhead profiler (jcmd <pid> JFR.start).

7.12 Removed and deprecated

Item Status Replacement
Java EE modules (JAXB, JAX-WS, JAF, CORBA, JTA) Removed in 11 Jakarta artifacts as normal dependencies
Nashorn JavaScript engine Deprecated 11, removed 15 GraalJS, or standalone Nashorn library
Applets, appletviewer Deprecated 9, appletviewer removed 11, Applet API deprecated for removal 17 None — browsers dropped plugins
SecurityManager Deprecated for removal 17, permanently disabled in 24 Containers, OS-level sandboxing, module encapsulation
Object.finalize() Deprecated 9, deprecated for removal 18 try-with-resources, java.lang.ref.Cleaner
CMS garbage collector Removed 14 G1, ZGC
Biased locking Disabled/deprecated 15, removed 18 Nothing needed: modern code uses java.util.concurrent locks
RMI activation, Pack200, experimental AOT/Graal JIT Removed 14–17 —
Thread.stop/suspend/resume Throw UnsupportedOperationException (20+) Interruption
--illegal-access Removed 17 Upgrade libraries, --add-opens
String templates (preview in 21–22) Withdrawn in 23 formatted(), MessageFormat

7.13 Preview features in Java 21

Use them only with --enable-preview on both javac and java, never in production code you must support across JDK upgrades. Know what they are:

  • String templates (JEP 430): STR."Hello \{name}" — template processors with embedded expressions. Preview in 21 and 22, then withdrawn for redesign. Good interview point: "previews can disappear".
  • Unnamed patterns and variables (JEP 443): _ for unused variables and pattern components: catch (NumberFormatException _), case Circle(_, var r), for (var _ : list). Final in 22.
  • Unnamed classes and instance main methods (JEP 445): void main() { System.out.println("hi"); } in a file with no class declaration — aimed at teaching. Finalised as compact source files in 25.
  • Structured concurrency (JEP 453): StructuredTaskScope treats a group of subtasks as one unit — if one fails, siblings are cancelled; the scope cannot outlive its block. Still evolving after 21.
  • Scoped values (JEP 446): immutable, bounded-lifetime alternative to ThreadLocal, cheap with millions of virtual threads: ScopedValue.where(ORG, org).run(() -> handle()). Final in 25.

7.14 Migrating from Java 8/11 to 17/21 and Spring Boot 3

Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+ and Jakarta EE 9+ (the jakarta.* namespace). These are the steps of a real migration, in the order that keeps the build green:

What breaks and how to fix it:

  1. javax → jakarta. javax.persistence, javax.servlet, javax.validation, javax.annotation (@PostConstruct), javax.transaction all become jakarta.*. javax.sql, javax.crypto, javax.net stay — they are part of the JDK, not Java EE. Every library compiled against javax.servlet (old filters, old Swagger/springfox) must be replaced by a Jakarta version (springdoc-openapi 2.x). OpenRewrite's UpgradeSpringBoot_3_x recipe automates most of it.
