  2. Spring Security 6: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter removed — declare a SecurityFilterChain bean; antMatchers → requestMatchers; authorizeRequests → authorizeHttpRequests; lambda DSL required for most config.
  3. Spring MVC 6: trailing-slash matching is off (/api/runs/ no longer matches /api/runs); PathPatternParser is the default matcher.
  4. Hibernate 6: different default sequence naming (one shared hibernate_sequence becomes a per-entity <entity>_SEQ), stricter HQL, new type system (@Type changes), ID generation changes — test persistence thoroughly.
  5. Properties: add spring-boot-properties-migrator temporarily; it logs renamed keys at startup (spring.redis.* → spring.data.redis.*).
  6. Tracing: Spring Cloud Sleuth does not support Boot 3; move to Micrometer Tracing with the OpenTelemetry or Brave bridge.
  7. JDK-level: removed JAXB/JAX-WS (add dependencies), strong encapsulation errors (upgrade libraries), changed default charset in 18 (explicit charsets everywhere), SecurityManager uses removed.
  8. Build: Maven compiler <release>21</release>, Surefire/Failsafe recent versions, Docker base image to a 21 JRE, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage instead of fixed -Xmx in containers.

Interview tip: tell the migration as a story with numbers and order. A template, to fill with your own numbers from a migration you actually did: "We had N services on Boot 2.7 and Java 11. We first moved every service to Java 17 on 2.7, which surfaced library upgrades (Lombok, Mockito) without mixing in Spring changes. Then one pilot service went to Boot 3 using OpenRewrite for javax→jakarta; the painful part was Spring Security 6 configuration and Hibernate 6 sequence naming. With a checklist from the pilot, the rest took a couple of sprints. Afterwards we adopted records for DTOs and enabled virtual threads on I/O-heavy services." The order (JDK first, then framework) is what shows seniority: it isolates failures.

RefinePoint: RefinePoint started on Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.4.3, so all 13 services and ryfn-platform were written in the jakarta.* world from day one. The shared library's auto-configurations (PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration, PlatformWebAutoConfiguration) use Boot 3's AutoConfiguration.imports file rather than the old spring.factories key — another Boot 2 → 3 change worth mentioning when asked about auto-configuration.

7.15 Interview questions and answers

Q1. Which Java versions are LTS, and why does it matter?

8, 11, 17, 21 and 25. LTS releases get years of vendor patches, so enterprises and frameworks target them; the releases between are supported only until the next one ships, six months later. Spring Boot 3 requires 17 as a minimum, which pushed most of the industry off 8 and 11. Non-LTS releases are fine if you can upgrade every six months, and most teams cannot commit to that.

Q2. What is the difference between incubator, preview and final?

Incubator is an API in a jdk.incubator.* module that may change completely. Preview is a fully specified language or JVM feature that needs --enable-preview at compile and run time and may still change or be withdrawn. Final is standard and permanent. Class files compiled with preview features are tied to that exact JDK version. String templates are the proof that previews can vanish: preview in 21 and 22, withdrawn in 23.

Q3. What problem does JPMS solve?

It replaces the flat classpath with explicit modules that declare what they need and what they expose. That gives reliable configuration (a missing dependency or split package fails at startup, not with NoClassDefFoundError at runtime) and strong encapsulation (public no longer means visible to everyone). It also let the JDK itself be split up, which is why jlink can build small runtimes and why internals became inaccessible.

Q4. requires vs requires transitive vs requires static?

requires reads a module at compile and run time. requires transitive also makes the dependency readable by anyone who requires you, used when your API exposes its types. requires static is compile-time only, optional at runtime, the module equivalent of Maven's provided scope (annotation libraries, for example).

Q5. exports vs opens?

exports gives compile-time and runtime access to the package's public types. opens gives no compile-time access, but allows deep reflection at runtime, including private members. Frameworks need opens: Jackson on DTO fields, Hibernate on entity fields. exports p to m and opens p to m limit it to named modules. open module opens everything.

Q6. What are the unnamed module and automatic modules?

Everything on the classpath lands in the unnamed module, which reads all modules and exports all its packages, but named modules cannot require it. A plain JAR on the module path becomes an automatic module: it gets a name from Automatic-Module-Name or the file name, reads everything and exports everything. It is the migration bridge between the classpath and full modularity.

Q7. What is a split package and why is it a problem?

The same package present in two modules. JPMS forbids it, because a package must belong to exactly one module for readability to work, and startup fails. The classpath allowed it silently, so old libraries sometimes break when moved to the module path (the JSR-305 javax.annotation split is the classic). It stays invisible while everything runs in the unnamed module.

Q8. Do you use modules in your Spring Boot services?

No, and that is the normal answer. Spring relies on classpath scanning, reflection and runtime proxies, which would need opens almost everywhere, and many libraries do not ship proper descriptors. The benefit is mostly for libraries and small runtimes. RefinePoint has no module-info.java; the 13 services run on the classpath. For plug-ins we use ServiceLoader with META-INF/services (Plugins.load(DataConnector.class)), which predates modules and works without them. We still benefit indirectly, since the JDK itself is modular.

Q9. What are the properties of List.of, Set.of and Map.of?

They are unmodifiable (mutators throw UnsupportedOperationException), reject nulls with NPE (even contains(null) throws on List.of), and Set.of/Map.of throw IllegalArgumentException on duplicates. Set and map iteration order is deliberately randomised per JVM run with a salt, so tests that depend on it fail early. Arrays.asList differs: it is a fixed-size view over the array, set works, nulls are allowed.

Q10. List.of vs List.copyOf vs Collections.unmodifiableList?

List.of builds a new unmodifiable list from its arguments. List.copyOf makes an independent unmodifiable copy, and returns the same instance if the input is already an immutable list. Collections.unmodifiableList is a read-only view: changes to the underlying list still show through. For defensive copies in record constructors use List.copyOf.

Q11. Why were private methods added to interfaces?

So that default methods can share code without exposing a helper as part of the public contract. Before Java 9 a helper had to be another default method (visible and overridable) or live in a separate utility class. Private static interface methods are allowed too. Interface methods can never be protected.

Q12. What is JShell used for?

It is the JDK's REPL, for quick experiments without a class or a main. Useful for checking API behaviour, regexes and date arithmetic. It keeps state between snippets and supports /imports, /vars and /save. It is a learning and exploration tool, not a production one.

Q13. Is var dynamic typing?

No. The type is inferred at compile time and is fixed; the bytecode is identical to an explicit declaration. var x = 10; x = "s"; is a compile error. It reduces noise on the left side without changing the type system, and it is limited to local variables so that APIs always have explicit types.

Q14. Where can't you use var?

Fields, method parameters, return types, catch parameters, variables without an initializer, null initializers, array initializers (var a = {1,2}), and lambdas or method references without a target type. One lambda cannot mix var and explicit parameter types. var is allowed in for, try-with-resources and, since 11, lambda parameters.

Q15. Predict the type.

var a = new ArrayList<>();         // ArrayList<Object>
var b = List.of(1, 2.0);           // List<Number & Comparable<...>>
var c = new int[]{1, 2};           // int[]
var d = 'x' + 1;                   // int
var e = new Object() { int n = 5; };
System.out.println(e.n);           // 5, the anonymous type is usable through var

The diamond with var is the classic trap: with no target type, inference falls back to Object.

Q16. Can a variable be named var?

Yes. var var = 5; compiles. var is a reserved type name, not a keyword, chosen so that existing code using it as an identifier keeps compiling. Only a class or type parameter named var is forbidden. record, sealed, permits, yield and when are contextual in a similar way.

Q17. When would you avoid var?

When the type is not obvious from the right side and it matters to the reader: var result = service.process(x);. Also with numeric literals where the width matters, and when you want a variable typed as an interface (var list = new ArrayList<Run>() is an ArrayList, not a List). Good uses: long generic types, new expressions, loops over entrySet().

Q18. How does the Java 11 HttpClient compare with RestTemplate or RestClient?

HttpClient is the low-level JDK client: HTTP/2, async with CompletableFuture, WebSocket, no dependency. RestClient (Spring 6.1) and the older RestTemplate sit a level higher, adding message converters, error handling, interceptors and observability, and can use HttpClient underneath via JdkClientHttpRequestFactory. In a Spring service I use RestClient. Note that HttpClient does not throw on 4xx/5xx, its connect timeout and request timeout are separate settings, and it should be reused, because every instance has its own connection pool and selector thread.

Q19. trim() vs strip()? isEmpty() vs isBlank()?

trim() removes characters with code ≤ U+0020; strip() removes Unicode whitespace as defined by Character.isWhitespace, including an em space. Non-breaking space U+00A0 is removed by neither, because isWhitespace excludes it, which is a real headache with bank files pasted from Excel. isEmpty() means length 0; isBlank() means empty or all whitespace.

Q20. What does "a\nb\r\nc".lines() return?

A lazy Stream<String> of a, b, c. It handles all three line terminators and it is more efficient than split("\\R") because it does not build an array first. No trailing empty string is produced for a final terminator.

Q21. Switch statement vs switch expression?

A statement performs actions and may fall through; an expression produces a value, must be exhaustive and cannot fall through when using arrows. yield returns a value from a block. Arrow syntax can be used in statements too, and colon syntax in expressions (with yield), though mixing the two forms in one switch is a compile error.

Q22. Predict the output.

int day = 2;
String r = switch (day) {
    case 1, 7 -> "weekend";
    case 2 -> { String s = "mon"; yield s.toUpperCase(); }
    default -> "weekday";
};
System.out.println(r);

MON. There is no fall-through, and return is not allowed inside a switch expression block. It would have to be yield.

Q23. What happens if I add a constant to an enum used in a switch expression with no default?

At the next compile, every such switch fails, which is the point: the compiler lists every place to update. If an old class file runs against the new enum without recompiling, the compiler-generated default throws MatchException in Java 21 (IncompatibleClassChangeError on earlier releases). A default branch would silently swallow the new constant, so for closed sets I leave it out.

Q24. How is indentation handled in a text block?

The compiler strips incidental whitespace: the smallest indentation across all non-blank lines plus the line of the closing delimiter. Move the closing """ left and content gains indentation. Trailing whitespace is stripped, line endings become \n. Use \ at line end to join lines and \s to preserve a trailing space.

Q25. Predict the output.

String a = """
    hello
      world
    """;
String b = """
    hello""";

a is "hello\n world\n": the minimum indent is 4, the second line keeps its extra 2, and there is a trailing newline because the closing delimiter is on its own line. b is "hello" with no newline. """hello""" on one line does not compile, since the opening delimiter must be followed by a line break.

Q26. What is a record? What does the compiler generate?

A final, shallowly immutable data carrier declared by its components. The compiler generates private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessors named after the components, and equals, hashCode and toString over all components, through invokedynamic and ObjectMethods. It extends java.lang.Record.

Q27. Canonical vs compact constructor?

A canonical constructor has the full parameter list and must assign every field. A compact constructor omits the parameter list and the assignments: the body validates or reassigns the parameters, and the fields are assigned automatically at the end. Assigning this.x inside a compact constructor is a compile error. Any other constructor must delegate with this(...). The canonical constructor cannot be less accessible than the record.

Q28. What can't a record do?

It cannot extend a class (it can implement interfaces), be extended, declare instance fields beyond its components, have non-final component fields, or have native methods. It can have static fields and methods, instance methods, nested types, annotations and generics.

Q29. Are records immutable?

Only shallowly. The fields are final, but a mutable component can still be changed:

record Team(List<String> names) {}
var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
var t = new Team(list);
list.add("b");                // t.names() now has 2 elements

Fix with names = List.copyOf(names) in a compact constructor. Arrays are worse: equals compares the array reference, so two records with equal array contents are not equal.

Q30. Can a record be a JPA entity? How do you use records with JPA?

No. JPA needs a no-arg constructor, non-final fields for dirty checking and non-final classes for lazy-loading proxies. Records fit well as read models: JPQL constructor expressions, Spring Data projections and JdbcTemplate row mappers. Hibernate 6.2+ also maps a record as an @Embeddable value object such as Money. Reading into a record projection also avoids the persistence-context cost of loading entities for read-only screens.

Q31. How do records work with Jackson and Bean Validation?

Jackson 2.12+ deserialises through the canonical constructor and serialises through the accessors, and needs the component names, which records always retain. Validation annotations on components (@NotBlank String name) apply with @Valid on the controller parameter. @JsonProperty and @JsonIgnore work on components. No Lombok needed, which removes a build-time dependency for DTOs.

Q32. Records vs Lombok @Data / @Value?

Records are a language feature: no annotation processor, enforced immutability, canonical-constructor serialisation and pattern-matching support. @Data gives mutable JavaBeans with getters and setters, still needed for JPA entities and some frameworks. @Value is the closest, but it cannot be deconstructed in a pattern and it depends on Lombok. Records use name() rather than getName(), so old code expecting JavaBean getters (BeanUtils, some JSP or template engines) may need adapting.

Q33. How do you get a "with" style update on a record?

Java 21 has no built-in support, so write it by hand: public Money withAmount(BigDecimal a) { return new Money(a, currency); }. Each call goes through the canonical constructor, so validation always re-runs. Derived record creation (with expressions) has been proposed for a future release but is not in 21.

Q34. What is a sealed class and why would you use one?

A class or interface that restricts its direct subtypes to a declared list. It models a closed set of alternatives, keeps the hierarchy under the author's control, and lets the compiler check exhaustive switches with no default, so adding a subtype produces compile errors at every switch that must handle it.

Q35. What must a permitted subclass declare?

Exactly one of final, sealed or non-sealed. Records and enums are implicitly final. It must also directly extend the sealed type and be in the same module, or the same package if unnamed. non-sealed reopens that branch to any subclass, so exhaustiveness still holds at the permitted level: the switch covers the non-sealed type and all its unknown subclasses with one label.

Q36. Sealed classes vs enums vs final classes?

An enum is a fixed set of instances, each a singleton with the same shape. A sealed type is a fixed set of types, each with its own fields and any number of instances. final closes a class to all subclasses, while sealed allows a specific list. Use an enum for statuses, and sealed plus records for outcomes that carry different data.

Q37. What is flow scoping in instanceof patterns?

A binding variable is in scope wherever the compiler can prove the match succeeded. if (o instanceof String s && s.isEmpty()) is valid, while || s.isEmpty() is not. After if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;, s is in scope for the rest of the method. A binding can shadow a field, which is a subtle source of confusion.

Q38. Which of these compile?

if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 1) {}   // A
if (o instanceof String s || s.length() > 1) {}   // B
String t = "x";
if (t instanceof String u) {}                     // C
Integer i = 1;
if (i instanceof String v) {}                     // D

A compiles. B does not, since s is not definitely matched on the right of ||. C compiles from Java 21 (a total pattern in instanceof was an error before). D does not, since Integer can never be a String and the compiler rejects inconvertible types.

Q39. What are the rules of dominance in a pattern switch?

A label is a compile error if an earlier label matches everything it would match. Subtypes must come before supertypes, and a guarded pattern must come before the unguarded pattern of the same type. Constant labels must precede the pattern of their type (case "x" before case String s). default should come last; a pattern label after default is a compile error.

Q40. Predict the output or error.

static String f(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case CharSequence c -> "cs";
        case String s -> "s";
        default -> "other";
    };
}

Compile error: case String s is dominated by case CharSequence c. Swap them and f("a") returns s.

Q41. How does a pattern switch handle null?

It throws NullPointerException unless a case null label is present, keeping old behaviour for existing code. case null -> … handles it explicitly and case null, default -> … merges it with the default. default alone does not match null. Note that case null is the only place a null reaches a switch: a total pattern such as case Object o does not match it without that label.

Q42. How does a pattern switch compile?

To an invokedynamic call with SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch as bootstrap, which returns the index of the first matching label given a start index. The switch then jumps on that index, and when a guard fails it restarts from the next label. Compared with an if/instanceof chain, the checks stay in one place and the JVM may optimise them, but performance is rarely the reason to use it. Exhaustiveness and readability are.

Q43. What are record patterns and how do they nest?

A record pattern tests the type and deconstructs its components into bindings, recursively: case Rect(Point(var x1, var y1), Point p2). It calls the accessors, so an accessor that throws produces MatchException. A nested pattern against a null component does not match: Rect(Point(var x, var y), var p) fails when the first point is null, while var p itself accepts null.

Q44. What makes a switch exhaustive over a sealed type with record patterns?

The compiler computes coverage across the nested components. Given sealed interface S permits A, B, record P(S l, S r), covering P(A, A), P(A, B), P(B, A) and P(B, B) is exhaustive with no default; drop one and it is an error. Guarded labels do not count toward exhaustiveness, because the compiler cannot reason about a boolean expression.

Q45. What is data-oriented programming?

Modelling the domain as immutable data (records), alternatives as sealed types, and behaviour as functions using exhaustive pattern switches, kept separate from the data. It suits data pipelines, parsers, message handling and API boundaries. Use OOP polymorphism when new types are added often and behaviour belongs with state. Use data-oriented style when the set of types is stable and new operations are frequent.

Q46. Give a real example of sealed types and pattern matching from your work.

RefinePoint's rule language: Node is a sealed interface whose variants are nested records (Field, Column, Text, Num, Bool, Call, Arith, Negate and others), produced by the parser. The evaluator, the SQL compiler that targets DuckDB and the RuleWriter that renders a rule back to English are separate operations over the same tree. New node types are rare and new operations do come up, which is the textbook case for this style.

Q47. What are helpful NullPointerExceptions?

From Java 14, on by default from 15, the NPE message says which expression was null: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "User.name()" is null. The JVM derives it by analysing bytecode when the message is requested, so it has no cost until read. Chained calls such as a.b().c().d() no longer need to be split across lines just to diagnose production NPEs. Local variable names appear only with -g.

Q48. What are sequenced collections?

Java 21 interfaces SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap, added above List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet, LinkedHashMap and SortedMap, providing getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed. They give a uniform API for "has a defined encounter order". HashSet and HashMap do not implement them.

Q49. Is list.reversed() a copy?

No, it is a live view. Changes to either side are visible in the other, and it costs nothing to create. To get an independent copy use new ArrayList<>(list.reversed()). On an unmodifiable list the view is unmodifiable too. A class implementing both List and Deque (LinkedList) resolves reversed() to a type that is both.

Q50. What changed for virtual threads in Java 21 and what is the main gotcha?

They became final (JEP 444): cheap JVM-scheduled threads for blocking code, created with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() or Thread.ofVirtual(), enabled in Spring Boot 3.2+ with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. Main gotcha in 21: blocking inside synchronized or a native frame pins the carrier thread (the synchronized case was fixed in 24). Do not pool them, and limit downstream concurrency with a semaphore, since the database pool is still finite. Details in chapter 10.

Q51. What is generational ZGC and when would you turn it on?

ZGC split into young and old generations so most garbage is collected cheaply, giving lower allocation-stall risk and better throughput with the same very short pauses. On 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational. Consider it for large heaps or strict latency targets. G1 remains the sensible default for typical services. Chapter 12 goes deeper.

Q52. What did JDK 17 change about access to internals?

JEP 403 made strong encapsulation permanent: --illegal-access is gone, and reflective access to non-public members of JDK classes throws InaccessibleObjectException unless you pass --add-opens. The journey: warnings from 9, deny by default in 16, no global switch in 17. Upgrade the library rather than collecting --add-opens flags. Each flag is a documented debt.

Q53. What is the Key Encapsulation Mechanism API?

JEP 452 in Java 21: javax.crypto.KEM, an API for schemes where the sender derives a shared secret and an encapsulated form of it using the receiver's public key. It is the basis for hybrid public-key encryption and post-quantum algorithms. It has nothing to do with the strong encapsulation of JDK internals, and it is worth clarifying which one an interviewer means.

Q54. What was removed or deprecated, and what replaced it?

Java EE modules and CORBA removed in 11 (add Jakarta dependencies). Nashorn removed in 15 (GraalJS). CMS removed in 14 (G1, ZGC). SecurityManager deprecated for removal in 17 (OS and container isolation). finalize deprecated for removal in 18 (Cleaner, try-with-resources). Applet API deprecated for removal in 17 (nothing). Biased locking removed in 18. Thread.stop throws from 20 (interruption).

Q55. Why was biased locking removed?

It optimised uncontended synchronized for old APIs like Vector and Hashtable, which modern code rarely uses, while revocation needed costly safepoints and the code added heavy complexity to the JVM. JEP 374 disabled and deprecated it in 15, and the code was removed in 18. Thin locks are fast enough for today's workloads. Chapter 8 covers the mark word.

Q56. Which Java 21 features were still preview?

String templates, unnamed patterns and variables, unnamed classes with instance main, structured concurrency and scoped values. Later, unnamed variables were final in 22, string templates were withdrawn in 23, and scoped values and compact source files were final in 25. Do not depend on any preview API in production code on 21.

Q57. What is StructuredTaskScope?

A preview API on 21 that treats concurrent subtasks as one unit within a lexical block: fork subtasks, join, and handle results together. ShutdownOnFailure cancels siblings when one fails, ShutdownOnSuccess when one succeeds. No subtask outlives the scope, which removes thread leaks and gives clear thread-dump hierarchy. The API was reshaped in later previews, so treat it as direction rather than a stable contract.

Q58. Scoped values vs ThreadLocal?

A ThreadLocal is mutable, lives until removed, and each thread (and each inherited copy) carries its own map, which is costly with millions of virtual threads and leaks in pools. A ScopedValue is immutable within a bounded where(...).run(...) block, cleaned up automatically, and shared cheaply with child tasks under structured concurrency. Preview on 21, final in 25.

Q59. What is new in the JDK's default charset behaviour?

From Java 18 (JEP 400) the default charset is UTF-8 on all platforms, regardless of OS locale. Before that, new FileReader(f) and getBytes() used the platform charset, so a Windows server with cp1252 corrupted non-ASCII data that worked on Linux. Migration check: code that relied on the old default (or files actually written in cp1252) now behaves differently. Use explicit charsets, and -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT as a temporary bridge.

Q60. How do you approach a migration from Java 8 to 21?

Run jdeps --jdk-internals for internal API use. Upgrade build tools and libraries first, then the JDK to 11 or directly to 21 with --release left at the old value, fix removed-module dependencies (JAXB) and InaccessibleObjectExceptions, run everything including integration tests and GC-log comparison, deploy a canary, and only then raise --release and adopt new syntax. Review GC flags, as many old ones are removed and make the JVM refuse to start.

Q61. What exactly changes in javax → jakarta?

Only the Java EE namespaces moved, because Oracle's transfer to Eclipse did not include the javax trademark: persistence, servlet, validation, annotation, transaction, mail, jms, websocket and so on. JDK packages like javax.sql, javax.crypto, javax.net and javax.naming stay. No behaviour changes, but binary compatibility breaks, so every library compiled against javax.servlet needs a Jakarta build. OpenRewrite handles the source changes; the hard part is third-party dependencies.

Q62. What else breaks going from Spring Boot 2 to 3?

Spring Security 6 (SecurityFilterChain, requestMatchers, no WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter), trailing slash no longer matched, AutoConfiguration.imports replacing spring.factories for auto-configuration, renamed properties (spring.redis → spring.data.redis), Hibernate 6 semantics, Sleuth replaced by Micrometer Tracing, and HttpStatus usage changed to HttpStatusCode in some APIs. spring-boot-properties-migrator flags properties at startup.

Q63. Why move the JDK first and the framework second?

Each step then has one cause for each failure, which makes breakage easy to diagnose and revert. Boot 2.7 runs on 17, so the JDK upgrade can ship on its own and get production mileage. Doing both together means an InaccessibleObjectException, a jakarta import failure and a Hibernate query change all land in one big branch. Small, independently deployable steps are the senior answer.

Q64. How would you test a JDK upgrade beyond the unit tests?

Integration tests with real dependencies (Testcontainers), a load test comparing throughput, p99 latency and GC logs against the old version, a startup log check for warnings, and a staged rollout (one instance or a canary) with JFR recordings to compare allocation and lock behaviour. Check container memory too: heap ergonomics and native memory use can shift between releases.

Q65. Which Java 21 features do you use in your project?

RefinePoint runs on Java 21: records for DTOs and for the LlmClient contract (LlmRequest, LlmResponse, Message, Attachment), a sealed Node hierarchy for the rule language, instanceof patterns throughout (OrgContextService uses attrs instanceof ServletRequestAttributes servlet), switch expressions and text blocks for SQL in JdbcTemplate work queues such as RefreshWorker.claim(). Being honest about what you did not use (JPMS, preview features) is as credible as listing what you did.
